• Accredited Entities should provide summary information in the proposal with cross-reference to
annexes such as feasibility studies, gender action plan, term sheet, etc.
• Accredited Entities should ensure that annexes provided are consistent with the details provided in
the funding proposal. Updates to the funding proposal and/or annexes must be reflected in all
relevant documents.
• The total number of pages for the funding proposal (excluding annexes) should not exceed 60.
Proposals exceeding the prescribed length will not be assessed within the usual service standard
time.
• The recommended font is Arial, size 11.
• Under the GCF Information Disclosure Policy, project and programme funding proposals will be
disclosed on the GCF website, simultaneous with the submission to the Board, subject to the
redaction of any information that may not be disclosed pursuant to the IDP. Accredited Entities are
asked to fill out information on disclosure in section G.4.

B
A.21. Executive summary
1 This Multi-country Project (MCP) proposal is part of a global initiative to advance Early Warnings for All (EW4All) as
announced by the United Nations Secretary General in March 20224 and articulated in the EW4All Executive Action Plan
(EAP).5 The project will improve the production, dissemination and effective use of Multi-Hazard Early Warning Systems
(MHEWS), aiming to reach the most vulnerable communities in the targeted seven countries, namely Antigua and
Barbuda, Cambodia, Chad, Ecuador, Ethiopia, Fiji, and Somalia. National projects tailored to each participating country's
needs will establish Early Warning Systems (EWS) infrastructure, set up systems for its long term operation, support local
capacities in the generation and dissemination of early warnings products and help institute relevant policies and
governance mechanisms for end-to end MHEWS. This MCP aims to accelerate the delivery of EAP priority actions by
stimulating the design and funding of multiple regional delivery mechanisms to support the financial and technical needs
of the targeted countries.
2 The project will follow the approach of the ADB CRPP project6. An EW4All Global Funding Proposal (FP) serves to provide
details on the global program and financing architecture, its theory of change, alignment with the GCF investment
criteria, and other relevant information common to all participating countries. Eligibility criteria for the selection of
interventions, activities, sites and beneficiaries are provided in Appendix 3.
Climate change problem
3 Rising annual global near-surface temperatures associated with anthropogenic climate change have already exceeded 1.5
°C above pre-industrial levels,7 exacerbating disaster risk triggered by different types of hazardous events. Societies and
the natural systems on which they depend are unable to cope with and adapt to the effects of climate change, some of
which are irreversible.8 The intensity, geographic extent and frequency of both slow and rapid onset disasters has
increased, exacerbated by changes in the weather and climate, including increases in temperature (leading to heat-
waves, damages to agriculture and human health) and the intensity of rainfall, storms and cyclones (causing floods,
landslides and coastal inundation), as well as decreases in rainfall (leading to agricultural and hydrological droughts).
4 These changes in climate increase the risks faced by communities and the livelihoods on which they depend. They create
food and water insecurity for millions of people by reducing production from agriculture and natural resources and
disrupting ecosystem services.9 These impacts are reflected within National Determined Contributions (NDCs) which
identify freshwater resources, food production and nutritional security and terrestrial and wetland ecosystems as the top
priority areas and sectors. National Adaptation Plans (NAPs) 10 submitted by 48 countries identified drought, floods, heat
waves, increasing temperatures, sea level rise, and land and forest degradation as critical impacts of climate change, with
cyclones, typhoons and storm surges major concerns in most of the SIDS. The impacts of these hazards are numerous and
include reduced crop yield, soil degradation, animal diseases, loss of livestock, reduction of water supplies, salinization of
water resources, human migration, ecosystem and biodiversity loss, increased coastal erosion, damage to infrastructure
4 World Meteorological Organisation (WMO), “Statement of Antonio Guterres, Secretary-General of the United Nations,” March 2022.
5 The UN Global Early Warning Initiative for the Implementation of Climate Adaptation, “Early Warnings for All - Executive Action Plan 2023-2027”
(World Meteorological Organization (WMO), 2023).
6 FP215: Community Resilience Partnership Program Multiple Countries: Asia and Pacific Region | Asian Development Bank | Decision B.37/12, 24
November 2023
7 WMO. ‘State of the Climate 2024-Update for COP29’. World Meteorological Organization, 2024. https://library.wmo.int/idurl/4/69075.
8 David I. Armstrong McKay et al., “Exceeding 1.5°C Global Warming Could Trigger Multiple Climate Tipping Points,” Science, September 2022.
9 Valérie Masson-Delmotte et al., “Global Warming of 1.5 C,” An IPCC Special Report on the Impacts of Global Warming of 1.5°C above Pre-Industrial
Levels and Related Global Greenhouse Gas Emission Pathways, in the Context of Strengthening the Global Response to the Threat of Climate Change,
Sustainable Development, and Efforts to Eradicate Poverty, 2019.

Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, 2023.

and increases in forest fires. They further highlight the need for establishing national MHEWS, including community-
based systems, or sector specific systems 11.
5 EWS(EWS) to monitor climate and weather variability and change are a critical investment that can warn against
impending shocks and enhance climate resilience of governments and communities by providing critical information to
guide risk management, including anticipatory action and make informed long-term decisions that help avoid otherwise
crippling damages and losses to communities and livelihoods. Early warnings furthermore save lives and assets and can
be worth more than ten times the investments and can also mitigate millions of cases of morbidity (cholera, dengue,
diarrhea, malaria, etc.). Twenty-four hours warning of a coming storm or heat wave can cut the ensuing damage by 30%,
while spending USD 800 million on such systems in developing countries could avoid losses of $3–16 billion per year.12
Key climate change induced risks in participating countries
A summary of key climate change risks in each of the seven participating countries in the MCP is provided below. Antigua
and Barbuda
6 Ranked as the 5th highest in the World Risk Index in 2023, Antigua and Barbuda is highly exposed to an array of baseline
hazards, including hurricanes, extreme rainfall, droughts, and rising sea levels. Hurricanes are considered the country’s
main climate hazard, having faced 15 hurricanes and 14 tropical storms between 1995 and 2021. By 2030, the general
building stock in Antigua and Barbuda, using the Representative Concentration Pathway (RCP) 8.5, will experience direct
losses from storm surges and wind in the amount of USD 451M for a historic event, USD 4.03 billion for a 1:100-year
event, and USD 9.4 billion for a maximum credible event13. Additionally, the islands endured 14 drought episodes
between 2000 and 2020, resulting in droughts being considered the 2nd major climate threat. 14
7 Rising sea levels and increasing land and sea surface temperatures are expected in the future. The low-lying geography of
Antigua and Barbuda makes it particularly susceptible to land loss due to sea-level rise, as projected under all future
scenarios assessed by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC). Moreover, hurricane intensity is
anticipated to increase by 18% for category 4 and 5 hurricanes over the next 30 years, based on General Circulation
Models. Under the RCP 4.5 scenario, models predict nine drought years for the period 2040–2069, representing an 8%
increase.
Chad
8 Chad faces severe environmental degradation, and climate change is aggravating already challenging climatic conditions
by increasing the frequency and magnitude of extreme events. The current and projected warming is increasing
evapotranspiration, and while rainfall projections for the region are very uncertain, they suggest that extreme rainfall will
increase while overall precipitation decreases. As a result, both floods and longer droughts are very likely15.
9 The food production and livelihood systems in Chad are highly dependent on climatic factors, particularly rainfall patterns
and distribution. Extreme heat, heavy rainfall and flooding pose risks to crops, health, farmers’ and herders’ livelihoods,
food security and farm workers’ productivity. Since 1995, Chad has been ranked at the bottom of the ND-GAIN Country
Index (the country ranked 184th from 1995-2004 and 185th from 2005-2021) due to a combination of high poverty,
frequent conflicts, and the risk of both droughts and floods. This underlines the country’s great need for investment and
innovations to improve readiness, and a great urgency for action.
Ecuador
11 UNFCCC, “Report of the Conference of the Parties Serving as the Meeting of the Parties to the Paris Agreement on Its Third Session, Held in Glasgow
from 31 October to 13 November 2021 Addendum Part Two: Action Taken by the Conference of the Parties Serving as the Meeting of the Parties to the
Paris Agreement at Its Third Session,” March 2022.
12 Global Commission on Adaptation. ‘Adapt Now: A Global Call for Leadership on Climate Resilience’, September 2019.
13 GoAB 2022. Adaptation Communication for Antigua and Barbuda
14 GoAB 2022. Adaptation Communication for Antigua and Barbuda.
15 https://dicf.unepgrid.ch/chad/climate-change

=== PAGE 10 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 7
B
10 In Ecuador, projections foresee changes in the frequency and magnitude of precipitation and temperature, both for
average and extreme values16. Climate change is project to increase melting of glacier cover, increase variations in sea
surface temperature, cause spatial and temporal changes precipitation regimes, increase flood-prone areas, intensify
droughts, reduce water quantity and quality, expand the range of disease-transmitting vectors (dengue and malaria), and
increase loss of biodiversity17. The increased intensity and frequency of extreme and slow-onset climatic events is
projected to cause economic and non-economic losses and damages to goods and services18.
Fiji
11 Daily maximum temperatures in Fiji have increased at the rate of about 0.2°C per decade. There has been a clear shift
towards more years being warmer than average during the warm/wet season, especially since the 2000s. Fiji is becoming
hotter, with more intense temperatures occurring more frequently. An increase in the frequency and intensity of
extreme rainfall events is also projected. The 1-in-20-year daily rainfall is projected to increase by approximately 5-7 mm
by 2030 and by 36 mm by 2090. Whilst climate projections suggest a decrease in the total number of cyclones, their
severity is expected to increase19. This is expected to result in increased floods, flash floods and landslides. Coupled with
projected changes in sea level rise, increased storm surges and coastal erosion is expected. The increased temperatures
are expected to contribute to drought and together with changes in precipitation result in accelerated ecosystem
degradation leading to bleached coral reefs and saline water intrusion into aquifers.
Ethiopia
12 Projections20 indicate that temperatures in Ethiopia will rise by 1.5-2.5°C by mid-century under RCP4.5 and up to 3-4°C
under RCP8.5. Rainfall will become more erratic, with prolonged dry spells worsening drought conditions, wild land and
forest fires, and intensified rainfall events leading to severe flooding, land and mudslides. Significant impacts of climate
change in Ethiopia include reduced water availability, frequent crop failures, and heightened food insecurity. South-West
Ethiopia is facing devastating floods causing widespread destruction of homes, public infrastructure and affecting
essential services like water, sanitation, and hygiene.
13 In July 2024, torrential rains in the Gambella region triggered floods and landslides severely affecting 143,000 people and
causing more than 2,300 fatalities. Wildfires have ravaged ecosystems, including humid forests and protected areas. The
International Organization for Migration (IOM) Displacement Tracing Matrix DTM, 2024 reports that drought in the
Somali region is causing the highest number of displacements caused by climate-induced events (17% of Internally
Displaced Persons (IDPs)), followed by floods, landslides and fires (9% of IDPs).
Cambodia
14 Cambodia faces a high level of disaster risk, ranking 58th out of 191 countries in the 2024 INFORM Risk Index. The
country is especially vulnerable to flood and drought events, with about 80% of its land in the Mekong River and Tonle
Sap regions. Underlying vulnerabilities such as economic and environ-mental challenges further heighten the risk from
climate hazards for disadvantaged populations.
15 Climate change is projected to exacerbate flooding and drought risks and decrease Cambodia’s GDP by as much as 10%
by 2050 compared to projected GDP in 2050 in the absence of climate change21. Agriculture, infrastructure, forestry,
human health, and coastal areas are most affected by climate change. The observed impacts of climate change include

more intense rains leading to floods, delayed rainy season and longer dry seasons affecting rain-fed and irrigated crops,
unexpected dry periods during the rainy season, and untimely rains which affect agricultural planning. Dams and poor
river management exacerbate climate change related impacts, increasing vulnerabilities and risks, especially near
waterways such as the Mekong River.
Somalia
16 Critical climate change impacts in Somalia are drought and flood.22 Drought affects nomadic and agro-pastoral
communities who are more vulnerable to prolonged dry seasons and consequent water scarcity and reduced pasture.
Droughts in Somalia result in reduced livestock production and agricultural productivity, livestock loss, food insecurity,
and ultimately, famine and the loss of human life.23 Somalia experiences regular river floods and flash flooding that result
in human casualties and major impacts on the economy and damage to infrastructure. Riverine flooding typically occurs
along the Juba and Shabelle Rivers in southern Somalia and flash floods, in the north along intermittent watercourses.24
Intense rainfall events and subsequent floods have become more frequent, washing away fertile soil and causing
widespread devastation.
Proposed Interventions
17 The project interventions, delivered through two Outputs, intend to assist vulnerable countries in making continuous
strides towards meeting the EW4All vision. This will be achieved by supporting concrete investments in the seven
countries in Output 2, and by establishing a sustainable architecture at the global and regional levels to continuously
support more countries in promoting country-level actions towards EW4All (Output 1).
18 The project addresses critical barriers that prevent the effective generation, dissemination, communication, and use of
early warnings for climate change adaptation, preparedness and response to warnings, through two broad outputs
tailored to specific country needs.
19 Output 1 aims to accelerate and scale up national access to global and regional technical and operational support for
countries to develop comprehensive MHEWS and respective capabilities. Recognizing the need for continuous and
significant efforts to achieve the goal on universal access to early warnings, enabling conditions will be enhanced globally
and regionally to promote country-level actions toward a global coordination and support architecture for EW4All that
will be sustained beyond the project implementation period. The output will be led by the World Meteorological
Organization (WMO) and United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR).
20 Output 2 addresses barriers that prevent the implementation of a comprehensive and end-to-end MHEWS in the seven
countries including: 1) Gaps in policies, inter-agency coordination and lack of coherent strategies; 2) Inadequate technical
and scientific capacities; 3) Missing observations particularly in SIDS and Least Developed Countries (LDCs); and 4)
Barriers that prevent effective local actions. The activities will mirror the four pillars of the EW4All EAP and will be
implemented through the national governments with support from UNDP, the EW4All Pillar leads (WMO, UNDRR, ITU,
IFRC) and their in-country national offices and other partner agencies where relevant.
21 The two outputs will work in tandem to accelerate the delivery of the EW4All EAP and provide long-term and
uninterrupted support to critical baseline capacities on which MHEWS are built. These are: i) robust scientific information
and analytics on weather, water and climate hazards and vulnerabilities within National Meteorological and Hydrological
Services (NMHSs), National Disaster Risk Management Authorities (NDMAs) and relevant sectors to support greater and
more diverse understanding of disaster risk and its underlying factors, with greater Impact Based Forecasting (IbF) to
inform decision-making and planning; ii) effective internal coordination among various government entities that are
responsible for different elements of managing a national EWS; and iii) a long-term financing plan to maintain the
necessary hydrometeorological infrastructure, and community level capacities to receive, understand and respond to
EWS thus enhancing adaptive capacities at national levels to protect lives and livelihoods.

22 Summary of proposed interventions in participating countries
23 To be able to address the climate change induced and exacerbated risks highlighted above, through MHEWS and
associated early actions/responses ahead of an anticipated weather/climate event, each country will need to develop
and strengthen their existing MHEWS, strategies, policies and protocols to mobilize resources and people. This MCP will
address these country-specific requirements, which are given below and based on extensive consultations with national
stakeholders (government, NGOs and CSOs), as well as the EW4ALL Pillar leads (UNDRR, WMO, ITU, IFRC).
Antigua and Barbuda
24 This project will update and align disaster management legislation and policies with international standards, including
modernizing the Disaster Management Act, integrating disaster risk reduction (DRR) into sectoral policies, and
strengthening EWS for pandemics. The nationally defined EW4All implementation plan emphasizes improving national
strategic plans for emergency management agencies and promoting data-sharing collaborations. Enhancing public
awareness and understanding of hazards and disaster risk, including exposure and vulnerability, through a
comprehensive communication strategy is also proposed. An online risk data platform will be created which is accessible
to stakeholders and the public. Hazard maps will be updated along with exposure and vulnerability models and climate
change analyses for critical sectors covering both hazards and risks across multiple scenarios will be conducted. The
project will incorporate indigenous knowledge and practices into the national EWS and improve disaster risk knowledge
in schools.
25 The project will strengthen the Antigua and Barbuda Meteorological Services (ABMS) by improving infrastructure for real-
time monitoring of hydro-meteorological data, for hydrological and marine monitoring and for routine operations and
broadcasting activities. It will improve telecommunications and broadcasting infrastructure, conduct country assessments
on network infrastructure resilience, and set up communication campaigns to raise awareness of EWS. Under the project,
a National Emergency Telecommunication Plan (NETP) will be developed and adoption of the Common Alert Protocol
(CAP) will be supported. The project will implement networks configured to respond to assistive technologies for people
with disabilities. It will also support the adoption of the Caribbean Disaster Emergency Management Agency (CDEMA)
Model MHEWS Policy 2020, and integrating CAP procedures and impact-based forecasting (IbF) into local response
systems. Finally, the project will enhance community disaster response teams, providing training and equipment for first
responders, and will support the government to adopt a dedicated financing mechanisms and structured early action
measures for pre-impact actions based on the needs of vulnerable groups.
Cambodia
26 The project proposes to improve and update platforms for data integration by enhancing data management protocols
and security and generating risk knowledge at the national level. It will develop a comprehensive approach to disaster
management, focusing on human resource development in EWS, particularly for women and those with disabilities.
Additionally, early warning dissemination strategies and platforms will be developed to ensure timely and accurate
information reaches all stakeholders.
27 At the sub-national level, the project will develop DRR capacities and implement community-based EWS for floods and
lightning to ensure access to improved weather information. It will provide training for community members in
emergency preparedness and response, focusing on the most vulnerable populations using the government's Shock
Resistant Social Protection frameworks. By strengthening local capacities and integrating community-focused strategies,
the project aims to build a more resilient and prepared Cambodia at all levels.
Chad
28 The intervention in Chad will cover the four pillars of EW4ALL and address underlying institutional and regulatory barriers
through a cross-pillar approach to governance and coordination issues, considering the critical need for data
interoperability and holistic, multi-hazard knowledge generation and management. It will complement existing
programmes including the Systematic Observations Financing Facility (SOFF) Investment Funding and will build on
community based early warning initiatives by bringing in innovations allowing the dissemination of intelligible and
actionable alerts, risk education and preparedness information to the public.

29 The intervention will promote a people-centered approach by strengthening risk knowledge, gender analysis, and
community-based research to identify and act on trust and perception issues. It will support local and devolved
authorities responsible for crisis management while integrating anticipatory action into response frameworks. Significant
stakeholder engagement, and preparatory work on institutional and regulatory frameworks, will be needed to ensure
that coordination and governance approaches are set in motion to support these activities and outcomes.
Ecuador
30 Strengthened governance and coordination will be established through a robust regulatory and institutional framework
for MHEWS. The project will support the establishment of a functional regulatory framework for MHEWSs and the
development of a National Framework for Climate Services (NFCS), including coordination with National Gender and
Development (GAD) initiatives. A National Climate Finance Framework will be developed to ensure sustainable climate
services and create a comprehensive climate data management strategy with standardized data frameworks, including a
climate data centre with a user interface. Governance capacities will be enhanced through the definition of Standard
Operating Procedures (SOPs) for each hazard. A harmonized Monitoring, Evaluation, Accountability, and Learning (MEAL)
strategy will ensure effective tracking of project outcomes and integration of lessons learned.
31 Disaster risk knowledge and observations will be enhanced through developing methodologies for risk assessments and
implementing these assessments to create a robust data collection and risk database. Specific actions include conducting
hazard and risk assessments and establishing a Multi-Hazard Risk Platform for the dissemination of risk information.
Observations and monitoring networks will be strengthened by rehabilitating and integrating existing monitoring systems
and improving data management and telemetry capabilities. Strengthening MHEWS forecasting capacity through
improving access to, and use of Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) models will focus on extending forecasting
capacity, enhancing now-casting, improving assimilation processes, and adopting ensemble forecasting techniques. IbF
will be developed for specific hazards such as floods, landslides, droughts, and extreme temperatures, including pilot
projects to test these forecasts.
32 Warning dissemination systems will be strengthened through mapping stakeholders and focal points for receiving and
disseminating alerts, establishing a multi-level and inter-institutional communication protocol, and generating binding
documents to ensure effective communication. Permanent operational mechanisms will be set up for warning
dissemination and activation of necessary actions. The project will enhance message dissemination by identifying priority
alert mechanisms, implementing cell broadcasting, strengthening alternative communication means, and developing a
warning platform using CAP. The project will analyze existing warning content, standardize communication bulletins, and
generate alerts and notices in various languages with an inclusive approach. Raising awareness through educational
communication strategies and drills at national and local levels will also be emphasized, along with integrating Indigenous
Knowledge Systems (IKSs) into MHEWS Preparedness protocols will be developed by assessing regulatory frameworks
and standardizing methodologies for Community Emergency Plans and supporting their implementation. The project
aims to strengthen disaster response capacities by assessing and enhancing municipal disaster management units,
including improving technical capacities and equipment. Anticipatory action protocols will be developed, including
reviewing and implementing existing protocols for El Niño and droughts.
Ethiopia
33 The project will address gaps in the implementation of each of the four EW4All pillars, identified in the Ethiopia Impact-
Based Multi-Hazard Early Warning Early Action National Roadmap 2023-2030, complementing existing programmes and
projects and contributing to the EW4All objectives. The project will support and ensure coordination with national Pillar
leads and stakeholders, and relevant UN, non-governmental organizations (NGO) international organizations and civil
society organizations (CSO) supporting the EW4All initiative in Ethiopia.
34 A national disaster risk database will be created, coordinated by the Ethiopian Disaster Risk Management Commission
(EDRMC), with contributions from all sector Agencies/Ministries to collect and develop multi-hazard data and risk
analyses and strengthening the Woredas risk profiles in priority areas with compilation and analysis of hazard, exposure
and vulnerability data. The Ethiopia Meteorological Institute (EMI) will upgrade observing stations and coverage in East
and South-East areas of the country, improve data sharing, and develop specific gender-based EWS focusing on women,
elderly and children.

Fiji
36 The project will strengthen governance and coordination through development and implementation of protocols and
relevant mechanisms, including protocols and SOPs for data sharing among MHEWS agencies to enhance collaboration
and legal frameworks. It will establish interagency working group for data exchange, analyze laws related to data
exchange, establish Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs) between authorities for early warnings, and create protocols
for data sharing. The project will additionally enhance coordination among stakeholders in developing MHEWS plans and
establish collaboration mechanisms among government, non-government, and community levels. Training workshops for
national and sub-national trainers will be undertaken along with strengthening of community disaster management
committees.
37 A robust tracking system for assessing hazard impacts and future risks will be established. It will expand the necessary
location-specific and targeted forecasting to all areas are affected by hazards. The project will address challenges in
accessing and sharing disaster data by improving infrastructure and data utilization. It will standardize risk assessment
methodologies and parameters in Fiji, including disaster data; creating a centralized database system to store risk
information across sectors and disaggregated by gender, age, and disability; and improving infrastructure to collect and
analyze data for climate projection applications. The project will improve the expansion of river gauges to un-gauged
locations. The project will upgrade observation networks, including Automatic Weather Station (AWS) installation,
spares, and training. It will upgrade TB3 and AWS data loggers to utilize historical climate data for enhancing EWS and
expand location-specific predictions and develop a scientifically based drought risk map for Fiji. A drought monitoring
system for health and food security will be established. It will strengthen the use of AI and a centralized database for
forecasting and early warning.
38 The project will support the implementation of cell broadcasts and help establish a regulatory framework for mobile
manufacturers to support it, specifically focusing on automated systems and mobile coverage in rural areas and for
fishermen at sea. The project will activate the National Emergency Telecom Cluster, develop SoPs/contingency plans,
automate EWS communication dissemination and improve warnings through mass messaging, utilize traditional
knowledge and enhance national and regional communications. Communities based response plans will be developed to
respond to early warnings based on previous successful implementations, focusing on how they access and act on
received messages. Traditional and local knowledge will be incorporated into the local level EWS, as well as reviewing and
integrating anticipatory actions into national and community-based disaster management plans.
Somalia
39 Somalia’s EW4ALL project activities contribute directly to the realisation of the proposed activities under Somalia’s
National Roadmap for Implementation of EW4All 2024-2027. The project will develop a comprehensive Risk Assessment
Framework including hazard risk assessment methodology harmonised with regional approaches and international
framework-based targets and indicators. Using the framework, hazard risk assessments will be undertaken for national
and local levels and applied/interpreted and translated for critical considerations of key vulnerability factors. A database
of disaster impact data and loss and damage tracking is also to be established. The project will develop disaster risk
knowledge materials and communication for national and local levels, which include maps of multiple hazards that
identify specific geographic areas, sectors and groups, tailored for EWS and DRR plans and local risk management plans.
Climate risk summaries of key vulnerability factors will be developed which are accessible for national and local levels.

Climate results/benefits
42 The MCP will establish and strengthen the role of MHEWS in informing decision as a foundation for risk informed
development processes. It is aligned with the Agenda for Sustainable Development,25 specifically SDG 13 and SDGs 1, 2,
9, 11, 12 and 15. The project will reduce disaster risk and the impacts of shocks and hazard events by supporting national
strategic guidelines and frameworks towards achievement of the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015-
203026, and create a regional support framework as well as direct action in selected countries to address the four
priorities of the Sendai call for action.27 It contributes specifically to target G of the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk
Reduction.28 The project contributes to the priorities identified in Article 8 of the Paris Agreement29 by supporting the
following areas of cooperation: i) EWS; ii) emergency preparedness; iii) slow onset events; iv) events that may involve
irreversible and permanent loss and damage; v) comprehensive risk assessment and management; and vi) resilience of
communities, livelihoods and ecosystems.
43 In sum, the project supports achieving global targets in reducing exposure to climate changes impacts, with a strong
focus on those most vulnerable. It will lay the foundations for further projects and the supporting mechanisms that are
needed by countries in establishing, operating and expanding the coverage of effective, end-to-end MHEWS. Regional
and global facilities and networks for technical and financial support will be strengthened. Implementation strategies and
approaches from past projects and initiatives will feed into effective and pragmatic project design, which address the
unique constraints under which NMHS, NDMA and other stakeholders operate. This will specifically include the
challenges and contexts of SIDS and LDCs, those with limited infrastructure or in fragile and conflict affected states.

PROJECT/PROGRAMME INFORMATION
B.1. Climate context
44 Climate hazards and associated risks (impacts, exposures and vulnerabilities)
45 Approximately half the global population of 3.3 to 3.6 billion people live in countries or regions that are highly sensitive
to climate change30. Most live in LDCs, SIDS and Africa with limited MHEWS and are unable to undertake anticipatory
action and risk reducing measures at scale.31 The acceleration of climate risks is outpacing the financial flows towards
adaptation, the requirements of which are estimated to be 5-10 times higher and will increase to USD 160-340 billion by
2030 and USD 315-565 billion by 2050.32 Human populations will be exposed to the highest magnitude of one to three
climate hazards concurrently by the turn of the century. Some coastal regions will face up to six different hazards
concurrently.33
46 The Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC) region has seen the strongest warming trend of about 0.2 °C per decade on
record, warming faster than global averages with temperatures projected to rise by 1.5 to 2.5 °C by 2050. Prolonged
droughts have affected multiple sectors, including agriculture, energy, transportation, and water supply. Droughts
combined with higher temperatures and lower humidity have triggered wildfires in the region. Sea levels have risen at a
higher rate than the global mean and tropical storms such as Fiona, Lisa and Ian caused extensive damage as did floods
and landslides triggered by heavy rain which also caused hundreds of deaths.34 Climate change-driven impacts and risks
are amplified for small islands, where more severe and frequent hurricanes compound the impacts of sea level rise,
storm surge and coastal erosion, flooding and salinisation of water bodies and aquifers, threatening coastal communities
and infrastructure.35 In Central and South America, changes in the timing and magnitude of precipitation and extreme
temperatures are affecting agricultural production among subsistence farmers. This includes more frequent long dry
spells, reduced precipitation and altered rainfall during the start and end of the rainy season. Warming temperatures
have further increased the transmission of vector borne diseases.36
47 In Antigua and Barbuda these regional changes lead to (see Appendix 1 for further details):
• Increases in the frequency of high intensity (category 4 and 5 hurricanes), leading to increases in storm surge,
coastal flooding and high winds;
• Increases in drought intensity, reducing freshwater in groundwater and increasing saline intrusion;
• Rising sea levels lead to increases in coastal flooding, exacerbated by low-lying geography.
48 In Ecuador climate risks include (see Appendix 1 for further details):
• Increases in rainfall and temperature extremes which increase the risk of flooding, landslides and mudflows
compounded with volcanic ash;
• Intensification of droughts reduce water quantity and quality;
• Increasing temperatures expand the range of disease-transmitting vectors (dengue and malaria).

49 In the South-West Pacific, TCs, floods, droughts, sea level rise and ocean acidification have had significant impacts on
people, economies and ecosystems. The region is influenced by both the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and the
Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD)37. Most of the South-West Pacific shows upper-ocean (0–700 m) warming since 1993, with
rates exceeding 2–3 times the global average in the tropical Pacific. Sea-level rise in the eastern Indian Ocean, western
tropical Pacific, and south and north mid-latitude Pacific are also higher than the global mean. Observed sea surface
temperatures have increased in tropical western Pacific Ocean and Rainfall has decreased in parts of the Pacific islands.
This drying trend is expected to continue in the coming decades, except in parts of western and equatorial Pacific. Heavy
rainfall events will increase in the western tropical Pacific and the higher evapotranspiration is expected to amplify or
partially offset the effect of decreases or increases in rainfall respectively, resulting in increased aridity in parts of the
Pacific under the 2°C global warming and above scenario. The intensity and frequency of TCs will increase and, together
with sea level rise will contribute to storm-surges leading to extreme coastal water levels in most regions in the Pacific
islands38.
50 In Fiji these regional changes lead to (see Appendix 1 for further details):
• Current warming of 0.2C per decade is expected to accelerate, reaching 1.3-2.5C above pre-industrial
temperatures by 2070;
• Greatest impacts are due to typhoons (F$500 million in annual expected losses – 5% GDP), the most intense of
which are expected to increase in frequency due to climate change;
• Increases in rainfall intensity will increase the likelihood of 1/100 yr floods with expected losses of F$ 2 billion;
• Drought and coastal salinization due to SLR and storm surge affects crop production, leading to food imports.
51 Climate hazards in sub-Saharan Africa include floods, droughts, storms and landslides. Floods have caused widespread
damage to infrastructure and crops and have contributed to waterborne diseases. Droughts have resulted in crop failures
leading to food and water insecurity while storms have damaged infrastructure and crops and lead to loss of lives.
Landslides, which are linked to heavy rain have also contributed to deaths and damages to infrastructure and crops. Most
African countries will face increasingly high temperature climates, with increased mean and extreme temperatures,
including increased heat waves as a consequence of climate change. Increased droughts are expected over large parts of
southern Africa, decreased precipitation in Northern Africa at 2°C global warming. The intensity of heavy rainfall is also
expected to increase, increasing exposure to pluvial and riverine flooding across all but north and southwestern Africa39.
52 In Chad these regional changes lead to (see Appendix 1 for further details):
• Successive droughts have affected the food security and livelihoods of households across large swathes of the
country, with 1.5 million people affected in 1981-85, and 2.4 million people affected in 2009-2010. The most
recent drought in 2022 affected 2.1 million people;
• Floods (riverine and pluvial) rendered 121,088 people homeless. These disasters led to a total of 10,556
recorded deaths, of which 67% were a result of viral or bacterial disease epidemics such as cholera, meningitis
and measles;
• Climate change is expected to increase temperatures 2.1°C to 4.3°C (very likely range) by 2080, with more very
hot days leading to greater incidences of heat stress and reduced agricultural labour production;
• More variable rainfall is likely to lead to great extremes of drought and flood, with reductions in yields of maize
and other crops.
53 In Ethiopia climate risks include (see Appendix 1 for further details):

54 Somalia is considered to have the least capacity to respond and recover from extreme weather events.40 Climate risks for
Somalia include (see Appendix 1 for further details):
• The frequency and intensity of heavy precipitation events are projected to increase with potential impacts of
flooding and soil erosion.41 The higher rainfall and runoff expected across the various climate scenarios, are
likely to lead to increased flash flooding.42 In 2023 around 2.48 million people were affected, with over 1.2
million displaced. 43 The 2023 floods also resulted in the loss of 188 lives.44
• Increased frequency, persistence and intensity of droughts in Somalia are likely.45 Climate change projections
suggest that the duration, frequency and intensity of droughts will increase by the end of the 21st Century under
all scenarios and that drought areas will increase by 16 per cent, 36 per cent and 54 per cent under increasing
Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs) (2.6, 4.6, 8.5 respectively).46 Prolonged dry seasons result in
water scarcity, reduced grazing land, reduced livestock production, livestock perishes, reduced agricultural
productivity, food insecurity, and ultimately, famine and the loss of human life.47 During 2015 – 2022, 6.1 million
people were affected by drought, and 760,000 - 1.2 million people were displaced by drought.48
• Daily temperature maximums have also increased over the last two decades49 and are projected to continue
over the next decade.50 The very southern areas of Somalia are projected to experience extreme heat, and the
southern and some parts of the northern areas are projected to experience very high heat.51

55 In Asia, surface temperature has increased in the past century with large increases and extremes in West and Central
Asia, resulting in an increasing trend of growing-season length across the continent and causing strong, more frequent
and longer heat-waves in South and East Asia. There is a decreasing trend of the South Asian summer monsoon
precipitation during the second half of the 20th century. On the other hand decreased precipitation and increased
evapotranspiration in West and Central Asia have contributed to drought conditions and decreased surface runoff52.
56 Climate projections suggest rising temperatures increase the likelihood of the threat of heat-waves across Asia, droughts
in arid and semiarid areas of West, Central and South Asia, floods in monsoon regions in South, Southeast and East Asia,
and glacier melting in the Hindu Kush Himalaya region. A greater warming in North Asia, including the Tibetan Plateau,
Central Asia and West Asia are also projected. The highest levels of warming for extremely hot days are expected to occur
in West and Central Asia with increased dryness of land. Elevation-dependent warming is expected to continue and
leading to glaciers shrinking at varying rates among regions, Temperature rise will be strongest in winter in most regions,
while it will be the strongest on summer in the northern part of West Asia and some parts of South Asia where a desert
climate prevails. The wet-bulb temperature, a measure of heat stress, is likely to approach critical health thresholds in
West and South Asia under the RCP4.5 scenario and in East Asia, under the RCP8.5 scenario. The occurrence of extreme
heat-waves is likely to increase in Asia with a sizeable part of South Asia experiencing heat stress conditions in the future.
A large percentage increase in annual precipitation is projected in South and North Asia, but decrease over the northwest
part of the Arabian Peninsula and increase over its southern part. Both heavy and intense precipitation are projected to
intensify and become more frequent in South, Southeast and East Asia. Monsoon land precipitation is likely to increase in
East, Southeast and South Asia due to increasing moisture convergence by elevated temperature53. There will be a large
increase in flood frequency in monsoon regions in Southeast Asia, Peninsular India, eastern Africa and the northern half
of the Andes54 which without further mitigation efforts, will lead to continued loss of lives and infrastructure55. On the
other hand, the warming in higher latitudes in the Himalayas is likely to adversely affect glacial melt, increasing the
likelihood of glacial lake outbursts and significantly affecting water resources over time56.
57 In Cambodia these regional changes have resulted in the following (see Appendix 1 for further details):
• Over the past 25 years riverine and flash floods have caused the most deaths, with droughts and lightning
causing fewer deaths but higher damages;
• Rising temperatures and decreases in average rainfall during the dry season are expected to increase the
demand for irrigation for most crops, including rice;
• Increases in extreme rainfall during the monsoon are likely to increase riverine and flash flood risks;
• Whilst it is not clear if lightning risk will change, the availability of more moisture, energy and a deeper
convective monsoon under climate change may potentially increase the risk.

59 Climate change has a disproportional impact on the poor and vulnerable who lack assets and access to information and
resources and are therefore less able to anticipate, adapt or mitigate these impacts.61 Often these communities are
reliant on livelihoods linked to climate sensitive sectors such as agriculture, or are located in regions more exposed to
climate risks, including on small islands, along coastlines and in flood and land-slide prone regions. Many live in un-
planned settlements and shanty-towns and lack basic facilities and infrastructure. Furthermore, vulnerable groups within
communities, including women, women-headed households,62 households with infants, children and elderly, people with
disabilities,63 often lack the means to receive information and respond to climate related disasters.
Well-functioning MHEWSMHEWS allow people, institutions and businesses to prepare for and respond to multiple
hazards (see Table 1), including those occurring simultaneously or whose impact accumulates over time, and their
potential interrelated impacts.64
60 Disaster impacts in countries with high risk and high poverty can negatively affect welfare and cause major setbacks in
human and economic development, with long-term consequences65 to resilience building and well-being. MHEWS are a
proven, effective and feasible climate change adaptation measure that saves lives and provides at least a tenfold return
on investment66. The socio-economic benefits of weather prediction are approximately USD 160 billion per year and
improvements in forecasting and EWS could provide additional annual benefits of US$30 billion67. Economic assessments
in several countries have found strong positive cost-benefit ratios for investment in weather and climate services
between 1:4 to 1:36 from reduction in weather-related economic losses, reduced humanitarian relief costs and
maladaptive risk-coping strategies68.

63 Differences in regional climate between the present day and warming between 1.5 °C and 2 °C are expected to be
widespread across temperature increases and extremes, heavy precipitation events, significant increases in runoff and

preparedness activities and preventative and anticipatory action to attenuate the impacts of climate-induced shocks.78
Goal outputs and activities
64 The objective of this MCP is to accelerate the design and implementation of the EW4All initiative through coordinated
global support involving all the key actors across the early warnings value chain. This project, through its country
interventions, will target communities whose livelihoods depend on climate sensitive sectors, those with greater physical
exposure to climate hazards, with clear emphasis on women, poor and vulnerable groups within these communities. It
will lead to the enhanced production of actionable multi-hazard early warnings and IbFs to inform and trigger
preparedness, early and anticipatory actions. It will strengthen multiple channels of communication to ensure timely and
effective dissemination of these warnings and information to the last mile. The project will also prepare disaster
management and supporting agencies at national and the sub-national level as well as communities to make effective use
of these early warnings and advisories for early and anticipatory action which allows them to adapt to, avoid and
facilitate recovery from climate change hazards. Finally it will address barriers to mobilizing financial resources that
prevent many countries from translating early warnings into on-ground action.
65 The underlying assumption for the theory of change of the project is: IF generation, delivery and adoption of multi-hazard
early warning information is improved for effective early and anticipatory action, THEN avoidance of and adaptation to
climate induced natural hazards will be enhanced and the loss of lives and disruption of livelihoods, services and
productive assets will be reduced BECAUSE of improved, effective and timely disaster mitigation and response by
national and sub-national governments, communities and businesses supported by multilateral agencies and private
entities.

constraints and resource mobilization.79 The effective development, generation and use of MHEWS is challenged by the
absence of consistent, reliable and robust sources of technical, human and financial support to and within countries. In

this regard, it is important to strengthen the internal mechanisms and capacities by which institutions at the national

Some of the root causes and barriers associated with these aspects of MHEWS and that need to be addressed are

Poor strategic planning for long term financial support to MHEWS
67 There is insufficient capital at the global, country and community levels to establish and maintain the observation
networks and equipment needed to generate meaningful weather, climate and hydrological forecasts. Critical socio-
economic observations are also difficult to gather in real time because suitable crowd sourcing and other technologies
are underutilized. These observations are needed to improve our understanding of multi-hazard exposure and
vulnerability and hence risks faced by people and communities. Resources at national, sub-national, and community
levels are not enough to translate forecasts into warnings, share these warnings effectively, and prepare communities,
especially those at risk and vulnerable, to use and respond to them through mitigative actions that have been proven
effective.
68 Limited financial resources and human/institutional capacity to establish and maintain observation networks has led to
gaps in data needed to meet the requirements of the WMO Integrated Global Observing System (WIGOS) and the Global
Basic Observing Network (GBON) systems. These systems are used to generate early warning products at the regional
and global levels. The SOFF has been established to address this resource constraint in SIDS and LDCs, and this project will
ensure that investments through SOFF are leveraged and coordinated through additional GCF investments. Many
countries face similar challenges in operating and maintaining their hydro-meteorological and communication
networks.80 Limited awareness about the value of hydrometeorological and communication networks in reducing climate
risks constrains opportunities to raise necessary public budgets. This often leads to the deterioration of existing
installations or the use of equipment that fails to meet required standards, creating challenges in quality control and
interoperability.
69 Efficiency and efficacy of preparedness and early response efforts is constrained by lack of forecast-based planning and
financial resources at the grassroots and municipal levels. This is critical as local governments are often mandated with
maintaining local EWS, particularly last mile access. The inadequacy of mechanisms through which necessary funds and
other resources can be rapidly released before and during emergencies is a significant barrier to early response and
anticipatory action to early warnings needed to mitigate disasters. There is a lack of financing to put in place and
maintain the mechanisms, systems and capacities needed for anticipatory action. Funding is also needed for the actual
implementation of anticipatory action, including within national systems81.
70 Many countries lack a coherent and long-term financing strategy for establishing, rehabilitating and/or maintaining their
soft and hard infrastructure for early warning services. In some countries, it has become challenging to effectively
coordinate available resources to ensure end-to-end systems. Even fewer have the fiscal frameworks to allow for funding
of EWS, particularly those that are maintained by local actors. Such strategies should explore raising resources from
private sources. They need to enhance the capacities and resources to develop comprehensive and compelling proposals
that help unlock funding for projects to set up EWS and address different national priorities and vulnerabilities and
contexts. The absence of a comprehensive gap analysis at the national level prevents these countries from benefiting
from the global and regional support architecture and facilities, such as GCF or the Global Environment Facility (GEF), or
from global financing campaigns which targets donors across different sectors.

Limited global, regional and national support for country level actions for a comprehensive MHEWS
71 Technical, scientific and institutional barriers prevent the generation and development of reliable, meaningful and
actionable weather and climate information, as well as its effective communication and use by people, government,
communities and businesses. Absence of such information contributes to the low level of awareness and appreciation of
the value of MHEWS and its associated components, including among policy makers. Many LDCs and SIDS fail to leverage
regional facilities and partnerships for necessary and sustained technical assistance due to limited human capital and
capacities. Consequently, they are excluded from the knowledge exchange, peer-to-peer learning, coordination and
collaboration with key initiatives and frameworks which provide contextual operational support across a wide range of
hazards. This is a barrier to access technical support and information services from regional climate centres, regional
centres of excellence including national and regional academic institutions, initiatives and projects.82.
Inadequate policies and strategies for inter-agency coordination, data sharing and governance for preparedness and
response
72 Inconsistencies in policies, institutional structure and mechanisms that govern the collection and sharing of
hydrometeorological, vulnerability and exposure data can pose a barrier to implementation of international agreements
and frameworks for EWS and DRR.83 National policies often fall short of a comprehensive framework to facilitate private
financing and fail to provide suitable structures to strengthen inclusive, people-centred approaches to early warnings.
Capacity gaps exist in transformational planning for such approaches which would address each country’s unique
"paradigm shift" needs. There are barriers within regions and countries which prevent the effective use of available
climate information and EWS (CIEWS) by line agencies for different sectors, and those responsible for national disaster
response, relief and recovery, particularly civil protection organizations at the district and community levels.
73 In most countries, ministries or departments with independent administrative structures and procedures are involved in
the generation, analysis and use of climate information. Meteorological and hydrological services often reside in different
ministries or departments from those whose expertise is needed in co-developing advisories and provide the sectoral
expertise, for example health and agriculture. Inadequate and inefficient mechanisms for data sharing and coordinated
action between these agencies prevents the development of targeted and IbF84 and scenarios for triggers to inform early
and Anticipatory Action85 or Forecast based Financing86 for relevant sectors and areas87. Furthermore, the Information
and Communication Technology Ministry and telecommunication regulatory authority and private telecommunication
companies are not actively involved or consulted in the design of communications strategies which includes data
transmission from observation stations, dissemination of early warnings and advisories and obtaining feedback from
targeted stakeholders. Insights from behavioral science about how end-users respond to early warnings are also neither
contextualized nor institutionalized in national EWS. Their exclusion results in missed opportunities to take advantage of
the growth in networks and services.
74 The NMHSs often do not have staff or facilities below the provincial or district level, de-linking the generation and use of
CIEWS. The inadequacies and deficiencies in SoPs is a barrier to the dissemination of CIEW using public and private
communications infrastructure. SoPs are often lacking in the development of easily understood, targeted, tailored and

actionable CIEWS for different audiences. Sub-national agencies are often excluded from the dissemination or the use of
CIEWS. There are very few sub-national agencies where procedures exist for the use of CIEWS by communities, for who
they are intended, this is particularly the case in un-planned settlements and remote areas where national services may
not available. Institutional structures at the settlement, village or community level are often weak, have limited roles in
governance and weak linkages with government agencies. Consequently, the mechanisms needed to effectively prepare
for disasters and to implement mitigation and adaptive action at the grassroots are not enabled and/or do not exist.
Inadequate technical and scientific capacities
75 NMHS in developing countries, face a number of technical and scientific challenges and constraints in the generation and
delivery of timely, targeted and contextual CIEWS. The transition to IbF, Anticipatory Action / Forecast Based Financing
increase the requirement for higher resolution spatio-temporal data, technical and scientific expertise as well as facilities
for statistical downscaling, and the ability to develop models and interpreting model outcomes to build scenarios and
triggers to activate early and anticipatory action, including through scalable social protection systems88.
76 NMHS often have insufficient training and capacities required to develop and run models locally. There is therefore a
need to develop in-house skills in these areas, but also, to have the parallel development of CIEWS through regional and
global support arrangements. There is an urgent need for regional centres and relevant academic and research
institutions to support weather and seasonal forecasts as much as possible through provision of data to NHMS and other
agencies involved in the early warning/early action value chain, who in turn need to use those data in conjunction with
other forecasts available through global producing centres, for e.g. the UK Met Office (UKMO), the European Centre for
Medium-Range Weather Forecast (ECMWF), and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).
77 Many countries have a shortage of staff with field data collection, analytical and modelling skills required for the
generation of IbF to inform anticipatory and early action. In many countries the subject course for hydrometeorology is
not existent, resulting in a systemic barrier in the development of skilled professionals to support met services, much less
at a sub national level. The localised nature of CIEWS, creates a greater need to develop national and sub-national
systems as they have better access to local information and contexts. Agencies need to be in a position to conduct local
level monitoring and data gathering on factors that are important for impact-forecasting, such as the changing dynamics
of hazard exposure, social vulnerabilities and disaggregated distribution of assets, access to services and infrastructure at
risk. While regional centres have a role in making first order estimates, it is national institutions that must undertake
more detailed risk mapping and assessments based on both historic loss and damage data as well as risk data that
enables outlook and foresight on the possible impacts of climate change. The number of countries that have accessible,
understandable, usable, and relevant disaster risk information and risk assessments available at the national and local
levels represents the lowest of all Sendai Framework Target G indicators. In large part this is a result of a lack of field
capacities within hydrometeorological systems as well as those related to data processing through new technologies. For
example the field data required for IbF include multidisciplinary vulnerability assessments and tracking of bio-physical
and hydrologic variables such as those pertaining to vegetation (land use and cover), soil properties (saturated
conductivity, erosivity) and hydrology (flow-generation/accumulation and discharge). Processing and visualising this data
require programming skills and use of programming languages and tools. Skills are also required in analysing spatial data
and hydrologic modelling using tools/software and cloud-based tools which leverage large data infrastructure without
the costs associated with setting up such systems locally. Capacities to link forecasts with hydrologic models and the use
of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools are also lacking. It is these new innovative technologies that paradoxically would allow
met services to address in a more a cost-efficient manner existing gaps in CIEWS coverage and in some cases can provide
solutions to data gaps.
78 Gaps in observational data are particularly severe and persistent in SIDS and LDCs and even in middle income economies.
This is a bottleneck at the start of the EWS value chain about which the international community has been concerned
88 UNDRR, “Analysis of Barriers to Financing and Operationalizing Linkages between Anticipatory Action and Social Protection Systems”, 2023,

about for decades. Many attempts have been made to address the problem. However, substantial investments in
observing systems have not translated into increased observational data sharing or in addressing data gaps effectively.
79 The lack of technical and financial capacities at a national level has acted as a barrier to adoption of innovative digital
technologies. These technologies can enable a transformational shift towards solutions that address the lack of
consistent and reliable field monitoring such as the use of IoT based sensors to autonomously measure and transmit data
using mobile networks. Generation of timely early warnings, particularly in remote areas, requires use of sensors and
systems which are autonomous and "off-grid". Many of these, such as water level recorders, have dual channels for real-
time warnings to local communities as well as transmission of data to NMHS for further analysis and interpretation.
Nonetheless, operation and maintenance (O&M) of these systems can present challenges for NMHS who have a shortage
of ground personnel and for communities without the necessary technical skills.
80 Effective local actions based on MHEWS are prevented by a number of barriers.
Ineffective or absence of dissemination to the last mile
81 Many countries have significant gaps in telecommunication networks which exclude some of the most climate vulnerable
communities in rural areas, especially nomadic and migratory pastoral groups and forest dwelling communities. Access to
early warnings and advisories can also be a serious constraint among poor rural communities who may not own phones
or have electricity to power radios. Insufficient capacities for translation, contextual rephrasing and packaging of early
warning information and advisories for multiple channels can prevent end-users from receiving such information. Most
MHEWS are developed through a centralized process. In large and diverse countries, this fail to sufficiently address local
contexts and tailor risk communications to diverse audiences, and tend to use technical terms in major national
languages. They are not adequately designed around end-users, are not people-centred and warning messages are often
not timely, actionable or understood by local actors. Warning messages and advisories usually lack the local context and
are not tailored to the different needs of targeted communities, including the elderly, persons with disabilities and health
impairments, female-headed households, ethnic minorities and IDPs, and vulnerable children. The design and content of
early warnings often fail to address the differential needs of end-users arising from differential access to information,
resources and representation. This prevents the most vulnerable members of communities to access early warnings or
take appropriate action.
Insufficient national and local level disaster preparedness and anticipatory action planning
82 There is a major gap in terms of national and/or local plans setting out anticipatory action and development and use of
triggers which determine when to act, roles of different actors in the early warning value chain, to define the relevant
and most appropriate and effective types of anticipatory actions for these actors. Under one third of countries globally
have reported on the percentage of local governments that have plans to act on early warnings (Sendai Framework
Monitor, Target G indicator G4 ), suggesting they may not have these plans. Furthermore, the percentage of local
governments that have a plan to act is very low even among the countries that have reported on this indicator. Few
governments have integrated anticipatory action into their national systems, although their number is growing.
83 Equitable and meaningful decision-making opportunities and roles for women in the design and management of MHEWS
and related areas are significantly limited.89 There are gender gaps in access to information, technology and digital
services. For example, in South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa where, more than half a million women are excluded from
the mobile connection and the gender gap scores are 41% and 37%, respectively.90 Inadequate resources at the local
institution level often prevent women from leading preparedness and coordinating effective inter-agency responses to
follow up warning messages with local action. Barriers that limit effective use of CIEWS by first responders and
communities include local socio-cultural and economic contexts, infrastructure and services that determine the ability of
communities to adopt measures that mitigate the impact of climate-induced disasters.91 First responders and
communities include technical limitations in accessing CIEWS, their contextual interpretation, particularly in the case if
89 UNDRR, “Inclusive and Accessible Multi-Hazard Early-Warning Systems: Learning from Women-Led Early-Warning Systems in the Pacific,” 2022.
90 GSMA, “The Mobile Gender Gap Report 2022,” Mobile for Development, June 2022.
91 Pörtner et al., Climate Change 2022, 2022.

indigenous and minority populations, and inadequate procedures and plans to take anticipatory action or to mitigate
impacts of disasters. There is almost a complete absence of information on dissemination and evacuation procedures
that consider people with visual or hearing impairments, physical disabilities. In the few cases where evacuation
procedures and facilities exist, they are male-centred and designed for persons without disabilities.
B.2 (a). Theory of change narrative and diagram
84 Addressing the barriers to effective end-to-end MHEWS require engagements at different levels of organisation,
governance systems and across multiple institutions. The project will need to operate at different scales and leverage
new and innovative technologies while ensuring the interventions engage meaningfully with local communities, their
own knowledge, understanding and coping strategies for climate related disasters.
85 The project is structured so that Output 1 provides support at the regional and global levels to set up, scale up and
accelerate technical and operational support to countries with the ambition to enhance their MHEWS coverage and
capacities. This output will catalyze regional and global collaboration among actors active in EWS support, including
through regular coordination, joint action, and exchanges to reduce duplication, save scarce resources, and better
leverage the comparative advantage of diverse actors to deliver shared value to countries aligned to the EW4All call to
action. The output will strengthen strategic planning for long term financing for maintaining such a support architecture
to avoid fragmented, discontinuous, and uncoordinated support to countries in improving end-to-end MHEWS.
86 Output 2 ties together the four key components of the EW4All EAP by addressing barriers in observations, risk
knowledge, dissemination and disaster preparedness and response at the country level. Activities under Output 2 address
gaps at the national level, these are designed to ensure effective use of MHEWS for disaster preparedness and response.
Hence the investments in observations will be guided by the vulnerability analysis and specifically seek to facilitate
development of impact based and actionable early warnings for early and anticipatory action by national actors on the
ground. Engagements with the governments will also seek strengthening of institutional mechanisms and governance for
more effective preparedness and response to attenuate the scale of recovery needs. Dissemination systems will be
improved to ensure usable multi-hazard risk information is transferred to end-users, including women and vulnerable
groups within communities, along with guidance on effective mitigation actions to reduce impacts (loss and damage).
Finally, the work with communities will ensure disaster planning and preparedness as well as community-based systems
that hybridize new technologies and local knowledge.
87 The project will improve technical support mechanisms and financial flows to meet the needs of countries (particularly
LDCs and SIDS) to establish, operate and maintain their national end-to-end MHEWS. To do so, it will establish regional
and national collaborations, multiple funding instruments and complementary mechanisms that maximize country
ownership and impact. The project will facilitate national investment planning into the MHEWS value chain, including the
development of national roadmaps, investment pipelines, and approaches to sustain national EWS through state and
private sector resources, and innovative finance. This will help address gaps across the continuum of country-specific
technical and financial support needs for end-to-end MHEWS, translating country visions into concrete investments.
88 The project has two broad outputs and associated activities which address the barriers described above. These outputs
and activities are mutually supportive and reinforcing (Figure 1).

B.3. Project/programme description
92 This project addresses the four key elements of MHEWS, i) disaster risk knowledge; ii) detection, observation, monitoring,
analysis and forecasting of hazards; iii) warning dissemination mechanisms and communication; and iv) preparedness and
response capabilities.92
93 Effective MHEWS depend on coordination with and across different sectors and at multiple levels and require feedback
mechanisms which allow for their improvement.93 The involvement of both national and local institutions and
communities in dissemination of warnings and response is a critical component of successful MHEWS.94
94 Addressing persistent gaps in establishing and managing an end-to-end MHEWS at the country level is a key requirement.
The proposal recognises that there are multiple on-going initiatives and mechanisms that aim to enhance countries'
climate information and EWS. These programmes and initiatives in the participating countries is summarized in Table 2 in
the appendices. The proposal also recognizes that an effective end-to-end MHEWS can only be built on timely and long-
term support for critical baseline capacities such as: i) robust scientific risk information and analytics on weather,
hydrology, environmental conditions, climate hazards and socio-economic, infrastructure and other dynamic
vulnerabilities; ii) optimised internal coordination among various government entities that are responsible for managing
different elements of a national EWS value chain; and iii) a long-term financing plan to maintain the necessary
hydrometeorological infrastructure, and community level capacities to receive, understand and respond to EWS through
risk-informed preparedness and response actions. These baseline capacities in many countries, especially in LDCs and
SIDS, can be built only through long-term support; the project will therefore strengthen the existing architecture and
create the environment in which countries can better utilise timely, long-term, uninterrupted support.

96 Targeted countries will be provided global and regional assistance to mobilise technological resources for upgrading and

and mechanisms will be instituted to coordinate and collaborate between NMHS, NDMAs, government ministries

Component/Output 1: Enhancing enabling conditions globally and regionally to promote country-level actions towards
the EW4All goals
97 Output 1 aims to scale up and accelerate global and regional support for national efforts to increase Multi-Hazard EWS
(MHEWS) capacity, coverage and performance. Three key activities are envisaged: Activity 1.1 focuses on enhancing
global and regional coordination and providing coordinated technical support for the implementation of the EW4All
initiative; Activity 1.2 emphasizes the strengthening of monitoring and evaluation (M&E) processes to support EW4All
implementation; and Activity 1.3 aims to reinforce knowledge management, evidence from national practice, and the
dissemination of lessons learned to inform national progress in EWS. Together, these outputs are designed to improve
the effectiveness and reach of EWS, ensuring that more communities are better prepared for multiple hazards.
98 The output will support the global and regional coordination and support architecture for EW4All that will be sustained
beyond the project implementation period. Activities through this output will help the EW4All Pillar leads build on the
Climate Risk and Early Warning Systems Initiative (CREWS), SOFF, and similar financing and coordination mechanisms to;
i) achieve substantive synergies with other partners providing similar support towards the EW4All target; and ii) to help
unlock required funding for sustaining EW4All support architecture to 2027 and beyond. The latter will target
conventional and emerging donors such as bilateral donors, multilateral financing institutions, and philanthropists. A
long-term financing strategy will be developed which is informed by detailed needs assessment from LDCs and SIDS,
including fragile and conflict-affected states. EW4All pillar leads are simultaneously engaged in global advocacy for EWS
finance with the G20 Presidency, the ‘Friends of EW4All’, a coalition of 17 major bilateral donors, MDBs, the private
sector, and non-traditional donors to unlock funding for national EWS. These efforts will also include finance gaps in the 7
countries. The private sector will be prioritized as part of EW4All financing, with several entities already actively engaged
in EW4All through provision of technical services, pro bono cloud bandwidth, and satellite mapping, e.g., Microsoft,
Google, Insurance Development Forum, and representation of the high-level EW4All Advisory Panel.
99 The output will augment on-going support for synthesis of knowledge, experience and lessons by providing operational
and technical assistance aligned with international standards and best practices towards the effective implementation of
the EW4All initiative. This will involve the development, dissemination and application of comprehensive normative
guidance, tools, and methodologies across all four pillars of EWS and at the inter-pillar level. Specifically, this includes the
development of detailed guidelines, strategic orientation documents, and AI-based tools designed to improve processes
along the entire early warning value chain and the provision of tailored technical assistance to strengthen national EWS
capabilities. National and regional DAEs, as well as sectoral representatives and associated ministries will be included in
the knowledge exchange to ensure they can contribute to discussions on practically implementing MHEWS within
different contexts and sharing innovations, lessons, and evidence of national EWS effectiveness.
100 In addition, this output will support the integration of EWS into national priorities, roadmaps, and financing strategies,
including governance and legal frameworks. Technical support will also be provided to facilitate simulations and testing
of national EWS operational effectiveness, develop coordinated funding requests, strengthen the global EW4All M&E
framework and develop a knowledge management system to document and disseminate key learnings. Collectively,

these global and regional activities aim to establish robust, sustainable, and effective national EWS globally, ensuring that
