Activity 1.1: Enhanced Coordination and Technical Support for EW4All Implementation
102 Activity 1.1 focuses on enhancing coordination and providing comprehensive joint technical support to ensure the
effective implementation of the EW4All initiative. This involves the development and application of normative guidance,
tools, and methodologies that span across all four pillars of EWS and integrate these efforts at the inter-pillar level. The
four Pillar lead agencies will collaborate to create detailed and standardized guidelines, training materials, and strategic
orientation documents. The goal is to provide countries and partners with the necessary resources to align their national
EWS initiatives with international standards and best practices. This includes integrating EWS into national development
and adaptation plans, roadmaps, and financing strategies, as well as supporting governance and legal frameworks for
EWS. Furthermore, the development and application of AI-based tools will be emphasized, ensuring that advanced
technologies are used responsibly to address gaps and improve the effectiveness of the entire early warning value chain.
Activity 1.1 further aims to accelerate harmonized technical support to countries by providing operational assistance and
facilitating simulations and testing of national EWS operational effectiveness. Capacity-building efforts will also be
undertaken to enable DAEs to fast-track access to GCF financing for early warning initiatives.
Sub- Activity 1.1.1: Develop normative guidance and tools across all four pillars & at the interpillar level
103 This sub-activity will result in the development of pillar-specific and joint inter-pillar guidelines, tools, training curricula
and methodologies, building on what exists and accounting for variations in regional and national contexts. Strategic
Orientation and Policy Guidance will be developed and provided to countries and partners in thematic areas such as:
improved access and harmonization of climate and disaster data and information for application in national EWS; global
standardization of loss and damage accounting for rapid and slow-onset hazard events for inform national tracking;
standardized EWS gap analyses and national EWS roadmaps and financial frameworks; global standards and diagnostics
of national data ecosystems related to risk, climate and disaster loss open-data sharing for IbF; national climate and risk
assessment capacity strengthening; and minimum standards for national climate and disaster risk hotspot mapping,
multi-channel warning dissemination and risk communications; and preparedness and response protocols.
104 This sub-activity will also focus on advancing the application of AI-based tools within the framework of EWS, offering
guidance and support to countries on the responsible and effective use of AI across the entire MHEWS value chain. This
effort aims to address existing gaps and emerging needs, leveraging the expertise and resources of the AI for EW4All sub-
group. AI is a key output identified in the EW4All EAP. The AI for EW4All sub-group will be leveraged to explore AI use
cases that align with the four pillars of EW4All, providing practical examples and identifying opportunities to enhance the
initiative's impact. This sub-activity will include the development of an EW4All Toolkit, which will include tools, models,
applications, and resources designed to enhance EWS. To ensure broad accessibility, a searchable webpage will be
designed to host the Toolkit, enabling countries to effectively leverage these resources for managing risk,
communication, and preparedness. This sub-activity will also involve cultivating strategic partnerships and collaborating
with stakeholders globally to support the implementation of AI in the EW4All initiative. Additionally, it will focus on
developing and delivering capacity-building and awareness-raising sessions. These sessions will demonstrate how AI can
significantly enhance the effectiveness of EWS, improve the flow of critical information during emergency response and
preparedness, and support the achievement of outcomes across all four EW4All Pillars.

Sub-Activity 1.1.2: Accelerate Technical Support to Countries for EWS implementation
107 Building on delivery of normative guidance and tools articulated in the preceding activity, Activity 1.1.2 focuses on
accelerating technical support for countries implementing EWS, focusing on providing operational and technical
assistance for the development and implementation of EW4All national roadmaps, supporting countries to test the
capacities of the MHEWS, and support the financing elements that underpin MHEWS systems and capacities. Efforts will
be focused on scaling up and enhancing the work of the Tropical Cyclone Programme (TCP), the Severe Weather
Forecasting Programme (SWFP), IbF and Warning (IBFW), and the CAP. WMO’s Regional Associations (RAs), working
groups and expert teams will be engaged to reach more countries with the afore mentioned capacity development
programmes to address a broader range of hazards, and provide better support to WMO Members.
108 Under this sub-activity operational and technical assistance will be provided to countries, ensuring alignment with
international standards and best practices outlined in sub-Activity 1.1.1. Pillar leads, WMO Regional Climate Centres
(RCCs), together with other global, regional and national agencies will co-design and implement analytic frameworks and
models for national adoption to scale-up use of data related to critical multi-hazard exposure, vulnerability, loss and
damage, and effective mitigation action to provide the basis of impact-based forecast warning services (IbWFS).
Alignment will also be sought with existing regional and global initiatives around early warning early action. This will
include providing and helping to design systems for climate and multi-hazard risk data sharing, archiving and access and
open-source software and scripts for data cleaning, analysis, visualisation and modelling. Regional centres will also be

countries via Output 2. In particular, the existing WMO supportive frameworks such as SWFP, TCP, CAP, IbFW and RAs
will be expanded geographically to provide real time operational support to more countries and also cover a wider range
of hazards to match country needs. These activities will be closely coordinated with SOFF investments which directly
support WMO corporate priorities and frameworks.
109 The sub-activity will support the integration of EWS into national priorities, roadmaps, and financing strategies. Technical

Activity 2.1: Strengthened Governance and Coordination
125 The activity will focus on legislation and policies governing the exchange of information to facilitate coordinated
dissemination of warnings between different actors. It will establish clear functions, roles and responsibilities of agencies
in the national warning dissemination process with associated updating of the WMO Register of Alerting Authorities
(RAA). Alert dissemination and feedback channels will be expanded to reach end users with targeted and actionable
information by leveraging community-based institutions, civil society and faith-based organisations. Considerations of
differential access to information and resources by women and vulnerable groups will be included in the dissemination
strategy. Partnerships with intermediaries will be established and training provided to local authorities and relevant
agencies for interpretation and dissemination of alerts to ensure delivery of clear and actionable warnings to end users.
This will include extension officers and other government staff in line departments and journalists.

Sub-Activity 2.2.1: Develop disaster risk knowledge systems
138 The sub-activity will increase production and access to risk information and effective application of risk information at
national, sub-national and local levels. It will result in improved capability of each country to produce quality, timely and
contextually relevant risk information for EWS which integrates community knowledge through a comprehensive

to a minimum defined level of vulnerability, exposure and risk across major climate-related hazards. Capacities of
relevant agencies in data access, metrics and analysis to support decision-making will be built to facilitate access to
updated risk information in standardised, inter-operable formats. Finally, the sub-activity will build institutional capacities
to incorporate risk knowledge into EWS. This will result in high resolution vulnerability (hazard, exposure) datasets for
each participating country and high resolution, forecast linked models for specific hazards (floods, dry-spells, heatwaves,

Sub-Activity 2.2.2: Broaden observation and monitoring networks
139 This sub-activity will focus on the strengthening and/or establishment of meteorological, hydrological and climate

Sub-Activity 2.2.3: Strengthen MHEWS forecasting capacity
144 The sub-activity will strengthen capabilities for data processing, forecasting and analysis. The network of Regional

G-6103. This will be achieved by developing and taking advantage of last mile connectivity and by establishing multi-

Sub-Activity 2.3.1: Strengthen early warning dissemination systems
147 The Sub-Activity will lead to expanded and strengthened communication network and services by supporting the
implementation of multi-channel systems for communicating and disseminating early warnings and alerts to the last mile.
Infrastructure and network services will be strategically strengthened by targeting the most efficient, trusted and
preferred communication channels, with at least one channel as backup where feasible. Geo-located mobile early
warning services based on cell-broadcast or location-based SMS systems will be implemented and strengthened by
working with mobile network operators, ICT regulators in countries and the GSM Association (GSMA), the global
association of mobile network operators. Best practices for data privacy will be put in place. Countries will receive
technical assistance to set up and implement mobile EWS. This will be further strengthened by supporting governments
to institute appropriate regulatory approaches and policies that mandate the use of geo-located alerts using satellite in
areas where people are at risk, but mobile networks do not exist (e.g. in remote mountainous areas). Here, alternative
networks, in particular, satellite-based and radio networks will be exploited as the primary dissemination channel. Funds
will be identified to pay for these systems where governments do not have resources to establish a basic satellite/mobile
EWS. Assessments will be carried out to understand how best to reach communities at risk and innovative and emerging
technologies will be used to develop "client profiles" to scale up targeted dissemination of actionable early warnings.
This activity proposes country piloting of the Disaster Connectivity Map and visualization tool to assess connectivity levels
and disaster risks using AI, helping visualise local connectivity, identify risk areas, and enhance national assessments and
communication strategies. Digital Connectivity Mapping (DCM) enables analysis of telecoms infrastructure vulnerabilitu
to extreme weather events and other hazards, enabling national authorities to take preventation action. Digital
connectivity is essential for early warning systems, and DCM visually demonstrates weaknesses that will disable message
disseminations in the event of shocks. This information is produced by ITU and will be shared through a very
detailed/granular map of the entire country to show exactly where people are within/outside of digital networks. This
map is shared with the telecommunication regulatory authority, for feedback and comments. This information on how
and where people have connectivity is critical to understand how many people can be reached via digital networks (such
as on mobile phones) but also to highlight areas where people at risk may be outside connectivity. This will allow
104 Human Rights Council (2015), Thematic Study on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities under article 11 of the Convention on the Rights of Persons
with Disabilities, on situations of risk and humanitarian emergencies. Report of the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights, A/HRC/31/30.
105 WMO, “Guidelines for Implementation of Common Alerting Protocol (CAP)-Enabled Emergency Alerting” (Geneva, Switzerland, 2013).

governments and operators to take informed policy decisions (for example, to expand networks, or to set up alternative
communication channels such as siren, radio etc to reach those at risk). For more information see here.
148 At the community level, the activity will promote and support inclusive, people-centered co-development of gender
responsive, disability inclusive actionable early warnings by targeted communities in accessible formats and local
languages using and extending approaches such as the Participatory Integrated Climate Services for Agriculture
(PICSA).106 Existing community-based systems including Indigenous Knowledge Systems (IKS) and flood and drought
warning systems set up through other agencies such as the IFRC will be leveraged and feedback mechanisms from end
users, including women and vulnerable groups, will be established to facilitate improvements in the development and
delivery of early warning services. Innovative systems that leverage mobile communications and Internet of Things (IoT)
will be used to set up low-latency autonomous systems (described in Activity 2.3.3) with local communities. Communities
will be supported in accessing and interpreting forecasts and weather data to better manage their risks.
Sub-Activity 2.3.2: Develop adaptation and preparedness protocols
149 Actions under this sub-activity will lead to comprehensive procedures and protocols for climate change adaptation and
preparedness, with emphasis on supporting communities most at risk in each country. Its actions will build on the
strengthened coordination mechanisms and governance (Activity 2.1) and better disaster knowledge and observations
(Activity 2.2). Actions under this sub-activity will include: i) Communication protocols and identification of focal persons
for each interest group, including a disability protocol incorporating accessible communication formats; ii) Protocols for
graduated warning levels to have heightened awareness during periods of increased risk exposure; iii) Protocols for
evacuation during disasters; and 4) Protocols for relief, extension and health services to deliver appropriate services to
communities.
Sub-Activity 2.3.3: Strengthen disaster adaptation and response capacity
150 This activity will result in the development of disability inclusive disaster preparedness/contingency plans to ensure
effective response, including provisions for early warning and early/ anticipatory action. Capacities for preparedness
based on risk-informed and impact-based forecasts will be ensured at the local levels to enable local authorities, first
responders and communities to act quickly and effectively based on the early warning alerts. Training of local
governments and first responders including agencies such as National Red Cross or Red Crescent Societies will be done
and their preparedness capacities, systems and procedures will be strengthened based on the integrated community and
national EWS. A National Early Warning Service training programme will be developed and implemented to enhance
capability, develop a sustainable knowledge base, and ensure the training programme is disability inclusive in line with
the Inter-Agency Standing Committee Guidelines on Inclusion of Persons with Disabilities in Humanitarian Action.107
Institutional and operational level capacities will be built by scaling up investments in preparedness, cash systems, supply
chains and logistics, as well as enhancing accountability of local responders.
151 Communities will be engaged in developing holistic early warning and anticipatory action in local disasters management,
DRR and climate change adaptation plans based on feasibility studies, climate information and local knowledge. These
will include evacuation routes and plans for future construction and retrofitting of small infrastructure for emergencies.
Specific attention will be given to the needs of women, persons with disabilities and vulnerable groups, specifically
building awareness of the increased risk of gender-based violence during emergencies and need for accessibility of
facilities to persons with disabilities, including physical, visual and hearing impairments. As part of CIEWS, communities
will be trained on O&M of early warning devices such as water level recorders, rain-gauges and anemometers. Support
and oversight may also be provided for small scale infrastructure for emergencies such as installing water storage tanks,
minor improvements to existing access paths, and small repairs or improvements to buildings (such as waterproofing,
installing toilets). Existing preparedness systems and operational protocols should reflect the roles, needs and rights of
106 Center for Independent Evaluations (CIE), “Participatory Integrated Climate Services for Agriculture (PICSA) Under Saving Lives and Protecting
Agriculture-Based Livelihoods in Malawi: Scaling up the Use of Modernized Climate Information and EWSs (M-CLIMES) Project,” Final Evaluation Report,

107 Inter-Agency Standing Committee (2019), Guidelines on Inclusion of Persons with Disabilities in Humanitarian Action.

Country based project description and strategy summary
152 A summary of climate hazards across critical sectors and proposed interventions for the participating seven countries is
provided in Error! Reference source not found.in Appendix 2, Pg. 106 in this document. A description of these
interventions is provided below.
Antigua and Barbuda
153 The project approach for Antigua and Barbuda (A&B) was developed through an extensive multi-stakeholder engagement
process, which culminated in an implementation roadmap for reinforcing a people-centric MHEWS in the country. The
roadmap identified several key principles which underpin the approach, focused on: i) strengthening the national
governance framework; ii) data-sharing collaborations and consolidation; iii) bridging the gap between technical
information and community comprehension; and iv) enhancing capacity for emergency management. Moreover, several
key sectors/areas have been prioritized to fill gaps in the existing MHEWS, particularly focused on the marine
environment – including ocean conditions and environmental impacts – and the introduction of an EWS for Barbuda that
is not wholly reliant on already stretched services in Antigua.
154 From a governance perspective, interventions in A&B will focus on modernizing the disaster management policy and
legislative framework, including through integration of disability issues, and integrating DRR considerations into sectoral
policies – including for the built environment, land-use planning and urban development. These policy actions will be
aligned with existing plans on a national and regional level and reinforced by a national strategic plan for national
emergency management agencies, together providing a solid foundation for the effective functioning and sustainability
of MHEWS and ensuring clarity and alignment among all involved parties. A key component of the governance support is
the establishment of a Disaster Preparedness and Response Fund. This fund will provide a sustainable mechanism to
channel resources toward critical disaster preparedness and response activities. The cross-cutting governance
interventions will be underpinned by improved disaster risk knowledge in the country (Pillar 1), focused on creating a
seamless information flow between relevant government agencies, supporting organizations and the public to improve
coordination and enable more holistic developmental planning, with risk data and information readily available to all
stakeholders. This will include increasing the availability of sector-specific risk data, disability inclusive risk data,
knowledge and best practices for critical sectors such as tourism, energy, agriculture, education, telecommunications and
health, as well as added focus the marine environment and social risks. At the heart of this effort is the development of
an online risk data platform, designed to centralise and manage critical risk information across all relevant sectors, as well
as undertaking comprehensive and disability inclusive hazard and risk assessments, addressing significant knowledge
gaps, particularly in Barbuda.
155 Under Pillar 2, a core focus of interventions will be on increasing the operational capacity of the Antigua and Barbuda
Meteorological Service (ABMS) – including supporting actions to direct additional budget to the services, hiring and
training of technical staff, and improving the hurricane resilience of the ABMS offices through structural enhancements
and the installation of backup power and communication systems. In addition, the project will improve existing
hydrological observation infrastructure and monitoring systems to enhance flash flood forecast system for urban and
rural areas, as well as introducing additional marine monitoring infrastructure for swells and potential environmental
changes. The enhancements to these networks will include provisions for real time monitoring and analysis of
hydrometeorological data, ensuring interoperability with risk data in place at ABMS through the introduction of a
platform to consolidate geospatial hydrometeorological and disaster risk information.
156 Pillar 3 will focus on simpler warning messages that are easily understandable by the public, including persons with
disabilities, ensuring that warning messages are clear, concise, and actionable in accessible formats during emergencies.
This will be supported by awareness actions to build trust among communities in the warnings being presented and their
associated anticipatory actions. A national emergency telecommunication plan will be developed alongside a common
alert protocol that integrates multiple dissemination platforms, including cell broadcasts, radio and television
broadcasting, sirens, among other traditional forms of mass warning, as well as accessible formats to reach persons with
a variety of disabilities.

=== PAGE 44 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 41
B
157 Finally, interventions under Pillar 4 the project will support the scaling of community-based EWS (CEWS) to empower
local communities, including persons with disabilities, to take an active role in monitoring, disseminating, and responding
to potential threats — developing specialized risk-informed response/contingency plans for extreme events based on the
needs of vulnerable communities, including persons with disabilities. The plan also emphasizes enhancing community
disaster response teams, providing training and equipment for first responders, as well as providing resources for rapid
evacuation and shelter services, and strengthening scenario-based planning with IbF to improve response capabilities.
and establishing dedicated financing mechanisms and structured early action measures for pre-impact actions based on
the needs of vulnerable groups, including persons with disabilities. The anticipatory action will be closely linked with the
governance support interventions – ensuring that relevant legislation is updated to accommodate the emerging functions
of key response institutions.
Chad
158 The intervention in Chad will ensure that EW/EA are impact based by building capability to carry out disability-inclusive
post-disaster needs assessments and loss and damages reporting, promoting longer-term adaptation planning and
knowledge management. It will ensure EWS are functional, by developing a sustainable finance plan with expertise in
public financial management in the context of Fragile and Conflict Affected States (FCAS). The project will promote the
development of a pipeline of supporting projects, ensuring data collected is transmitted in a timely way, ensuring data
governance, disability disaggregation, and mapping of location and collection of information on the support needs of
persons with disabilities through consultation, and developing rights and protocols for issuing and disseminating
warnings including in accessible formats for persons with disabilities. It will move from a siloed approach centred on food
security, towards a multi-hazard system, considering wider adaptation challenges. It will be people centred, based on the
right to information on risks, advice on preparedness measures, and warnings/advisories that are locally relevant and
respond to the needs and expectations of people including women, the elderly, people with disabilities, refugees and
minorities.
159 The project will develop an offer of audio recordings developed through mobile phones, conduct regular surveys and
qualitative community research, and develop national capability for cell broadcasts. It will consider preferences for
communication, including accessible formats for persons with disabilities, and monitor trust in existing and new
communication channels being developed. It will provide end-to-end integration of early warning and early action,
ensuring anticipatory action protocols are tested and adapted, providing capability to carry out simulations, lessons
learned and post disaster needs assessments, supporting crisis response capacity at devolved levels, while bringing
together contingency planning information with a register of responsibilities for disaster management, and defined
alerting rights. The project will respond appropriately to the needs of people concerning transparency, accountability and
the management of grievances, and be sensitive to conflict dynamics. Significant stakeholder engagement, and
preparatory work on institutional and regulatory frameworks, will ensure that coordination and governance approaches
are set in motion to support these activities and outcomes, and address critical institutional, financial and regulatory
barriers.
Fiji
160 The proposed interventions in Fiji primarily focus on strengthening and enhancing the existing functions of partner
organizations to address well-known priorities for improving understanding and communication and governance and
coordination mechanism amongst the national stakeholders relevant to EWS in Fiji. The project aims to unify risk
assessment methods in Fiji, focusing on historical data, climate models and local knowledge.
161 The project will expand or upgrade weather/climate/hydrometric observation network for EWS: Investments will be
made to improve monitoring and warning for severe weather, and localized and flash flooding, and droughts. Data
collected will be used to create models and forecasts of, enabling timely warnings and the development of disability
inclusive evacuation plans. The project will additionally Strengthen MHEWS forecasting capacity by enhance predication
accuracy through integration of AI and machine learning techniques, developing a centralized database/repository and
incorporating use of data science, e.g. AI to assist in forecasting and early warning. A slow drought monitoring IbF system
for food security will be established along with Drought EWS.

GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 42
B
162 For warnings dissemination and preparedness, the project will support the implementation of the National Emergency
Telecom Plan which includes automation of a geo-targeted, location-based messaging through the CAP and cell
broadcasting. This will require a review and revision of the current licensing of the national mobile providers to ensure
they upgrade their infrastructure to enable cell broadcasting. The project will also support expansion of Starlink network
and maritime radio to achieve 100 % EWS coverage in Fiji. This plan will ensure inclusion of formats accessible for persons
with disabilities.
163 The project will develop and implement community-focused communication strategies based on findings from risk
perception studies, and incorporating accessible communication formats for persons with disabilities. It will improve
translation and interpretation of early warning messages by incorporating message translation, caption generation, and
text-to-speech capabilities in EWS messaging to enhance inclusivity for persons with disabilities and the elderly. Train-
the-Trainer workshops will be run for key stakeholders, such as ground actors, government officers, Red Cross officers,
and sugarcane extension officers and Technology Transfer Officer and community-level awareness campaigns will be run
on how to respond to early warning information, including for persons with disabilities and OPDs. The project will
evaluate the reach and effectiveness of disaster preparedness campaigns, and integrate the lessons learned into revised
communications and training. Local contingency plans will be developed which are behaviourally informed, inclusive and
community driven and a community-based DRM (CBDRM) Training Toolkit will be developed used to and run Train of
Trainer workshops on CBDRM and early warning messages with inclusion of early actions.
Cambodia
164 The EW4AII intervention for Cambodia provides a comprehensive plan for governance and coordination, disaster risk
knowledge and coordination, and warning dissemination and preparedness in Cambodia. The plan includes developing a
disability inclusive data-sharing protocol, upgrading the Cambodia Disaster Damage & Loss Information System (CamDi),
and implementing disability inclusive EWS at the national and sub-national levels. It also emphasizes the need for gender,
disability and inclusion considerations, as well as the establishment of river gauges and drought gauges in target
provinces to address weather information needs. Furthermore, the plan focuses on raising awareness of emergency alert
systems and enhancing warning dissemination through various channels, including mobile networks, online platforms,
and accessible formats for persons with disabilities.
165 The governance and coordination aspect of the plan involves establishing a collaborative early warnings secretariat,
addressing gaps in the legal and financial context, and implementing a cross-pillar approach to gender, disability and
inclusion. The disaster risk knowledge and coordination section emphasize upgrading the CamDi, preparing preparedness
and contingency plans in target provinces (incorporating specific needs of persons with disabilities and preparing persons
with disabilities to respond effectively to warnings), and installing river gauges and drought gauges. Additionally, it
highlights the development of a comprehensive human resource plan to meet early warning requirements.
166 The warning dissemination and preparedness component focuses on raising awareness of emergency alert systems,
coordinating mobile network providers, and upgrading online presence and dissemination channels. It also entails
equipping local authorities with early action capacity, implementing community-based disability inclusive EWS, and
providing shock-responsive social protection for preparedness and anticipatory action in target provinces. The plan places
particular emphasis on the needs of vulnerable communities, including women, persons with disabilities, children, and
youth.
Ecuador
167 The MHEWS project proposed in Ecuador is designed to significantly enhance the country's ability to anticipate, prepare
for, and respond to various climate-related hazards, such as floods, landslides, droughts and extreme temperatures. The
impact of these hazards is increasing in Ecuador in the last years due to climate change. The project aims to establish a
robust and integrated multi-hazard EWS that leverages advanced forecasting techniques, standardised climate data
management, inclusive communication strategies, community emergency plans and anticipatory actions. The primary
activities include the development of a functional legislative framework, the development of a National Framework for
Climate Services (NFCS), the establishment of a comprehensive climate data centre, the implementation of national risk
assessments for the relevant hazards, the improvement of the hazard forecasting, the integration of Indigenous
Knowledge Systems (IKS) into early warning practices, the integration of rights of persons with disabilities into early

=== PAGE 46 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 43
B
warning laws, policies, systems, data collection, communication strategies, risk management strategies, and protocols,
the improvement of the communication strategies and the creation of gender-sensitive disaster preparedness protocols.
168 These activities are strategically aimed at addressing the pressing climate challenges in Ecuador. The country is highly
vulnerable to natural hazards due to its geographical location in the Andean region, which is prone to extreme
meteorological events, droughts, floods, and landslides. The project’s focus on strengthening governance structures and
enhancing institutional capacities ensures that EWS are effective and sustainable. By improving disaster risk knowledge,
enhancing monitoring and forecasting capabilities, and ensuring timely and inclusive communication of warnings, the
project will mitigate the adverse impacts of climate-related hazards on vulnerable communities.
169 Key activities of the project, such as the establishment of a National Climate Finance Framework and the enhancement of
data management systems, address specific gaps identified in Ecuador’s national climate strategy. These include the need
for more robust and sustainable financing mechanisms for climate adaptation, as well as improved coordination among
different governmental and non-governmental stakeholders involved in DRM. Furthermore, the project’s emphasis on
gender-sensitive and disability inclusive approaches and the inclusion of Indigenous Knowledge Systems (IKS) aligns with
Ecuador’s commitment to social inclusion and equitable climate adaptation. By ensuring that EWSs are accessible and
responsive to the needs of women, persons with disabilities, Indigenous peoples, and other vulnerable groups, the
project contributes to a more resilient and inclusive society.
170 In summary, the MHEWS project addresses the key challenges identified in Ecuador’s national climate strategy, including
gaps in institutional capacity, financing, and community preparedness. Its activities are specifically designed to
strengthen the country’s preparedness and resilience in the face of increasing climate variability and extreme weather
events, ensuring that Ecuador is better equipped to protect its people and assets from future climate-related risks.
Ethiopia
171 The project interventions address critical barriers that prevent the effective generation, dissemination and use of early
warnings for climate change adaptation, preparedness and response to warnings, through three broad outputs tailored
to specific country needs, which are aligned with the tree activities under Output 2 of the Global FP. The project will
support the collection and dissemination of multi-hazard, multi-sector, disability inclusive risk data through the
development of a central National Risk Data Hub managed by EDRMC and accessible to all. This will enable the
development and sharing of impact-based disaster risk profiles focusing on highly vulnerable areas especially looking at
floods risk and drought. It will support the upgrade of hydro-meteorological observing stations and improve coverage in
under-covered areas. An analysis on most relevant communications channels to address early warning to vulnerable
populations, including accessible formats for persons with disabilities, will be undertaken and used to develop a disaster
risk, early warning linked to mitigation and Anticipatory Action messaging. Early warnings systems will be operationalized
at community level in priority high risk locations, linking with Anticipatory Action. An emergency call number and service
will be developed.
172 Multi-sector line ministries will be engaged to agree on sector-specific early warning and Emergency Thresholds, and
multi-hazard Anticipatory Action plans will be integrated into Preparedness Planning in highly vulnerable areas, linking
with a financial support mechanism and a disability inclusive social protection scheme.
173 A National Risk Data Hub coordinated by EDRMC with contributions from all sector Agencies/Ministries will be formed to
collect and develop multi-hazard disability inclusive data and risk analyses and undertake capacity development for
expert human resources including IT and connectivity capacities to enable data sharing amongst all actors. Woreda level
risk profiles in priority areas will be developed with compilation and analysis of hazard, exposure and vulnerability data.
The project will improve data sharing by establishing requisite protocols and procedures and will support the integration
of geo-hazards in EWS. A gender based, disability inclusive EWS focusing on elderly and children will be developed as part
of this exercise which will also lead to the establishment of community-based, disability inclusive EWS in priority areas.
174 A survey will be undertaken to identify most relevant media communications channels according to types of audience,
including vulnerability, disability inclusive and gender-based issues. This will be used to build capacities of
communications specialists to address media, and to journalists to communicate about disaster risk.

175 The interventions proposed for Somalia under the EW4All project fall predominately within the Country’s EW4All
Roadmap identified activities and the resourcing requirements for these. In collaboration with the UNDP Somalia country
office, the Early Warning for All (EW4All) 2024-2027 Roadmap will be operationalised under the leadership of the Somali
Disaster Management Agency (SODMA) and the National Multi-Hazard Early Warning Center (NMHEWC). Three outputs
under the four pillars, corresponding to the three activities under Output 2 of the Global FP, form the interventions
proposed for Somalia, and contribute directly to the realisation of Somalia’s Early Warning for All (EW4All) 2024-2027
Roadmap through the identified activities and the resourcing requirements for these. The activities under the three
outputs include the following:
176 To improve disaster risk knowledge and capacities the project will undertake the development of a comprehensive risk
assessment framework and database. Disaster risk knowledge materials and communications will be developed for
national and local levels, and capacity building and coordination provided for the application of improved disaster risk
knowledge at national and local levels. The project will also support integrated actions for detection, monitoring, analysis
and forecasts of weather and climate; harmonising the collection of early warning data, its analysis and exchange
modalities among federal line ministries, sectorial offices, and regional bodies. The proposed project will support
improved data automation, modelling and forecasting of early warning coherency among sectorial offices and the
improved interoperability and early warning information exchange between sectors. Disaster risk knowledge activities
will ensure mapping the location of persons with disabilities and gathering information on their support needs, consulting
with persons with disabilities and their representative organisations.
177 The project will support nationwide warning dissemination and communication access by supporting the development
and implementation of early warning communication strategies and standard operating procedures (SOPs) for
governance, functions, roles and responsibilities for early warning information, communication and dissemination. These
will include early warning communication strategies and SOPs being established for early warning information,
communication and dissemination governance, functions, roles and responsibilities, impact-based forecast and warning
services (IBFWS), and CAP. It will establish comprehensive infrastructure networks and early warning dissemination
services and equipment which cover simulation exercises, CAP adoption, telecommunication service provider
agreements, automated system setups and protocols for AA and communication strategies and feedback mechanisms,
amongst others. The project will invest in accessible nationwide warning dissemination and communication.
Communication strategies and SOPs will also incorporate risk and warning information in accessible formats for persons
with disabilities.
178 The proposed project will establish comprehensive functional infrastructure networks and early warning dissemination
services and equipment and ensure inclusive, people-centred EW4ALL at the local level. Finally, the project will enhance
preparedness for timely responses and early actions by supporting improved response and recovery disaster
preparedness measures established for early actions and the development of supporting risk management policy,
legislation and strategies. This will include ensuring preparedness and response plans (i) address the needs of persons
with disabilities, including through their consultation and meaningful participation, (ii) are tested, and (iii) prepared
persons with disabilities to respond effectively to warnings.

B.4. Implementation arrangements
181 UNDP will be the Executing Entity of the EW4All-MCP and will be responsible for the overall project execution. It will
collaborate with the EW4All pillar leads in the provision of technical assistance and support.
182 The UNDP will enter into a Funded Activity Agreement (FAA) with the GCF, on approval of the project. This will be in
accordance with the Accreditation Master Agreement (AMA). UNDP’s overall role as an Accredited Entity is to provide
oversight and quality assurance through its Headquarter and Country Office units. This role includes: i) project
preparation oversight; ii) project implementation oversight and supervision, including financial management; and iii)
project completion and evaluation oversight. It also includes oversight roles in relation to reporting and knowledge-
management. The ‘project assurance’ function of UNDP is to support the Project Board by carrying out objective and
independent project oversight and monitoring functions. This role ensures appropriate project management milestones
are managed and completed. Project assurance has to be independent of the Project Manager; therefore, the Project
Board cannot delegate any of its assurance responsibilities to the Project Manager. A UNDP Programme Officer, or M&E
Officer, typically holds the Project Assurance role on behalf of UNDP. The ‘senior supplier’ role of UNDP is to represent
the interests of the parties which provide funding and/or technical expertise to the project (designing, developing,
facilitating, procuring, implementing). The senior supplier’s primary function within the Board is to provide guidance
regarding the technical feasibility of the project. The senior supplier role must have the authority to commit or acquire
supplier resources required. If necessary, more than one person may be required for this role. Typically, the
implementing partner, UNDP and/or donor(s) would be represented under this role.

AMA (the “Project Document”). For the avoidance of doubt, as the Accredited Entity will act as the Executing Entity for
the implementation of the Funded Activity, the Project Document shall not be considered a Subsidiary Agreement. This
EW4All global project will be implemented in multiple countries and therefore will use the multi-country project type

other subject experts brought in on an as needed basis.

B.5. Justification for GCF funding request
198 Investments in and around MHEWS are largely public goods including the networks, capacity building at the institutional
level as well as community level. While there are a few elements that are conducive for private sector engagement, in
developing countries, particularly in the aviation and telecommunications sectors, such opportunities are largely
untapped due to under-developed markets. Markets can also be constrained due to challenges in insecurity, access and
limitations of government support and available financial services. Public investments in MHEWS have been limited and
sporadic partially because the value that MHEWS can bring is not recognised. The absence of technical capacities to make

--- Table 1 on Page 54 ---
 | B.5. Justification for GCF funding request | 

=== PAGE 55 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 52
B
use of existing CIEWS undermines the trust in maintaining such systems. As a result, countries’ needs for MHEWS have
been addressed largely through external financing, on a project-by-project basis. This approach addresses the short-term
equipment needs but has many shortcomings considering that the “ecosystems” that make use of MHEWS require long-
term support and financing.
199 This GCF program focuses on establishing a global support architecture that intends to be long-lasting, is built on the
principle of multi-partners to address a wide range of needs which to date have been addressed, if at all, in a fragmented
manner, and offers a platform for regional and global south-south, north-south, and public-private information exchange.
The quantum of GCF financing allows a program of global/multi-country coverage to establish a pathway towards EW4All
not just for the initial 7 countries but more; and their mandate allows multiple partners not only the pillar leads but also
CREWS, SOFF and other initiatives, to come together to overcome the fragmentation. The multi-partners approach,
particularly the involvement of the likes of ITU, allows exploring the possibility of meaningful public-private sector
collaboration around the dissemination and use of CIEWS.
Key characteristics and dynamics of the private sector
200 Considering that EWS also affect various economic sectors, project interactions with the private sector are expected to be
diverse, and the nature and the extent of private sector engagement in this project will show significant variations
depending on country contexts. However, the following commonalities can be drawn to guide private sector engagement
within the proposed project.
201 The private sector, especially in the telecommunication industry, plays a critical role in both the collection/transmission
of basic observational data and dissemination of early warnings. This project will, with the help of ITU and GSMA seek
collaboration and partnerships with the telecommunications sector in each of the countries. This is critical as universal
coverage of early warnings will not be met unless the existing mobile cellular networks, managed by private operators,
are utilized to assist in automatic collection of observations and to complement radio, TV and other networks in
disseminating alerts. However, in many developing countries, regulatory barriers exist in effectively engaging these
private operators in the dissemination of early warning information.
202 Telecommunication infrastructure is vulnerable to extreme weather events and therefore, companies owning such
infrastructure are also prospective clients for climate services. The same infrastructure can also be leveraged to host
observation systems such as lightening sensors and generic weather observations, particularly in remote areas with
limited power infrastructure and security challenges.
203 Limited public-private partnerships with providers of digital networks and services limit the reach of early warnings and
weather information through multiple communication channels including radio, TV, internet, mobile phones, satellites
and social media. In remote locations (particularly mountainous environments) satellite-based transmission and
dissemination mechanisms may offer the only effective means of communication and therefore also need to be
considered.
204 Private sector engagement in the project will also take place at a different scale involving multi-national corporations
who are expected to supply hydrometeorological equipment to target countries. National governments will be supported
to adopt requisite policy frameworks and principles for successful public-private partnerships between government
entities and private businesses. This will facilitate alignment with corporate social responsibility and help leverage
mechanisms such as the UN Global Compact which offer businesses the opportunity to adopt sustainability principles and
support UN goals. The project will leverage the global commitments and engagement of the private sector as part of the
EW4All Advisory Panel e.g. GMSA, for the telecom industry, IDF for insurance and Microsoft and Planet Labs for
digital/frontier technologies.
205 This will also facilitate the adoption of emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence and provide access to new and
innovative digital platforms, social media and technological platforms such as remote sensing systems for high resolution
hydrometeorological data acquisition, big-data and cloud computing. This can facilitate data analysis and delivery to the
most vulnerable, enhance warning, improve dissemination and increase awareness about disasters and early warnings.

=== PAGE 56 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 53
B
At the other end of the spectrum, private companies and innovators can help design low cost, autonomous EWSs and
alarms that are managed by communities, for example for floods109 and landslides.110
206 The insurance sector plays an important role in using improved weather and climate data. This project will explore how
CIEWS can be used for development of weather indexed insurance products that the population can benefit from. In
many developing countries, risk transfer mechanisms using insurance are significantly underdeveloped due to the
absence of weather/climate and other socioeconomic data needed for product development, lack of awareness about
insurance products, underdeveloped regulations, all of which increase risks for insurance providers to enter into the
market. Globally, economic losses from natural hazard-related disasters in 2022 amounted to USD 270 billion and 55% of
the losses were uninsured. In emerging and developing countries, less than 10% of their losses were insured.111 The
absence of insurance as a mechanism to mitigate the impact when climate-induced extreme events strike continues to be
a major impediment for resilient development in many developing countries.
B.6. Exit strategy
The global support structure
207 The speed and scale of interventions required to deliver on the EW4All objectives can only be achieved through
coordinated global support involving all key actors across the EW4All value chain. The needs of LDCs and SIDS to
establish, operate and maintain their national end-to-end EWSs, effective communication systems and disaster
preparedness at the level of vulnerable communities requires multiple funding instruments. These instruments need to
bring together complementary mechanisms that maximize country ownership and impact.
208 There is a need to facilitate national investment planning to achieve EW4All goals around which finance can coalesce to
achieve shared value and results. This includes the development of national roadmaps and investment pipelines and the
communication of a common vision of needs, priorities, and opportunities across all four pillars of EWS. It is necessary to
recognize the respective business practices, funding cycles, and operational practices of various financial instruments to
accelerate GCF co-finance. This will help address gaps across the continuum of country-specific technical and financial
support needs for end-to-end EWSs, translating country vision into concrete investment.
209 The absence of a consistent, reliable and robust source of holistic technical and financial support to countries is the
essential challenge to the effective generation and use of MHEWS. Support available to countries is fragmented and
tends to be driven through project financing. Global initiatives such as EW4All and mechanisms like CREWS are therefore
necessary for countries to receive consistent, continuous support that meets the global standards, allows them to
exchange knowledge and sustainably develop and expand MHEWS to cover all sections of their vulnerable communities.
210 Recognizing that responding adequately to the SG’s call for EW4All will require concerted efforts at the global level for a
sustained period of time, developing a strong exit strategy for this project will become one of the critical deliverables of
this GCF project. In particular, the global support architecture supported by the project will continue to finance itself
through various channels including bilateral or multilateral public financing, philanthropists, private sector financing, or
other innovative financial instrument. Sustainability and replicability of the project will be facilitated and supported
through key partnerships and its alignment with key frameworks and strategies at the global and regional level. The
project is aligned with the WMO Global Framework for Climate Services (GFCS), designed to facilitate delivery of best
practice climate services.
211 This project is designed to address existing root causes and barriers to sustainable climate information services, MHEWS
and Anticipatory Action in the most vulnerable countries among the LDCs and SIDS. The following strategy is proposed to
ensure sustainability beyond the project’s lifespan.

GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 54
B
Institutional strengthening
212 The project will strengthen the existing institutions and governance at the global, regional and national levels, rather than
creating new parallel structures. Sustainability will be supported by the establishment of holistic national and regional
frameworks, with associated institutional coordination mechanisms such as road-maps, to ensure effective governance,
coordination and management of national climate services. The project will support integration of climate services in key
policies, strategies, plans and budgets which will provide a foundation for uptake of climate information in decision-
making and facilitate sustainable service provision in the long term. The identification of funding modalities for climate
information products and anticipatory action including by integration in the national/regional budget/pools will also
contribute to sustainability.
213 State of the art hydrometeorological monitoring equipment and tools for observations, monitoring, modelling and
prediction will be integrated in the existing hydrological and meteorological institutions, based on available data
management infrastructure. Institutional capacity will be further strengthened through upgrading relevant IT and
communications equipment. Special attention will be given to building capacities for O&M of both equipment and data
infrastructure. The project will also help NHMS and NDMAs in developing and implementing long-term sustainable
strategies for O&M through financial arrangements such as SOFF, for which it will provide support. NHMS will be
supported in designing and disseminating a suite of tailored climate information products for national ministries,
departments and agencies and the private sector to ensure some cost recovery. Transfer of Equipment: Equipment
purchased through GCF Proceeds will be transferred to the governments per standard processes as detailed in Article III
of each SBAA entered between UNDP and each respective government in a mutually agreed upon manner that places a
priority of the sustainability of project results and objectives.
214 In order to ensure long term technical and capacity support, the project will support NMHS and NDMA to participate in
networks based on regional and national centres of expertise. This will ensure long-term and sustainable engagement
with governments and policy makers. It will allow network actors to apply to a wide variety of other funding sources,
including utilising academic grants to support research as part of MEAL. This national and regional technical capacity will
furthermore benefit DAEs, regional institutions and national government by increasing access to technically rigorous
support and their capacity to submit transformative proposals in the future. By including DAEs and NDAs in the
development of proposals, this programme will also expose them to new ideas and enhance their proposal development
capacity.
Community level capacity strengthening
215 The project will adopt a broad multi-stakeholder approach and bring on board government agencies, multilateral and
international agencies and NGOs, Organisations of Persons with Disabilities (OPDs), Red Cross and Red Crescent network,
private sector actors and communities as users of climate information, early warnings and anticipatory actions as well as
front-line agencies in climate adaptation and disaster response. When possible, this will be done through existing
government-led coordination mechanisms. Institutional linkages will be strengthened by enacting enabling policies and
procedures that improve effectiveness of delivery and use of CIEWS. Local, community-based institutions, in particular,
will be strengthened to effectively access CIEWS, interpret and co-develop anticipatory action, adaptation and response
strategies and plans. These activities will be implemented through government agencies and institutions with a mandate
for decentralized disaster preparedness and response. Lessons learned will be used to fine tune and improve the
strategies and plans and successes will be scaled up through the relevant agencies to other vulnerable regions in the
country.
Programmatic alignment
216 This multi-country project will unlock opportunities for coordinated action and serve as an accelerator and amplifier for
EWS support co-financed through complementary instruments. It will work closely with other important programmes
such as CREWS and SOFF, and other mechanisms for funding such as from GEF and multilateral donors. This will be
achieved by building on multilateral mechanisms such as CREWS and the GCF, which mobilizes a significant number of
diverse national entities ranging from Ministries to national NGOs operating through a collaborative and partnership-
based business models. This will ensure scaling up of projects supported by these agencies, particularly under SOFF and
CREWS.

=== PAGE 58 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 55
B
Financing
217 Establishing a financing strategy in each participating country is one of the deliverables of the project to address the
critical challenge of financial sustainability. The strategy will assess the feasibility of various possible sources of finance,
including both public and private sources, to expand and maintain end-end-to end MHEWS in the selected countries,
based on their specific needs. This includes the national hydrometeorological monitoring network including public and
private financing sources. The financing strategy will include financial mechanisms that ensure the sustenance of: i) the
national hydrometeorological monitoring network; ii) development of climate products including IbFs, models for
scenario and trigger development; iii) support to anticipatory actions including ex-ante forecast-based financing and
resilience bond or ex-post climate risk transfer mechanisms; and iv) support disaster preparedness and response
capabilities down to the level of communities. These mechanisms will be operated at multiple levels and tailored to each
countries fiscal policies and capacities for effective and efficient fund transfer for DRR. Contingency funds will thereby be
released to targeted agencies and communities to take early action and avoid and/or mitigate the impact of disasters
through effective action built on CIEWS. This arrangement applies to countries where contingency funds are already
available for early and anticipatory action. Deployment of these funds is based on agreed approaches built by consensus
between governments and donors. Where this coordination is lacking the project will help coordination mechanisms
between relevant agencies and the government.
218 .
219 The financing plan will explore public-private partnership on data usage, analysis and dissemination. It will develop and
implement campaigns and consultations with various development partners, seek synergy among donors and coordinate
funding requests, including GCF submissions, across pillars to unlock financing at the global level. The project will support
Direct Access Entities to fast-track access to GCF financing on early warnings. Countries will be supported in sourcing
financing from international financial institutions, international organisations, vertical funds and corporate donors
seeking to support climate adaptation.
Policy strengthening
Project activities will fill gaps in policies and governance arrangements to strengthen national level EWS coordination
among government actors at the national and local level across sectors. Relevant national strategies and plans will be
updated or developed for NMHS and NDMA agencies in each country contributing to Sendai Target G Indicator 4: All
countries' local governments have a plan to act on early warnings. The project will strengthen legislation and policies
governing coordination, exchanging of information, coordinated dissemination of warnings and establishing DRR
structures for preparedness and response. This will mainstream early warning and anticipatory action and will leverage
supportive framework and legislation within the respective countries. The strategy will be linked to social protection and
DRM based on local priorities and will address assignment of roles and responsibilities at the national and subnational
level for government agencies, communities and local institutions as well as other actors such as NGOs. Coordination
platform will be established and inter-institutional arrangements will be specified for data sharing, inter-operability of
systems, co-design of services.

C.3 Capacity building and technology development/transfer (max. 250 words, approximately 0.5 page)
C.3.1 Does GCF funding finance capacity building activities? Yes ☒ No ☐
C.3.2. Does GCF funding finance technology development/transfer? Yes ☒ No ☐
220 The project is expected to support capacity building, technology development and technology transfer through multiple
mechanisms. Under Activity 1.3 knowledge exchange between countries and across initiatives with a focus on countries
seeking to improve their MHEWS and Anticipatory Action approaches and systems and through development of analytic
frameworks and models for IbFs and scenarios to inform early and anticipatory actions.
221 Under Activity 2.1 the project will support capacity development towards meeting the needs of Sendai Framework Target
G. This includes collection of risk data, information and its analysis leading to improved production and use of risk
information to support IbFs, better integration of relevant agencies with the work on NDMAs and NMHYS for more
efficient use of this information and improved monitoring, evaluation and learning systems.
222 Under Activity 2.2, the observation and forecasting capacities of NMHS will be enhanced by addressing technical gaps
leading to better accuracy and timeliness of these forecasts leading to GABON compliance. This will also lead to
installation of EWS and forecasting services for all priority services leading to meeting Sendai Target G Indicator 4.
223 Activity 2.3 will lead to improved use of technological solutions for data integration and sharing for development and
broadcasting alerts, communications and dissemination of early warnings across multiple channels, but specifically
focusing on mobile cellular networks and communications. This will lead to the strengthening or establishment of the
Common Alerting Platform in all countries backed with multiple channels of dissemination by working with network
operators. The activity will also build capacities of extension services in co-development of early warnings which
integrate weather forecasts and information with indigenous knowledge and practices. Innovative technologies for
autonomous community based EWSs will be transferred for relevant hazards to adapt to local EWS needs, particularly in
remote, “off-grid” locations and areas with poor reach of the NMHS and most dissemination channels.

GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 59
D
EXPECTED PERFORMANCE AGAINST INVESTMENT CRITERIA
This section refers to the performance of the project/programme against the investment criteria as set out in the GCF’s Initial
Investment Framework.
224 Globally, 3.3 to 3.6 billion people are highly vulnerable to climate change112. Between 2015 and 2021, 1.05 billion people
were affected by disasters and $330 billion USD in economic losses of 145 countries reporting to the Sendai Framework.
Yet, only 4.1% of disaster-related development assistance was allocated to ex-ante prevention and preparedness, of
which the majority was for emergency response113. As of 2022 half the countries in the world, less than half of LDCs and
less than a third of SIDS had a MHEWS.
225 Numerous studies have assessed the costs and benefits of EWSs. EWSs save lives and assets worth at least ten times their
cost. Just 24 hours warning of a coming storm or heat wave can cut the ensuing damage by 30 percent, and spending
$800 million on such systems in developing countries would avoid losses of $3–16 billion per year. Such investments
benefit from high benefit-cost ratios. For each of the 7 countries included in this project, an economic analysis will be
conducted following the GCF Guidelines. The outcome of these 7 analyses will be aggregated into a single economic
analysis for the entire proposed project.
226 The project contributes to the achievement of GCF strategic-level impacts through increased resilience and enhanced
livelihoods of the most vulnerable people and communities globally through a programmatic approach which accelerates
access to EWSs for the most critical climate hazards. It does so by investing in technologies and finance for generation,
dissemination of climate information and in its effective use through preparedness and anticipatory action. It will
enhance and increase the impact and long-term sustainability of these investments both at the national and regional
levels. It responds to the update of the GCF strategic plan 2024-20271 which contributes to the EW4All call of the
Secretary Generation with a dedicated target result on EWS.
227 Seven countries will receive holistic investment and technical assistance to establish an effective end-to-end EWS in
accordance with the actions proposed in the EW4All Executive Action Plan. A particular focus will be placed on improving
last-mile communication of and community-level capacities to receive, understand and act on climate information and
early warnings by ensuring each country prepares and updates disaster response plans and ensures communities have
access to communications, the capacities and knowledge and the preparation to react to warnings. These activities will
directly contribute to improving the resilience of people potentially at risk from climate-related extreme events and
hazards in LDCs and SIDS where communities are highly vulnerable to climate induced disasters on account of socio-
economic vulnerabilities and physical exposure.
228 Actionable climate information products for agriculture, energy and water management will increase resilience across
sectors, particularly agriculture, reducing the risks from climate-related hazards and thus reduce losses and damage to
crops, infrastructure and other assets. By the end of the project, it is expected that these target countries are well on
track to achieve the target of universal early warning coverage and hence the total population of the countries will be
receiving adaptation benefits from the project. Section B (pg. 43 to 48) summarizes the proposed interventions at the
country level which address barriers and gaps in governance, coordination, policies, implementation of EWS and in
delivering EWS services and response. The section also describes the expected adaptation benefits of these interventions
for vulnerabilities across relevant sectors and geographic areas.
229 The project will support existing WMO frameworks such as WIGOS, WIS, WIPPS and is aligned with existing initiatives

230 The project will contribute to the achievement of the GCF indicator of reduction in the number of people affected by

1. Improving the resilience of people potentially at risk from climate-related extreme events and hazards in LDCs
and SIDS where communities are highly vulnerable to climate induced disasters on account of socio-economic
vulnerabilities and physical exposure. It will provide early warnings to communities who are susceptible to

2. Strengthening NMHSs and NDMAs in participating countries through regional and global collaborations which

improved O&M of hydrometeorological infrastructure, access to innovative and state of the art tools and

based forecasts and targeted, actionable climate information products for early and effective on-ground action.
3. Enhancing regional and national MHEWS with targeted and timely IbFs which help communities take effective
measures to secure their lives, assets, and livelihoods during climate-related hazards and triggers to inform early
and anticipatory actions, including forecast based financing so that resources are made available to at-risk
communities ahead of disasters.
4. Increasing the safeguarding of assets and infrastructure from climate-related hazards through accurate, timely
and actionable early warning services. Actionable climate information products for agriculture, energy and water
management will increase resilience across sectors, particularly agriculture, reducing the risks from climate-
related hazards and thus reduce losses and damage to crops, infrastructure and other assets.
5. Strengthening national DRM legal frameworks and financing mechanisms as well as coordination, collaboration,
and knowledge sharing from the local to the international level leading to an effective DRM cycle and increased
opportunities for regional cooperation and up-scaling of climate resilient sustainable development.

D.2. Paradigm shift potential
232 This project will help shift the emphasis of DRM in countries from response to preparation and anticipatory action by
strengthening MHEWS, IbF. It will facilitate the generation and dissemination of critical climate risk information and the
design and implementation of evidence-informed transformative policies and plans which reduce the exposure and
strengthen the capacities of communities to prepare for and take pre-emptive action against disasters. It will thereby
reduce the vulnerability of communities and critical infrastructure and strengthen the resilience of vulnerable sectors to
climate-related hazards and their impacts of climate change. It will ensure the needs of most vulnerable population
groups during extreme events such as women, children, elderly and persons with disabilities will are reflected in relevant
policies, procedures and processes.
233 The global support architecture that the project establishes a sustainable mechanism to support countries both
technically and financially in rolling out a comprehensive MHEWS value chain. It will catalyse learning and impact beyond
one-off, project-based investments, which characterises investments in CIEWS in many developing countries. Elements
that contribute to the paradigm shift potential of this project include the emphasis on utilizing global standards for
assessing the gaps and needs and fostering synergies with other initiatives with complementary objectives. These include
the Alliance for Hydrometeorological Development, CREWS and SOFF, which will lead to support towards knowledge
generation; knowledge synthesis and sharing among countries; and long-term financing strategy for both countries and
for the global support architecture.
234 Finally, these investments and coordination between initiatives will be based in EW4All Roadmaps and standardized
assessments (CHD) leading to an unprecedented level of cooperation and collaboration among key actors across the
MHEWS value chain, from global to regional, national and even sub-national levels. This will leverage multi-institutional
partnerships at the regional and global level coupled with national frameworks and road-maps which ensure multi-
sectoral collaborations within government ministries and multi-level implementation mechanisms for disaster
preparedness and response. The mechanism will enhance partnerships between government and non-government
agencies, including societies and circles of Pillar Leads, iNGOs and national entities and mechanisms such as CREWS and
SOFF.
Potential for scaling-up and replication:
235 Scale-up and replication to other countries is feasible given the global support structure, should further funding be made
available. Substantively, the establishment of selected IbF schemes and Anticipatory Action initiatives have a high
potential for replication within and across the target countries. The use of appropriate technologies and innovations will
also contribute to scaling up and replications. For example: i) The implementation of the CAP and use of multiple
channels for dissemination, but those specifically leveraging on the cellular networks will facilitate uptake by different
telecommunication companies; ii) Successful applications of AI in for development of early warning products and
vulnerability assessments; iii) Co-development of agricultural advisories using PICSA and E-PICSA; and iv) Community
based autonomous early warning and alarm systems.
Potential for knowledge and learning:
236 The enhancement of MHEWS and production of IbF which utilise and combine traditional indigenous knowledge with
modern and scientific techniques will facilitate adoption of adaptation and responses to early warnings, facilitate
anticipatory actions for disaster preparedness and response by DRM institutions and grassroots communities. This will
catalyse wider acceptance and lead to safeguarding of lives, livelihoods and assets. It will support regional and country
level dialogues, knowledge exchange, coordination and collaboration with key initiatives such as on-going projects and
programmes of the UN, the Alliance for Hydrometeorological Development, CREWs and SOFF. Through these initiatives,
the project will also tap into communities of practice in place for knowledge sharing between countries and key actors

Contribution to the creation of an enabling environment:
237 The project will support enabling conditions at regional and global level, building on the significant investments of SOFF
in human and institutional capacity development and thereby promoting country-level actions towards the EW4All goals.
It will improve the hydrometeorological infrastructure of participating countries and strengthen capacities of NMHS and
NDMAs to improve observations and O&M of infrastructure as well as the generation of risk and vulnerability
information. It will streamline national and local protocols to improve institutional effectiveness of coordinating with
multiple actors in the dissemination of reliable, actionable IbF and climate information to trigger and support decisions
for anticipatory action. It will strengthen national DRM legal frameworks as well as coordination, collaboration, and
knowledge sharing from the local to the international level leading to an effective DRM cycle and increased opportunities
for regional cooperation and up-scaling of climate resilient sustainable development. It will help link sectoral and
technical government entities, science institutions, civil society and other stakeholders to promote anticipatory actions.
All of these will ultimately contribute to an enabling environment where climate risk information is effectively produced
and disseminated, in a sustainable fashion, to the most vulnerable groups to safeguard their lives, livelihoods and assets
in the long-term.
Contribution to the regulatory framework, policies and financial mechanisms:
238 The project will catalyse a systemic change in the operational procedures and processes of participating countries in the
generation and use of early warnings. It will facilitate the integration of climate information services in key decision
making, planning and operational processes by: i) revising institutional frameworks to optimise coordination between
hydrological and meteorological organisations with other governmental institutions by embedding early warnings, IbFs
and anticipatory action into government contingency plans and DRM budgets; ii) advocating for and providing links to
international financing opportunities for long-term funding arrangements for hydrological and meteorological institutes
to provide tailored climate information services on climate change threats; iii) linking with initiatives such as SOFF to
ensure funding for the installation and O&M of hydrometeorological infrastructure as well as human and institutional
capacity of NMHS as per WMO standards; and iv) delivering fine grained and updated vulnerability assessments to assist
in long-term disaster mitigation and adaptation planning.
Overall contribution to climate-resilient development pathways:
239 The development and dissemination of timely, tailored and targeted climate information products will be
transformational in building the long-term resilience of key economic sectors such as agriculture, tourism and health, to
climate risks. Delivered through a suite of outreach, learning and knowledge management activities, information
products will increase efficiency and provide more detailed and better-informed approaches and response actions to
climate risks.
