Antigua and Barbuda
Overall contribution to climate-resilient development pathways consistent with relevant national climate change
adaptation strategies and plans
241 The proposed approach for Antigua and Barbuda will create a paradigm shift in the end-to-end MHEWS process, enabling
effective anticipatory action and planning across multiple sectors. In particular, the project will be transformative in the
marine environment, significantly improving the monitoring and forecasting capacities for ocean swells, storms, strong
winds and sea temperature and other parameters. This will have a significant impact in terms of building resilience of
fisheries communities, as well as to enabling preparatory action to safeguard coastal infrastructure and related economic
activities – including shipping and tourism – against the impacts of swells, coastal flooding and erosion. The marine
monitoring will also enable tracking and forecasting of environmental impacts in coastal ecosystems – including coral
reefs early warnings and related links to the fisheries and tourism sectors. Additionally, the project’s focus on improved
disaster risk knowledge, monitoring, forecasting and response for Barbuda will enable a paradigm shift in disaster
preparedness and response on the island which is currently almost entirely reliant on information coming from Antigua.

Contribution to the regulatory framework and policies, and the creation of an enabling environment
242 The approach for Antigua and Barbuda is grounded in a strong cross-cutting governance and coordination component,
mainstreaming disaster preparedness and response into national sectoral policies and strategies, as well as ensuring
effective coordination between stakeholders in the full end-to-end process of MHEWS. The regulatory framework will be
enhanced by the development of a national strategic plan for national emergency management agencies, that together
with the policy updates will provide a solid foundation for the effective functioning and sustainability of MHEWS and
ensuring clarity and alignment among all involved parties.
243 In addition to strengthening the regulatory framework for MHEWS, the project will build capacity among key agencies
and response services, ensuring clear delineation of roles and responsibilities in preparedness and response processes.
Together with the strategic action plan, such capacity development will create an enabling environment for collaborative
actions, ensuring smooth and efficient implementation of preparedness and response strategies.
Potential for scaling up and replication
244 The expansion of Community Based Early Warning Systems (CBEWS) and the incorporation of localised response plans
offer a replicable framework for scaling CBEWS to additional districts or even other countries facing similar risks. These
scalable components, combined with robust training and capacity-building efforts, ensure that the project’s successes
can be replicated and adapted to enhance resilience in diverse contexts.
Potential for knowledge sharing and learning
245 By establishing a centralised online risk data platform and integrating it with sector-specific knowledge management
tools, the project facilitates the collection, sharing, and dissemination of risk information across government agencies
and the public. Antigua and Barbuda is also an active player in the Caribbean in terms of climate action and response,
positioning the country well to act as a catalyst for enhancing MHEWS and associated response actions in the region. As a
regional focal point for the CDEMA, Antigua and Barbuda actively participates in regional knowledge, learning and
support systems in the DRM space, creating a platform for sharing lessons and promoting the replication of actions across
the region. The involvement of the University of the West Indies (UWI) in the risk knowledge components further
facilitates knowledge sharing across the Caribbean region.
Ecuador
Potential for Scaling Up and Replication
246 The MHEWS project in Ecuador is designed with a flexible framework that can be adapted to different regions and hazard
types, making it highly scalable. The establishment of a NFCS and a comprehensive climate data management strategy
provides a model that can be replicated across other sectors or regions within Ecuador and even in other countries facing
similar climate risks. The use of innovative technologies for data collection and forecasting, the inclusion of
communication strategies and the implementation of community emergency plans in selected communities provides
support for replication and scaling up in other regions of Ecuador and countries in the region.
Potential for Knowledge Sharing and Learning
247 The project emphasises the development of a harmonized MEAL strategy, which will systematically capture lessons
learned and best practices. This creates a strong foundation for knowledge sharing at both national and international
levels. The integration of diverse stakeholder groups, including gender and development initiatives, ensures that a wide
array of perspectives and knowledge bases are shared, enriching the overall learning process. The focus on capacity
building and the creation of a robust data management framework will enable continuous learning and adaptation.
Contribution to the Creation of an Enabling Environment
248 The project contributes to the creation of an enabling environment by strengthening governance structures and
establishing inter-ministerial and multi-stakeholder coordination platforms. By developing a National Climate Finance
Framework and creating a sustainable funding mechanism, the project ensures long-term viability for climate services.
The development of standardised data frameworks and the establishment of a climate data centre will also foster an
environment where climate data is readily available, enhancing decision-making and planning across sectors.

Overall contribution to climate-resilient development pathways consistent with relevant national climate change
adaptation strategies and plans
251 This initiative will strengthen climate information systems by supporting the development of EWSs, the monitoring of
climate variables and observation facilities, and building the capacity of the stakeholders involved. It will contribute to
strengthening the capacity of relevant ministries and directorates dealing with DRM in Chad, the NDA, Red Cross
volunteers acting as first responders, local authorities, traditional leaders and communities at different levels of
governance (from the national to the local levels).
Contribution to the regulatory framework and policies, and the creation of an enabling environment
252 It will address the disconnect between climate information systems and the end-users in Chad, by investing across the
entire early warning value chain, supporting an inclusive multi-channel approach to disseminate early warning alerts to
the people most at risk of climate disasters, and build systems for two-way communication as a way of promoting a
culture of risk and an understanding of local capacities, and local knowledge systems for disaster preparedness and
disaster management. It will work closely with the range of national and international actors engaged in climate finance,
and in EWSs, to ensure a coordinated approach that contributes to a longer-term vision in Chad. This will include
advocacy at all levels for resourcing, regulatory evolution and ensuring that institutional mandates reflect the expected
roles and capacities of each of the national departments and institutions.
Potential for scaling up and replication
253 Qualitative research and dialogue conducted to inform the design and delivery of inclusive and people-centered EWSs
(including, language, gender and conflict sensitivity) will seek to address the global gap in community influence over
climate programming. This will ensure that anticipatory action programmes are aligned with community perceptions,
preferences, and priorities and foster greater community ownership and responsiveness in disaster preparedness.
Learnings from this process and its results will be relevant for comparable contexts, particularly in the Sahel and sub-
Saharan African countries with similar challenges.
Potential for knowledge sharing and learning
254 The project will invest substantially in knowledge management, M&E, accountability and learning. Research and dialogue
conducted to inform design and delivery will also shape and influence global and regional policy discussions on early
warning through sharing project findings, the process of developing the tools and learning. Broad dissemination of
findings, process and tools through targeted regional engagement, ensuring community views and voices are included in
targeted discussions with decision-makers, policymakers and donors. Data and learning will be shared at the global level
through the Anticipation Hub and the REAP. Community members and local organizations will be engaged in advocacy
efforts at both regional and global levels.

Cambodia
Potential for scaling up and replication

256 The Cambodia EW4AII project will form a central part of the already ongoing EW4AII initiative started in October 2023.

257 The EW4AII initiative is planning regular semi-annual meetings where facilitators will ensure a focus on cross-pillar

Contribution to the creation of an enabling environment
258 A key focus of the project will be on capacity development for the National Committee for Disaster Management (NCDM)

subnational levels. Training interventions will emphasise making the best use of regional centres of excellence and
investing in skills in newly emerging technologies such as AI and remote sensing capacities. In addition, trained local
youth will play a key role in accessing existing online early warning resources as part of Cambodia’s commitment to
digital transformation. In the target provinces, for the first time, the project will operationalise the newly developed
government Shock Resilient Social Protection mechanism.
Contribution to the regulatory framework and policies
259 In line with existing laws and decrees on disaster management115, in 2022 UNDP developed and advocated for the
implementation of Standard Operating Procedures for disaster preparation and response, on behalf of the NCDM. This
project will review these SOPs as well as develop protocols for shared data management collaboratively with government
ministries through the EW4AII initiative. In addition, as part of the planned DRR capacity development initiatives at
national and sub-national levels, existing DRR regulations will be publicised and further operationalised.

Somalia
Potential for scaling up and replication
268 The proposed activities will initiate Somalia's EW4All initiative, fulfilling the immediate programme of activities under the
Roadmap of the EW4All initiative 2024-2027, for building disaster resilient communities in Somalia. The activities under
the three project outputs, which represent the four pillars of the EW4All initiative and early warning more broadly, will
establish key needs and national apparatus for further future early warning activities to be implemented at local scales.
Potential for knowledge sharing and learning
269 The database of disaster impact data and loss and damage tracking (aligned with UNFCCC, Sendai and SDG targets and
indicators) will provide potential learning from past events alongside Interpretation and communication materials
developed. These materials are to include hazard maps that identify specific geographic areas, sectors and groups that
may be affected by particular hazards; tailored for EWS and DRR plans/local risk management plans. They will
incorporate climate risk projection summaries, tailored in clear, accessible language (as appropriate) that incorporate
traditional knowledge and understandings, developed and disseminated for the national and local levels and
applied/interpreted and translated for Somalia’s critical sectors (health, agriculture, livestock, forestry, fisheries and
aquaculture etc) and in considerations of key vulnerability factors (e.g. age, gender, disability, access to infrastructure
and services, IDP, conflict affected areas, economic diversity, social inequalities and environmental sensitivities). As
knowledge sharing and learning opportunities, these will complement the Early Warning Coordination and Information
Sharing Platform proposed to be established as a sub-structure of the National Platform for DRR (under the NMHEWC)
committed to coordinating and distributing early warning information across the country.

Contribution to the creation of an enabling environment
270 Despite establishing an NMHEWC as a central point for early warning coordination and information sharing, early
warning and information management in Somalia still need to improve in the early warning value chain. As a result,
competition and overlapping roles and responsibilities continue across the various government departments and
agencies. The Early Warning Coordination and Information Sharing Platform is therefore proposed for coordinating and
distributing early warning information across the country, with many of the activities (e.g. Comprehensive Risk
Assessment Framework and development of database, disaster risk knowledge materials and communication developed
for national and local levels) aimed to contribute to these. The activities of the EW4All Initiative, and therefore the
proposed activities under Somalia’s project, implement key areas of Somalia’s National Disaster Risk Management Policy
(NDRMP) and its accompanying national and local DRR plans, contributing to creating a better enabling environment for
enhancing the availability of disaster risk knowledge in the country.
Contribution to the regulatory framework and policies
271 The project's proposed activities include specific harmonisation of Somalia’s early warning with Somalia’s commitments
to the UNFCCC, Sendai Targets and SDGs. Specifically, seeking to harmonise the development of a comprehensive hazard
risk assessment methodology and assessments for key risks with regional approaches and UNFCCC, and Sendai and SDG
targets and indicators and the harmonisation of early warning data collection, analysis and exchange modalities among
federal line ministries, sectorial offices, and regional bodies and improved data automation, modelling and forecasting of
early warning harmonised among sectorial offices. The project directly contributes to Somalia’s commitment to the
Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction (2015–2030) Target G (substantially increase the availability of and access
to multi-hazard EWS and disaster risk information and assessments to the people by 2030) and Priority 4 (enhancing
disaster preparedness for effective response and to ‘build back better’ in recovery, rehabilitation, and reconstruction).
Furthermore, the project interventions align with Somalia’s commitment to the Paris Agreement (Article 7, paragraph 7c)
on adaptation and the Africa Program of Action for implementing the Sendai Framework in Africa. The EW4ALL initiative
is now operationalised at the national level under the NMHEWC leadership. The activities accompany the process of the
Roadmap, which establishes a systematic reform initiative aimed at aligning it to Article 3, para 6 and Article 7, para 2, of
the establishment Law 17/2016 of SoDMA. These Articles state the clear responsibility of SoDMA to gather information
and report on disasters and the risks facing the country and send out early warnings in collaboration with organisations
inside the country and abroad working on those activities. While implementing key aspects of the NDRMP and its
accompanying national and local DRR plans, the proposed project activities also interlace with Somalia’s NAP
Framework116, the 2021 NDC117, Somalia’s Biennale Update Report (BUR) to the UNFCCC118, and the 2021 National
Climate Change Policy119 which provides the framework for addressing climate change impacts focused on both
adaptation and DRR measures.
Overall contribution to climate-resilient development pathways consistent with relevant national climate change
adaptation strategies and plans
272 As noted, the proposed activities kick off the implementation of Somalia’s Roadmap, thereby contributing to climate-
resilient pathways consistent with national climate change strategies and plans. These contribute to climate-resilient
development pathways through the alignment with Somalia’s commitments on the Sendai Target G (substantially
increase the availability of and access to multi-hazard EWS and disaster risk information and assessments to the people

Fiji
Potential for scaling up and replication
273 Integration of AI-powered systems into EWS will provide more accurate forecasts, which will also enhance people’s faith
in early warning messages. By analysing historical weather data, AI can predict future events effectively, especially for
specific regions like agriculture and emergency services. It can optimize resource allocation and assess risks of extreme
weather events, improving preparedness and mitigation strategies.
274 Although Cell Broadcast (CB) is not a new technology for public warning systems, it has yet to be implemented in Fiji due
to the lack of infrastructure requirements for mobile service providers. However, the current infrastructure can be
upgraded to support cell broadcasting technology. Consequently, the project aims to establish cell broadcasting services
in Fiji and will enhance these mechanisms by integrating additional systems to disseminate early warning messages
utilising the Common Alert Protocol system.
275 The initiative to use selected sugarcane farms as reference points to monitor crop status and provide farmers with
guidance on necessary actions is a simple but effective way to implement an impact-based early warning system.
Although the system may not be perfect, it will be relatable to farmers. Furthermore, this system has the potential to be
extended to other crops in Fiji.
Potential for knowledge sharing and learning
276 Most importantly, people often do not take appropriate actions in response to early warnings; therefore, delays can be
critical in fast-moving disasters. This lack of action may be due to a lack of faith in the messages or insufficient knowledge
of the actions they could take to reduce impacts. It can also be attributed to resource or financial constraints, in the cases
of sugarcane farmers. Furthermore, false alarms can lead to people becoming desensitised to warning and are less likely
to take them seriously. Therefore, to have an effective EW4All system in Fiji, there is a need to change people’s mindsets
and attitudes towards early warning messages, so they are willing to take responsive actions, knowing that it may not
eventuate. This effort is required not only at the community level but also at the government level to adopt and
implement an effective Anticipatory Action system in Fiji.
277 It is important to understand how people perceive early warning messages and what influences their decision-making
and actions. This understanding can inform the development and implementation of innovative approaches and
technological advancements that enhance community capacity and inclusivity for people with disabilities and the elderly,
empowering them to respond effectively to early warning messages. It is anticipated that, over time, there will be
changes in people's mindsets regarding how to perceive and respond to early warning messages.
278 The project will facilitate a stocktake and harmonise multi-hazard risk assessment methodologies and tools across
government and non-government institutions in Fiji. It will encompass data on hazards, vulnerabilities, exposure,
capacity, and impacts. This will necessitate the development of a centralised database or repository system for disaster-
related data to be shared among all national and subnational EWS actors. Furthermore, the project will prioritise
enhancing the capacity to assess and gather information about risks at the local level. This will include documenting data
and information on community-specific risks, incorporating traditional, local, and indigenous knowledge. Once in a
mature stage, this centralised database can be used to inform the development monitoring of future EWS or DRR
initiatives in Fiji and other countries in the region.
Contribution to the regulatory framework and policies
279 The project will facilitate development of interagency protocols and SOPs for data access and sharing between relevant
MHEWS agencies. It will also strengthen coordination mechanisms for implementing MHEWS plans and protocols.
Furthermore, it will aim to enhance technical support for continuously collecting risk data, analysing it, and applying

D.3. Sustainable development (max. 500 words, approximately 1 page)
282 This project will contribute to long-term social, economic and environmental benefits from avoided human and economic
losses and support the objective of climate risk-resilient economies. Poor and vulnerable communities suffer
disproportionally from natural hazards due to increased exposure, fewer assets and economic resources and poor access
to information and financing to promote adaptation. In these countries, resources required to recover from disasters are
often covered through external borrowing, leading to significant debt and increased exposure to economic shocks that
result in large reductions in GDP and exports during global crises. Climate information services and MHEWS can be vital
tools in reducing these impacts and thereby promoting social development. This will enable preparation, planning and
anticipatory action based on early warnings which will result in avoidance, mitigation and adaptation to climate induced
hazards, directly contributing to health and safety for communities most vulnerable to such disasters.
The project is fully aligned with the SDGs, Paris Agreement and Sendai Framework, SDG 13 on urgent action to combat
climate change and its impacts and related target 13.1 to “Strengthen resilience and adaptive capacity to climate-related
hazards and natural disasters in all countries”. The project also speaks to the SDGs 1, 2, 9, 11, 12 and 15120.

preparedness; iii) slow onset events; iv) events that may involve irreversible and permanent loss and damage; v)
comprehensive risk assessment and management; and vi) resilience of communities, livelihoods and ecosystems. It is also

D.4. Needs of recipient (max. 500 words, approximately 1 page)
289 Least Developed Countries, SIDS and most African countries are particularly vulnerable to a range of climate change
impacts and climate-related hazards, which affect people, livelihoods, assets and economy. Affected countries have
highlighted the urgent need for better climate information and early warnings to help adapt to, mitigate and recover
from increasingly frequent climate induced disasters. Early warning systems are a critical need to improve the resilience
of their population to natural hazards and to strengthen and scale up early and anticipatory action. It is noted that
national policies on areas related to EWS and DRM often neglect the differential needs of people with disabilities and
those with special needs on account of age, gender and social and cultural exclusion129. The country projects will address
such gaps through an inclusivity strategy that is mainstreamed across project activities.
290 The project will address the following needs of recipients:
• Strengthening climate information services through enhancing institutions, coordination mechanisms, policies
and financial mechanisms and frameworks. This will sustainably address the needs and priorities of the NMHS
and NDMAs by leveraging modern technologies, automation, digitisation and establishing a MHEWS. The
enhanced capacity of these agencies will meet the needs for enhanced IbF , access to data and effective and
anticipatory actions to safeguard lives, livelihoods and assets against climate risks. The NMHSs and NDMAs will
be key responsible parties in the respective projects, which directly addresses their needs and priorities.
• Through this project, systems building of national and local actors will be addressed. This can include
strengthening the decision-making upon the early warnings received by setting up and equipping the national
emergency operations centres, improving logistics and supply chains for disaster preparedness and response
along with relevant procurement processes, establishing partnerships/MoUs between NMHSs, NDMAs,
ministries, agencies and departments responsible for critical climate vulnerable sectors, National Red Cross and
Red Crescent Societies and others.
• The project will address the needs of vulnerable groups within communities who are often neglected in the
design of MHEWS, their dissemination and for disaster preparedness and planning. These specifically include
people with disabilities, elderly, women, youth, cultural minorities, urban and rural communities. In addition,
specific attention will be given to women headed households, households with infants, elderly, children and
youth.
• Needs of communities exposed to climate-related hazard for timely and accurate early warning that will enable
them to take anticipatory actions. Populations living in coastal areas, along floodplains and in mountainous areas
are particularly vulnerable to climate-related hazards. The specific climate information needs of women, elderly
and disabled people require particular attention considering their increased socio-economic vulnerabilities and
relatively weaker representation and more limited access to resources and channels of communication.
• Communities dependent on natural resources, especially those reliant on rain-fed agriculture, pastoralism,
forest resources and fisheries are disproportionately affected by climate-related hazards. These communities are
often socially and economically more vulnerable and spend a high proportion of their income on subsistence
which limits their ability to adapt. Climate change impacts often undermine progress that has been made in
poverty reduction in countries with large proportion of such populations, adversely impacting food security and
economic growth, particularly in rural areas. This project will help these rural populations reduce these
associated risks.
• Pastoral communities practising transhumance, particularly those countries in Sub-Saharan, Eastern and the
Horn of Africa, face unique challenges associated with climate change. Pastoral communities are often forced to
migrate to wetter areas which are already inhabited in order to adapt to changing conditions and overgrazing.

Antigua and Barbuda
Vulnerability of the country and/or specific vulnerable groups, including gender aspects (for adaptation only)
292 As a SIDS, Antigua and Barbuda is particularly vulnerable to extreme climate events such as hurricanes, droughts and
coastal flooding, ranking 85th on the ND-GAIN index. The country’s NDC identifies five primary reasons for the country’s
vulnerability, including: i) inefficient planning and management of the built environment; ii) high costs of repairing
damage caused by recurrent extreme climate events; iii) the composition of the country’s economy; iv) high population
density in the coastal zone; and v) limited availability of freshwater resources.
Economic and social development level of the country and the affected population
293 Climate change is increasing the frequency of high-intensity hurricanes, which will have severe impacts on the country,
including loss of life, economic losses and damage to infrastructure. These impacts are further exacerbated by the
potential to disrupt key economic activities, including tourism which makes up the largest proportion of the country’s
GDP (~60%) and accounts for the highest overall investment, at ~40%. Antigua and Barbuda is also heavily reliant on
imports of basic supplies, including food, medicine and building materials, increasing vulnerability to disruptions to
shipping routes and associated increases in insurance costs during and after extreme events. Fisherfolk are also
particularly vulnerable given the limited availability of risk information and forecasts for ocean conditions or
environmental impacts of climate change on reef fisheries.
Absence of alternative sources of financing (e.g. fiscal or balance of payments gap that prevents government from
addressing the needs of the country; and lack of depth and history in the local capital market)
294 While Antigua and Barbuda invests heavily in building resilience, there capacity to do so is severely constrained by the
current economic conditions in the country. Although classified as high-income in terms of per capita GDP, the
distribution of wealth is largely skewed by a few high-income persons who have moved to the country from abroad, with
much of the local population having much lower income. Moreover, the country’s small tax and market base, as well as
its high public debt — more than 87% its GDP in 2022 — constrain the government’s ability to allocate funding from the
national budget for adaptation. External investment is therefore critical to enhance MHEWS and Anticipatory Action
measures needed to build climate resilience and preparedness of Antigua and Barbuda’s population.
Need for strengthening institutions and implementation capacity
295 The gap assessment conducted for Antigua and Barbuda identified several areas where capacity development and
institutional strengthening is needed to enable effective MHEWS and Anticipatory Action. This includes the need for: the
revitalization of the linkages between national development organisations and each major stakeholder ministries
responsible for key parts of the economy; updates to key policies for disaster management, emergency response, and
environmental management; strengthening the institutional and human capacity of ABMS.

296 Ecuador is highly vulnerable to a range of climate-related hazards, including floods, landslides, and droughts. These

women, who often have less access to resources and information needed for effective disaster preparedness and

297 Ecuador’s economic and social development is uneven, with significant disparities between urban and rural areas. Many

Cambodia
Vulnerability of the Country and/or Specific Vulnerable Groups, Including Gender Aspects (for Adaptation Only)
300 Cambodia, a country still recovering from decades of conflict, faces significant development challenges and is particularly
susceptible to compounding and cascading risks. These risks disproportionately affect vulnerable populations, including
rural communities, women, children, and ethnic minorities. Climate change intensifies the frequency and severity of
floods, droughts, and storms, exacerbating poverty and food insecurity. Economic downturns and health crises further
amplify poverty, unemployment, and inequality, while discrimination based on gender, ethnicity, and disability
exacerbates vulnerability to shocks and stresses. Specific examples in Cambodia include rural communities highly
vulnerable to climate-related shocks, women and girls facing gender-based discrimination and limited economic
opportunities, children affected by displacement and lack of education, and ethnic minorities experiencing discrimination
and increased vulnerability to exploitation.
Economic and Social Development Level of the Country and the Affected Population
301 Between 2014 and 2021/22, Cambodia made significant progress in reducing poverty, dropping the poverty incidence
from 36.7% to 16.6%. However, after the 2019 COVID-19 outbreak and economic shock, approximately 4.5 million people
were still classified as falling under ID poor 1 or 2, and at-risk households are in danger of falling into poverty due to
economic instabilities, natural hazard-related disasters, and environmental degradation. Cambodia is highly vulnerable to
the impacts of climate change, which is projected to exacerbate flooding and drought risks and decrease the country's
GDP by as much as 10% by 2050.
Absence of Alternative Sources of Financing
302 This GCF project will make a critical difference in its systemic approach to addressing the vital EW/EA value chain gaps,
from risk knowledge to early response. Over the years, funding has been ad hoc and has primarily focused on forecasting

Vulnerability of the Country and/or Specific Vulnerable Groups, Including Gender Aspects (for Adaptation Only)
304 Chad’s extreme vulnerability to the impacts of climate change is reflected in its position on the ND-GAIN index (185): a
combination of high poverty, frequent conflicts, and the risk of both droughts and floods have placed Chad as the lowest
ranked country overall, with a score of 27.0. In 2024, Chad had an Inform risk index of 7,8, placing it in the “very high” risk
class, meaning that the country is at substantial risk of a humanitarian crisis in case of natural or man-made disaster. The
gender inequality index is 0.7, indicating pervasive inequality in women’s empowerment. With a literacy rate of 28.1%
(compared to 57.6% for men), women face challenges in accessing information. The specific vulnerabilities of refugees,
returnees, minority groups and people living with disabilities also need to be considered.
Economic and Social Development Level of the Country and the Affected Population
305 Chad remains among the poorest and least developed countries in the world, with a 2023/4 Human Development Index
ranking of 189 out of 193. The World Bank estimates that 40% of Chadians live in poverty and face severe deprivation of
a range of basic needs. The percentage of households with access to electricity is 8% (NAP). Climate change itself is also
having a negative impact on the viability of rural production systems including agricultural production, rangeland
production capacity and livestock watering possibilities. This has led to increased competition between users of rural
areas and a deterioration in social cohesion.
Absence of Alternative Sources of Financing
306 Access to climate finance is insufficient to meet the acute challenges posed by climate change. There is a financing
shortfall to build climate resilience in Chad, with annual climate finance are estimated at a quarter of annual needs.
Recently-approved projects are investing in critical aspects of the EW/EA value chain, however additional financing is
needed to ensure that effective, actionable and intelligible communication and dissemination strategies are delivered, to
work specifically on institutional governance and coordination challenges, and to deliver a MHEWS that is functional,
impact-based, people-centered, and end-to-end.
Need for Strengthening Institutions and Implementation Capacity
307 Due to fragility and conflict within the country and beyond its borders, individuals, households and communities in Chad
are vulnerable to shocks and climate change. Fragile national and sub-national institutions (e.g. governmental, legal and
financial) are responsible for under-investment and weak systems for essential services, disaster and climate risk
management, and natural resource management.
Fiji
Vulnerability of the country and/or specific vulnerable groups, including gender aspects
308 Fiji faces a high risk from various natural hazards, including tropical cyclones, storm surges, floods, landslides, droughts,
extreme temperatures, earthquakes, and tsunamis. The country is particularly vulnerable to the anticipated effects of
climate change, such as rising sea levels, more severe tropical cyclones, and heavy rainfall. For Fiji, the probability of
catastrophic damage and loss of life from meteorological and geophysical hazards is considered very high. Fiji’s extreme
vulnerability to natural, human-induced, and technological hazards increases associated risks, particularly due to rising
population numbers, poorly regulated land use, and climate change. Although key hazards and risks have been identified
and priority issues recognised, they are not integrated into national and sector plans and policies, often resulting in a lack

=== PAGE 78 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 75
D
of preparedness. Agriculture in Fiji, mainly rain-fed and small-scale, supports over 117,000 people, primarily in rural
areas. Economic impact does not fully capture its nutritional and livelihood significance. However, agricultural livelihoods
are vulnerable to climatic extremes like cyclones, droughts, and floods.
Economic and social development level of the country and the affected population
309 Fiji’s GDP is around US$4.98 billion, with a per capita GDP of US$5,356.2. The economy is mainly driven by tourism and
agriculture with 91% of the population living near the coastline. By the end of the century, natural hazards may annually
push over 4% of the population into poverty. Cyclones result in loss of life, injuries, property damage, and disease spread.
A 100-year river flood in Fiji can lead to 12. 5% falling into poverty, with an average annual loss of $130 million attributed
to storm surges and high winds. In Fiji, impoverished remote communities face water security challenges and rely on
subsistence fishing. Climate change worsens their situation, impacting future extreme weather events. Recognized for
their vulnerability, these populations will suffer more from tropical cyclones and floods. There is a rising risk of disasters
and losses in Fiji due to increased vulnerability. Unplanned development rose by 24% between 2007 and 2015, with new
developments in hazard-prone coastal areas. Climate impacts such as floods, droughts, coastal erosion, and coral
bleaching pose significant threats to Fijian communities, the economy, and infrastructure, potentially resulting in loss of
life and displacement. Key sectors of Fiji's economy, including agriculture and tourism, are especially vulnerable to
changing climate conditions.
Absence of alternative sources of financing
310 Though Fiji has access to many global and regional donors and has been the recipient of numerous projects, either
bilateral or multinational, none have focused on establishing an end-to-end Early Warning System (EWS) in Fiji. Most
projects have been fragmented, concentrating on one or two pillars, mainly Pillar 2 (strengthening observation) and Pillar
4 (enhancing preparedness and response). This is the first project on EW4All in Fiji, and there are a few other
multinational projects in the pipeline or in their early stages that also focus on EWS, which includes Fiji (such as Weather
ready and CREWS 2.0). Directly relevant to this project, NDMO is currently leading a US$500K initiative titled "Mapping,
Assessing and Planning for Comprehensive Multi-Hazard Early Warning Capabilities for Fiji." This project aligns well with
the EWA4All Fiji component, particularly in the areas of risk management, multi-hazard early warning systems, and
capacity building. Consequently, it allocates the entire project budget of US$500K as co-financing.
Need for strengthening institutions and implementation capacity
311 However, despite efforts to improve the quality, reach, and effectiveness of an Early Warning System (EWS), there are
still gaps and challenges across four essential pillars in Fiji. These challenges stem from fragmented investments, limited
technical capacity, and a lack of coordination among key stakeholders in the EWS. To address these issues, it is necessary
to enhance observation equipment and ensure its proper use and maintenance. Additionally, there is a need to improve
the accessibility and inclusivity of early warning messages, establish community feedback mechanisms, and integrate
traditional knowledge into EWSs. The current early warning system faces challenges due to the absence of a designated
WMO Registered Alerting Authority and lack of cell broadcast implementation. The regulatory framework for mobile
manufacturers/importers to support cell broadcast is also missing. There is no automated systems in place to mitigate
impacts in the case of events with a short time frame. Certain remote areas have poor mobile coverage, hindering receipt
of warnings by fishermen at sea. Furthermore, there is no coordination stocktake among different actors working in
communities, which can lead to potential overlaps, gaps, and inefficiencies in response efforts. Coordination with other
stakeholders, including government agencies, NGOs, and community groups, can be challenging due to differing
priorities, mandates, and approaches. It is necessary to conduct studies to understand how people access and interpret
early warning messages. The findings from these studies should then be incorporated into message formats and
dissemination processes. Additionally, the lack of feedback mechanisms and surveys currently negatively impacts the
quality of warnings. Therefore, it would be beneficial to invest further in feedback mechanisms.

Vulnerability of the Country and/or Specific Vulnerable Groups, Including Gender Aspects
312 Somalia is one of the most climate-vulnerable countries in the world, with a ranking of 178 out of 182 countries on the
ND-GAIN Index 2024, and with the least capacity to respond and recover from extreme weather events.132 Somalia
consistently undergoes prevalent violence, conflict and fragility, which in turn has resulted in (and vice versa) harsh and
severe environmental conditions, affecting the depletion, use and access to natural resources and livelihoods. Moreover,
Somalia has a large number of IDPs and is one of the highest refugee-producing countries.133
Economic and Social Development Level of the Country and the Affected Population
313 Somalia is a low-income country with a fragile economy that relies largely on agriculture, livestock, remittances and
international assistance. Desertification is reducing the viability of rain-fed agriculture and livestock production.
Unemployment, particularly among youth, is alarmingly high while poverty rates are highest in rural areas.
Absence of Alternative Sources of Financing
314 Somalia has faced recurrent humanitarian crises, including droughts, famines, and displacement due to conflict. These
crises have exacerbated food insecurity, malnutrition, and displacement, with millions of Somalis reliant on humanitarian
assistance for survival. Somalia is considered the world’s fifth-poorest country134, and with ongoing and regular climate
induced disasters, Somalia’s early warning and response needs are significant, without the domestic resources to invest
effectively in MHEWS and Anticipatory Action.
Need for Strengthening Institutions and Implementation Capacity
315 In Somalia, interagency coordination gaps exist alongside overlapping mandates, resulting in poor coordination among
governmental agencies and non-governmental organisations as well as a duplication of efforts and inefficient resource
utilisation. There is a need for policy development and policy harmonisation, which means creating and enforcing
comprehensive climate policies that align with international standards. There is also the need for capacity building by
training policymakers and stakeholders to improve implementation and compliance.
Ethiopia
Vulnerability of the country and/or specific vulnerable groups, including gender aspects (for adaptation only)
316 Ethiopia is highly vulnerable to a range of climate-related hazards, including recurrent droughts, floods, landslides, and
wildfires, which are increasingly exacerbated by climate change. This vulnerability significantly impacts specific
populations, particularly women, children, and rural communities that heavily depend on agriculture for their livelihoods.
Women of reproductive age face substantial challenges due to systemic inequalities, with over 22% suffering from
chronic under-nutrition. Furthermore, more than 1.2 million children under five are affected by acute malnutrition,
illustrating the severe repercussions of climate-induced food insecurity on these vulnerable demographics. Addressing
these vulnerabilities is crucial for enhancing preparedness through effective EWSs, ensuring that critical information
reaches those most at risk, and empowering them to respond proactively to climate-related shocks.
Economic and social development level of the country and the affected population
317 Ethiopia, despite notable economic growth over recent years, remains a low-income country with a significant reliance on
agriculture, which is particularly susceptible to climate variability. Approximately 80% of the population resides in rural
areas where livelihoods are closely tied to rain-fed agriculture. Rural households are often severely impacted by climate
shocks, leading to food insecurity, displacement, and heightened poverty rates. This economic vulnerability is
compounded by limited access to essential services such as healthcare, education, and financial resources, further
exacerbating the challenges faced by these communities. As part of the feasibility preparation for the GCF-funded Multi-
Hazard EWSs (MHEWS) project, it is vital to improve resilience and support sustainable economic development by
integrating climate risk data into national and regional planning processes, thereby addressing the specific needs of the
most affected populations.

Absence of alternative sources of financing (e.g. fiscal or balance of payments gap that prevents government from
addressing the needs of the country; and lack of depth and history in the local capital market)
318 Ethiopia faces substantial fiscal constraints that hinder its ability to effectively address the extensive needs for climate
adaptation and disaster risk reduction. The country grapples with a persistent balance of payments gap, which limits the
financial resources available for critical climate resilience projects. Additionally, the depth of the local capital market is
insufficient to mobilize the necessary investments for large-scale climate initiatives. Consequently, the Ethiopian
government heavily relies on external financial support, such as that provided by the Green Climate Fund (GCF), to bridge
these funding gaps. This reliance underscores the urgent need for effective investment in EWSs, disaster preparedness,
and community resilience initiatives to mitigate the impacts of climate change on vulnerable populations as part of the
feasibility preparation process.
Need for strengthening institutions and implementation capacity
319 Ethiopia’s institutional capacity for managing climate risks and implementing EWSs requires significant strengthening.
While key institutions such as the Ethiopian Meteorological Institute (EMI) and the Ethiopian Disaster Risk Management
Commission (EDRMC) exist, they often lack the resources, coordination, and technical expertise necessary for effectively
managing multi-hazard EWSs. In the context of feasibility preparation for the GCF Early Warning for All project, there is a
critical need to support initiatives such as establishing a National Risk Data Hub for climate risk information, modernizing
and expanding hydro-meteorological observing stations, and integrating anticipatory action into emergency response and
disaster risk reduction programs. Additionally, strengthening or establishing Community-Based EWSs (CEWS) in priority
vulnerable communities is essential for ensuring that local populations are better prepared for climate-related events
and can respond effectively to emerging risks.
D.5. Country ownership (max. 500 words, approximately 1 page)
320 This project will equip countries to establish state of the art EWS which increase the resilience of the most vulnerable
communities to climate hazards. It will facilitate a paradigm shift wherein global and regional collaborations and
responsive, people centred policies will enable the production and delivery timely, targeted and contextual, community-
centred early warnings. These will be coupled with mechanisms for sustainable financial and technical support to NDMAs
and NMHSs. The project will substantively support the call of the UN Secretary General for EW4All by 2027.
321 By focusing on multiple delivery mechanisms, enhancing capacities to be able to deliver support and create a knowledge
base through national projects, the project will lead to participating countries developing timely, credible, holistic and
easily accessible climate, weather information designed to reach and equip communities with actionable and targeted
early warning. It will reduce vulnerability of communities to climate risks by supporting countries to reduce their own
exposure through timely alerts and protocols designed to reach the grassroots. Furthermore, the project will establish
links between participating countries and international financial and development institutions for sustainable financing
and support for adaptation and disaster recovery.
322 In each country, the NDA was approached with an idea note of the project to explain what the aim would be, and to
present the initial architecture of the project. There were extensive discussions and consultations with the NDA in each
country during the FP development. Furthermore, the NDA convened larger consultations with a wide range of
stakeholders including CSOs and CBOs, to anchor the project design as much as possible on ground realities. National and
regional DAEs were engaged with to establish their willingness to contribute to the design of country specific projects
(through both output 1 & 3). Where DAEs are financial institutions, these discussions and those with other lenders were
used to ascertain the potential for GCF grant funding to be used to unlock additional loans/lending through de-risking
measures.

the UNDP Somalia country office, the EW4ALL initiative is now operationalised under the leadership of the NMHEWC.

Ethiopia
Alignment with national climate strategy and frameworks
339 The GCF Early Warning for All project aligns strategically with Ethiopia's national climate and disaster management
strategies, reinforcing essential frameworks such as the NDRMP and the Climate Resilient Green Economy (CRGE)
strategy. Specifically, the Roadmap for Multi-Hazard, Impact-Based Early Warning and Early Action System (2023–2030)
provides a comprehensive plan for implementing a robust EWS that integrates IbF and anticipatory actions. The National
Framework for Climate Services, alongside the Strategic Programme and Investment Framework (SPIF), outlines priority
actions and investments needed to enhance Ethiopia’s DRM system. Additionally, the project supports Ethiopia's updated
Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC), emphasizing the integration of climate resilience measures into
development initiatives. As part of feasibility preparation, the project reinforces Ethiopia’s commitments to sustainable
development and climate adaptation by embedding EWSs into broader national and regional strategies.
Engagement with national stakeholders
340 The feasibility preparation for the GCF-funded Early Warning for All project has involved extensive engagement with
national stakeholders, coordinated through the Emergency Coordination Center (ECC) led by the EDRMC. The EW4All
Coordination Platform serves as an integrated framework to strengthen national EWSs by coordinating actions across
four key pillars: Risk Knowledge, Monitoring and Forecasting, Communication and Dissemination, and Response
Capability. This platform is designed to align stakeholders at all levels—government agencies, civil society organizations,
international partners, and local communities—ensuring that EWSs are effective, inclusive, and sensitive to the local
socio-political context. Given Ethiopia's complex landscape of socio-economic challenges, conflict dynamics,
environmental risks, and gender inequality, the EW4All platform will adopt a multi-sectoral and context-specific
approach, ensuring that early warning mechanisms are not only operationally effective but also conflict-sensitive and
gender-responsive.

341 This project will ensure a cost-effective alternative to reactive approaches to climate-related hazards that focus on ad-
hoc recovery and investment. It will significantly enhance the risk knowledge and early action capabilities of sectors and
communities and will contribute to the capacity building of relevant stakeholders. The enhanced risk knowledge will
enable stakeholders, particularly local communities and first responders, to take pro-active action based on timely and
accurate information, thereby reducing the impacts of disasters on lives, livelihoods and assets. The project will ensure a
larger spatial coverage of ibF for vulnerable regions and establish protocols, supported by national policies and
procedures, for communities to prepare for and take pre-emptive action against disasters.
342 A high expected benefit-cost ratio (BCR) on investments in strengthening the hydrological and meteorological agencies
and all partners in the MHEWS value cycle can only be achieved with a sizeable and multi-year investment which
addresses gaps in the value cycle and ensures that actionable warnings reach the last mile and those at risk being able to
respond. Improvements in MWEWS and preparedness make it possible to limit losses from hydrometeorological hazard-
induced disasters, which would not be possible without the informed use of constantly improving meteorological,
hydrological, social, behavioural and related information, which this programme will seek to do sustainably by leveraging
additional co-finance, as well as ensuring country ownership by governments that are able to fund the ongoing costs of
maintaining all elements of the MHEWS cycle.142
343 MHEWS are a public good and for under-developed countries and SIDS, the financial and technical barriers that prevent
the implementation of a reliable, robust, widely accessible and effective MHEWS for disaster preparedness and planning
can only be removed by public investment financed by grant resources from international development institutions. The
project does not entail revenue generation or cost recovery during its duration and cannot be expected to attract
investments from the private sector, which is nascent in many of the targeted counties. However, the project does plan
to engage the private sector by stimulating demand for climate information-based value-added products and services, by
engaging with the private sector particularly in telecommunications, agri-businesses, tourism and transport – with a focus
on aviation and financial services such as insurance. The level of engagement and the type of industry will be determined
by the national context. These engagements may generate some revenue and cost sharing or co-financing in the future
and could support the project’s financial sustainability beyond its proposed duration.
344 On the other hand, there is overwhelming evidence of substantial benefits of investing in weather and climate
information and DRR. Reported benefit to cost ratios are four and higher143, the socioeconomic benefits are estimated to
be at least US$ 160 billion per year144 and the net benefit of investing in the resilience of infrastructure in developing
countries would be $4.2 trillion over the lifetime of new infrastructure145. The return on investment from DRR offer
“triple dividends” from avoiding direct impact, enhancing economic potential and generating sustainable development
co-benefits.146
Efficiency and effectiveness
345 Efficiency and effectiveness will be ensured by building on existing national capacities and infrastructure across the
MHEWS value chain and leveraging investments from other donors, particularly from SOFF and CREWS. Existing
institutional capacities and linkages will be effectively used at all levels across government, non-government, private
sector – particularly telecommunications and among community based organizations. This will minimize time and costs
and provide a foundation to strengthen and enhance MHEWS to the community level.

346 Synergies between ongoing government initiatives and projects, including those supported through vertical funds will be

regional coordinating bodies (SPC, SPREP, SADC, IGAD, CCCCC, CAF etc) investments will be able to target the most critical
gaps and ensure the full MHEWS cycle is achieved, reaching as many people, businesses and communities as possible.

E.7. Monitoring, reporting and evaluation arrangements
348 Monitoring and evaluation will be at two levels, at the global project level and at the country level in each of the seven
countries. The global MEAL system will feed into overall project management and oversight, reporting as well as
knowledge management. It will prompt the global teams of experts to support national projects and to ensure a
continuous, two-way flow of information. The national MEL system will support adaptive management, reporting and
knowledge sharing at the national level.
349 Project-level monitoring and evaluation at both levels, will be undertaken in compliance with the UNDP POPP and the
UNDP Evaluation Policy. The primary responsibility for day-to-day project monitoring and implementation rests with the
respective Project Managers. The Project Managers will develop annual work plans to ensure the efficient
implementation of the project. The Project Managers will inform their respective Project Boards and the UNDP Country
Offices of any delays or difficulties during implementation, including the implementation of the M&E plan, so that the
appropriate support and corrective measures can be adopted. The Project Managers will also ensure that all project staff
maintain a high level of transparency, responsibility and accountability in monitoring and reporting project results.
350 The UNDP Bureau for Policy and Programme Support (BPPS) will support the global Project Manager through the
Technical Specialist on Climate Change Adaptation through regular meetings and oversight.
The UNDP Country Office will support their respective Project Managers as needed, including through annual supervision
missions.
351 The BPPS and the respective UNDP Country Offices are responsible for complying with UNDP project-level M&E
requirements as outlined in the UNDP Programme and Operations Policies and Procedures (POPP). Additional M&E,
implementation quality assurance, and troubleshooting support will be provided by the UNDP Regional Technical Advisor
as needed. The project target groups and stakeholders including the NDA Focal Point will be involved as much as possible
in national project-level M&E.
352 A project inception workshop will be held globally and at each country after the UNDP project document has been signed
by all relevant parties to: a) re-orient project stakeholders to the project strategy and discuss any changes in the overall
context that influence project implementation; b) discuss the roles and responsibilities of the project team, including
reporting and communication lines and conflict resolution mechanisms; c) review the results framework, re-assess
baselines as needed, and discuss reporting, monitoring and evaluation roles and responsibilities and finalize the M&E
plan; d) review financial reporting procedures and mandatory requirements, and agree on the arrangements for the
annual audit; e) plan and schedule Project Board meetings and finalize the first year annual work plan. The Project
Manager will prepare the inception report no later than one month after the inception workshop. The final inception
report will be cleared by the BPPS and the Technical Specialist on Climate Change Adaptationat the global level and the
respective UNDP Country Offices and the UNDP Regional Technical Advisor at the national level. These will be approved
by the respective Project Boards.
353 A project implementation report will be prepared for each year of project implementation at both the global and national
levels. The respective Project Managers, the BPPS and respective UNDP Country Office, and the UNDP Technical Specialist
Climate Change Adaptation and Regional Technical Advisor will provide objective input to the Annual Performance
Report (APR).
354 The global and national Project Managers will ensure that the indicators included in the project results framework are
monitored annually well in advance of the APR submission deadline and will objectively report progress in the
Development Objective tab of the APR. The annual APR will be shared with the respective Project Board and other
stakeholders. The UNDP Country Offices will coordinate the input of the NDA Focal Point and other stakeholders to the
APR. The quality rating of the previous year’s APR will be used to inform the preparation of the next APR. The final
project APR, along with the terminal evaluation report and corresponding management response, will serve as the final
project report package. The national APRs will be collated and consolidated into a global APR which will be reviewed and
shared with the global Project Board and other stakeholders for comments.

RISK ASSESSMENT AND MANAGEMENT
F.1. Risk factors and mitigations measures (max. 3 pages)
Please describe financial, technical, operational, macroeconomic/political, money laundering/terrorist financing (ML/TF), sanctions,
prohibited practices, and other risks that might prevent the project/programme objectives from being achieved. Also describe the
proposed risk mitigation measures. Insert additional rows if necessary.
For probability: High has significant probability, Medium has moderate probability, Low has negligible probability
For impact: High has significant impact, Medium has moderate impact, Low has negligible impact
Prohibited practices include abuse, conflict of interest, corruption, retaliation against whistleblowers or witnesses, as well as
fraudulent, coercive, collusive, and obstructive practices
Selected Risk Factor 1 Gaps in governance and institutional mechanism at the national level
Category Probability Impact
Governance Medium High
Description
Some countries may lack or have gaps in their NMHS and NDMA and in governance and institutional mechanisms necessary for coordinated
action required for an operational EWS, disaster preparedness and response. This is often on account of local or regional conflict and
insecurity, which is a risk to implementing the proposed activities, particularly under Output 2 of the project.
Mitigation Measure(s)
The project will work towards strengthening government structures for delivery of EWS to communities. It will simultaneously engage with
national and local agencies, including offices of pillar leads such as local societies of the IFRC, multilateral agencies and NGOs to implement
activities that are aligned with their core areas of expertise and comparative strengths. This implementation will, as far as possible, involve
government agencies and seek to build their capacities through partnerships and hand holding.
Selected Risk Factor 2 Operational delays due to cumbersome procedures
Category Probability Impact
Technical and operational Medium Medium
Description
Cumbersome procurement and administrative procedures may result in delays in procurement of critical equipment necessary to set up the
hydrometeorological observation networks and communications as well as hiring of technical expertise from outside the country.
Mitigation Measure(s)
The UNDP Country Offices will extend support to executing entities and responsible parties where necessary, including support for procuring
and importing equipment and technical expertise during project implementation. This will reduce the risk to low.
Selected Risk Factor 3 Risk of damage to equipment due to vandalism
Category Probability Impact
Governance Medium High
Description
Levels of insecurity in some participating countries may constrain the number and types of investments in observation and communications
equipment and its regular operation and maintenance. This may lead limit the gathering of observational data and dissemination of early
warnings affecting both the quality of climate information products as well as their effective communications to those in need.
Mitigation Measure(s)
The selection of equipment and its siting were done based on a comprehensive analysis of risks of vandalism and damage, keeping in mind
constraints on O&M operations. The project will site equipment in secure government owned and operated sites or on telecommunications
towers and installations where possible. The project will also utilise in-expensive IoT based community managed and operated EWS with an
emphasis on their ownership of the systems through mobilization and sensitization of local groups and leaders. The equipment will be
maintained and replaced as necessary, timing the field missions ahead of the relevant season, so that it is operational at the time when
climate hazards are most likely to occur.

Selected Risk Factor 4 Poor inter-agency coordination and collaboration
Category Probability Impact
Governance Medium High
Description
Poor coordination and cooperation both within and between government, multilateral and private agencies can reduce the collection and
sharing of observational data, the sectoral analysis of climate information, its dissemination and effective use for disaster preparedness and
response. Private telecommunication companies can be reluctant to adopt standards and share data on customers which may be required to
operationalize technologies such as cellular broadcast. Coordination and collaboration can be even more difficult for countries where climate
hazards are of a trans-boundary nature, such as floods that originate in a neighbouring country, or where communications networks in one
country overlap with another.
Mitigation Measure(s)
The project will strengthen institutional arrangements and governance mechanisms between agencies both at the national and regional level.
This will be done by leveraging the national and regional initiatives, programmes and facilities being led by the EW4All pillar leads and other
partner agencies. Where possible, policies, procedures and road-maps will be strengthened and formulated to ensure governments play a
coordinating role and ensure compliance and cooperation between agencies, including the private sector such as telecommunication
companies. This will ensure key dissemination mechanisms such as the CAP and technologies such as cellular broadcast can be deployed and
leveraged.
Selected Risk Factor 5 Poor community outreach and engagement in disaster preparedness
Category Probability Impact
Technical and operational Medium High
Description
The reach of government and non-governmental agencies to communities can constrains their ability to support communities to prepare and
plan for disasters or to build their capacities to adapt. Community level preparedness and planning is critical for effective early and
anticipatory action, particularly for marginalized and more vulnerable groups such as women, people with disabilities, elderly and households
with infants and children. This poses a significant risk to the project’s effectiveness in fragile and conflict affected countries as well as
countries with limited access to remote areas.
Mitigation Measure(s)
The analysis of hazards, exposure and vulnerabilities done in the feasibility studies identifies the regions where communities are most at risk.
This has informed the design of community engagement strategies, leveraging local actors from both within government and non-
government agencies and innovative technologies where available. The project will strengthen the capacities of relevant agencies such as
extension and health services and line departments to better equip them to support community level disaster planning and preparedness. It
will strengthen institutional linkages between sub-national agencies and community level institutions and invest in preparedness activities
and infrastructure at the village level with specific attention to vulnerable and marginalized groups.
Selected Risk Factor 6 Limited technical and financial capacities to sustain the EWS value-chain
Category Probability Impact
Technical and operational Medium Medium
Description
There is a risk that the gains made by the project are not backed up by sufficient resources, both technical and financial, to ensure the O&M
of equipment and infrastructure or to sustain the production of MHEWS, specifically IbFs and decision support systems to inform early and
anticipatory action. This is a risk to projects sustainability, particularly in poor and developing countries which have severe fiscal and technical
constraints.
Mitigation Measure(s)
The project will address this risk through a multipronged approach. The knowledge management strategy will specifically target policy
makers, presenting them with compelling evidence of financial returns from investments into the early warnings value chain, demonstrating
the savings through avoiding and mitigating the impacts of climate hazards through adaptation and early and anticipatory action. Institutional
linkages and collaborations will be established with national and regional agencies and academia to ensure ongoing and continuous support
to the NMHS and NDMA with the latest technologies and techniques. This will help steer these away from any dependence on consultancies
and one-off assignments for technical inputs. Finally, the project will strengthen existing regional financial facilities and funding mechanisms
for long term support to national governments in sustaining their MHEWS. As part of this effort, the project will also foster collaborations with
large technical firms to offset costs of data and computational facilities and technologies.

the project.

GCF POLICIES AND STANDARDS
G.1. Environmental and social risk assessment (max. 750 words, approximately 1.5 pages)
359 The UNDP Social and Environmental Screening Procedure (SESP) is provided in Annex 6 for the global project. The project
is assigned a risk category of "C" for GFC (and low risk based on the UNDP SESP). The project’s activities are mainly
focused on cooperation, dialogue, capacity building and training. The main risk of these activities is that they are not
inclusive of all stakeholders, including Indigenous peoples, women, people with disabilities and other marginalized groups
which is well-managed through project design as well as Stakeholder Engagement Plans (SEPs) and Gender Analysis and
Action Plans (GAAPs) prepared . In order to avoid these risks, Output 2 will involve extensive engagement with
communities, including vulnerable and marginalized groups. These consultations will ensure representation of and
equitable benefits and consideration to the needs of women, Indigenous groups, people with disabilities, elderly and
groups who may otherwise be culturally and economically excluded. The project recognizes the differential access to
resources, information and social roles and will proactively work towards overcoming cultural biases and other
limitations which may prevent women and marginalized groups from equitable participation and sharing of project
benefits. The project therefore embeds consultations and stakeholder engagement in its activities from project design
through implementation. Gender Analysis and Actions Plans (GAAP) , as well as Stakeholder Engagement Plans (SEP) have
been prepared, which will integrate considerations relevant for Indigenous peoples. These plans will help to ensure that
the project is inclusive of stakeholder’s needs, and that vulnerable groups access constraints and opportunities are taken
into account to ensure they can effectively benefit from the project’s activities.
360 Output 2 also has minor EWS small works activities that are being defined. These will be small-scale, such as small
hydrometeorological observation stations that carry small footprints which will need to be sited, small boreholes , or
repairs or small upgrades to buildings, such as waterproofing and installing toilets. The repairs/upgrade/installation of
these would be site-specific and contained, with limited, predictable, site-specific impacts that can be readily addressed
through standard mitigation measures. These impacts would mainly include limited pollution, waste and risks of
Occupational Health and Safety (OHS). The project excludes activities from project financing which require an ESIA/ESMP
or which would have a GCF Category A or B rating. The project has developed an Environment and Social Management
Framework (ESMF) which includes an assessment of all these risks and proposes mitigation measures, including through
an Environment and Social Code of Practice (ESCOP) which would guide the implementation of small works. There will be
no displacement of people or their livelihoods as a result of project interventions. No installation or works will be done in
sites of cultural, historical or environmental importance and as such no biodiversity impacts are expected. New
installations will be sited on government property or public areas free of encumbrances, with existing access so that
O&M operations do not require crossing private lands, biodiversity areas or other zones that would pose any impact to
the environment, workers or communities (including zones where there are ongoing conflicts). As a result of limited
numbers of staff, consultants and workers implementing project activities, there could also be some potential low risks of
Gender Based Violence (GBV)/Sexual Harassment (SH). Preventing SEAH guidance has been provided in the ESMF, as well
as guidance to prepare country-specific SEAH plans during implementation if SEAH risks (moderate or higher) are
identified.
361 In some countries, the population includes indigenous peoples. The project will not negatively impact Indigenous
Peoples. The project does not envision any small works on IP lands, and in the unlikely event this was identified during
project implementation, or any other impact to IPs identified, Indigenous Peoples Plans would need to be prepared
following the Indigenous Peoples Planning Framework (IPPF) annex in the ESMF. Nevertheless, it is important that
meaningful consultations are conducted with IP representatives during project implementation, to ensure their needs are
considered in EWs and that they are able to receive EW in a way that is meaningful to them. Guidance for consultations
and general stakeholder engagement, including specifically with IP groups, is included in the global SEP.
362

G.2. Gender assessment and action plan (max. 500 words, approximately 1 page)
363 A global Gender Analysis and Gender Action plan (GAAP) is provided in Annex 8. The project proposal emphasises gender
inclusiveness and gender responsive design of outputs and activities. It recognises the differential impacts of climate
change on women on account of the disadvantages they face in terms of representation in decision making, ownership
and access to resources, finances and information. The project also acknowledges the impact of gender roles and cultural
biases on the ability of women to prepare and plan for climate hazards and to receive timely and actionable early
warnings. The project design factors in the dependence of women on climate sensitive natural resources and their roles
in livelihoods, particularly those related to agriculture. Activities pertaining to climate change adaptation and
preparedness and response to climate mediated disasters, incorporate critical elements of gender mainstreaming and
equity.
G.3. Financial management and procurement (max. 500 words, approximately 1 page)
364 The financial management and procurement of this project will be guided by UNDP financial rules and regulations.
Further guidance is outlined in the financial resources management section of the UNDP Programme and Operations
Policies and Procedures (POPP), which also includes comprehensive procurement policies as outlined in the ‘Contracts
and Procurement’ section. These policies outline formal procurement standards and guidelines across each phase of the
procurement process and apply to all procurements in UNDP.
365 National projects will be implemented following the Direct Implementation Modality (DIM) by UNDP country offices. The
DIM project management and implementation approach takes full responsibility for executing a project, with no further
delegation of the implementation to a government entity or other partner.
366 If the NGO or private sector to be engaged as a Responsible Parties they will be engaged through Responsible Party
Agreements. Each Responsible party who will be engaged to support the implementation of project, following the
Framework for Cash Transfers to Implementing Partners (part of the Harmonized Approach to Cash Transfers - HACT). All
projects will be audited following the UNDP financial rules and regulations noted above and applicable audit guidelines
and policies. The HACT framework consists of four processes: (1) macro assessments; (2) micro assessments; (3) cash
transfers and disbursements; and (4) assurance activities. Assurance activities include planning, periodic on-site reviews
(spot checks), programmatic monitoring, scheduled audits and special audits. Weaknesses identified during micro-
assessments will require actions to addresses the gaps. When a spot check finds that the gaps are not addressed it will
mean that the level of assurance activities will have to remain higher and modalities of engaging with that implementing
partner will have to be reviewed if necessary, as described here.
367 The project will be audited in accordance with UNDP policies and procedures on audits, informed by and together with
any specific requirements agreed in the AMA established between GCF and UNDP, signed on 16 of March 2023 and
made effective in May 3, 2023. According to the current audit policies, UNDP will be appointing the auditors. Scheduled
audits are performed during the programme cycle as per UNDP assurance/audit plans, based on the implementing
partner's risk rating and UNDP’s guidelines. A scheduled audit is used to determine whether the funds transferred to the
implementing partner were used for the appropriate purpose and in accordance with the work plan. A scheduled audit
can consist of a financial audit or an internal control audit.
368 All GCF resources will be provided to the responsible party, less any agreed cost recovery amount. Under UNDP’s direct
implementation modality, UNDP advances cash funds on a quarterly basis to the responsible party for the
implementation of agreed and approved programme activities, in accordance with UNDP standard policies-. The
responsible party reports back expenditure via a financial report on quarterly basis to UNDP. Any additional requirements
will be in accordance with the AMA as and when it is agreed. A draft procurement plan (which will be further discussed
and revised prior to UNDP Project Document signature) is provided in Annex XIII.
