Appendices
Appendix 1: Climate hazards and associated risks (impacts, exposures and vulnerabilities) in participating countries
Antigua and Barbuda
369 Antigua and Barbuda is on the frontline of climate change, facing a range of intensifying climatic hazards that threaten
their very existence. Ranked as the 5th highest in the World Risk Index in 2023, the islands are exposed to an array of
baseline hazards, including hurricanes, extreme rainfall, droughts, and rising sea levels. These risks are exacerbated by
the islands' geographical position and limited land area, making them particularly vulnerable to the cascading and
compounding impacts of climate change.
370 Hurricanes pose the most significant threat in Antigua and Barbuda, with the country having faced 15 hurricanes and 14
tropical storms between 1995 and 2021. The devastation from Hurricanes Irma and Maria in 2017 serving as stark
reminders of the destructive power of these storms. These hurricanes not only caused widespread destruction of
infrastructure but also disrupted essential services such as healthcare, electricity, water, and waste management. In
Barbuda, nearly 90% of the island’s infrastructure was destroyed, rendering the island temporarily uninhabitable. The
increasing intensity of these storms, fueled by climate change, is expected to lead to even more catastrophic events in
the future. Moreover, hurricane intensity is anticipated to increase by 18% for category 4 and 5 hurricanes over the next
30 years, based on General Circulation Models (GCMs)149. By 2030, the general building stock in Antigua and Barbuda,
using RCP 8.5, will experience direct losses from storm surges and wind in the amount of USD 451 million for a historic
event, USD 4.03 billion for a 1:100-year event, and USD 9.4 billion for a maximum credible event (MCE). 150
371 Droughts, while less dramatic than hurricanes, pose a persistent and growing threat to the islands. Historically, droughts
have led to severe water shortages, impacting utilities, agriculture, and even leading to economic crises, such as the need
to import water during the drought of 1983-1985. With projections indicating a 30%-50% reduction in annual rainfall by
2090, droughts are expected to become more severe, further straining the already limited water resources. 151 Under the
RCP 4.5 scenario, models predict 9 drought years for the period 2040–2069, representing an 8% increase in drought
severity152.
372 The low-lying geography of Antigua and Barbuda makes it particularly susceptible to land loss due to sea-level rise, which
presents a long-term existential threat to Antigua and Barbuda. Projections indicate that by 2060, Antigua could lose
approximately 20 km² of land, while Barbuda could lose 15 km². This loss of land, combined with rising sea surface
temperatures and increased ocean acidification, threatens not only the islands' ecosystems but also the livelihoods of
those who depend on the sea, particularly in the tourism and fishing sectors. 153
373 The interplay of these climatic hazards creates a highly vulnerable environment for Antigua and Barbuda, where the
effects of one event can exacerbate the impacts of another. For example, a severe hurricane can lead to flooding, which
disrupts essential services and exacerbates water shortages caused by droughts. The cascading effects of these hazards,
coupled with the islands' low-lying topography and concentration of economic activities along the coast, underscore the
urgent need for comprehensive climate adaptation strategies.
374 Local stakeholders have identified several key areas that require urgent attention to strengthen the islands' resilience.
The first is the need for improved observation and forecasting systems, particularly for marine hazards. Given the islands'
exposure to ocean-related hazards such as storm surges and coastal erosion, there is a critical need for accurate and
locally specific advisories to protect vulnerable groups. The built environment is another area of concern, as many
buildings are not resilient to high-intensity storms due to the cost of building to code and the existence of outdated

375 The tourism sector, which employs a large percentage of the population and is heavily concentrated in exposed coastal
areas, also requires targeted preparatory actions. International visitors, who may lack local knowledge of climate hazards,
are particularly vulnerable, highlighting the need for better integration of the tourism sector into the islands' Multi-
Hazard EWSs (MHEWS) and Anticipatory Action systems. Finally, the island of Barbuda, still recovering from the
devastating impacts of Hurricane Irma, has been flagged as a key focus area for improving preparedness and response

Ecuador
376 Due to a combination of political, geographic, and social factors, Ecuador is recognized as vulnerable to climate change
impacts, ranking 115th out of 185 countries in the 2021 ND-GAIN Index154. When coupled with a low readiness score, this
makes Ecuador highly susceptible to climate-related impacts. These impacts, such as droughts, floods, and landslides,
undermine development and reduce the availability of natural resources, affecting the majority of the population. This
vulnerability was evident during the droughts of 2023155 and 2024156, as well as the floods of 2016157, 2023158, and
2024159.
377 Ecuador’s climate is highly diverse due to its location on the equator and its varied topography, which includes the
Amazon rainforest, the Andes mountains, and the Pacific coast.
378 From 1960 to 2010, Ecuador experienced increases in temperature as well as spatial and seasonal variations in rainfall
across its territory. The observed average temperature increase was 1.4°C, with maximum temperatures rising by 1.0°C
and minimum temperatures increasing by 1.1°C in the Galapagos Islands160. These changes varied across the country’s
regions, leading to impacts such as: (i) approximately 40% loss of glacier cover on the Antisana, Carihuayrazo, Cotopaxi,
and Chimborazo volcanoes; (ii) severe droughts affecting 66.7% of agricultural areas and 53.7% of livestock areas
(pastures); and (iii) extreme rainfall increasing the floodable surface area by 15.9%, affecting 49.5% of the population.
379 Projections foresee changes in the frequency and magnitude of both average and extreme precipitation and temperature
values. By the 2090s, average temperatures in Ecuador are projected to rise significantly, potentially increasing by 3.5°C
to 4.0°C under the highest emissions pathway (RCP8.5), compared to the baseline of 1986–2005161. Annual precipitation
is expected to decrease in the Amazon (by 2–6%) but increase along the coast and in the mountain areas under the
highest emissions pathway by the 2090s162. Intense precipitation is also expected to rise across the country, especially in
the central mountain region, with increases of up to 50 mm for the average largest 1-day precipitation163.
380 Floods are the most frequent hydro-meteorological disaster in Ecuador and rank second in terms of casualties, with
landslides, storms, and droughts also contributing significantly. According to the Desinventar database164, there has been
an increase in both the number of events and deaths over the past 40 years, although with significant fluctuations. The
rise in the intensity and frequency of these extreme climatic events has caused economic damages and losses to goods

climatic events will continue to cause economic and non-economic losses to goods, services, and human well-being167.
Fiji
382 Historical Climate Trends: According to the NextGen Projections report168, Fiji has warmed up by 0.7 degrees relative to
the pre-industrial baseline of 1850-1900, up to the period of 2011-2020. In Fiji, observed and projected warming shows
that 2°C of global warming corresponds to 1.2 to 1.9°C in Fiji. The temperatures in Fiji have increased at a faster rate in
recent decades, as shown by commonly used baselines (WMO – 1981 to 1991, AR5 – 1986 to 2005, AR6 – 1995 to 2014,
and 2011 to 2020). The strongest increase has been in daily maximum temperatures (around 0.2°C per decade) and a
similar increase in daily minimum temperatures (around 0.1°C per decade). There are no significant trends in gridded
rainfall datasets for the entire region of Fiji including surrounding oceans. Historical observations show large year-to-year
variability in rainfall with no significant trends since 1960. The average of all climate models considered shows no
significant change in annual rainfall for Fiji between the pre-industrial baseline of 1850-1900 to the more recent
baselines.169
383 Projected changes in climate: Projections for Fiji are presented for a range of ‘global warming levels’ (defined as the
warming of the global average temperature since the pre-industrial era), including the 1.5°C and 2°C limits from the Paris
Agreement. The range of possible change is larger under higher global warming levels compared to lower levels.170
384 Temperatures: Historical and projected changes in temperatures (relative to 1850 – 1900) are:
- There is a warming by 0.7°C up to 2011-2020.
- By 2030, the warming is 1.2°C regardless of the emission pathway.
- By 2050, the warming is 1.3°C (RCP2.6) to 1.9°C (RCP8.5).
- By 2070, the warming is 1.3°C (RCP2.6) to 2.5°C (RCP8.5).
385 According to the World Bank report, based on the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) models,
under the medium warming scenario (RCP4.5), Fiji is projected to experience a warming of 0.9°C by 2040-2059 and 1.3°C
by 2080-2099 and under the high warming scenario (RCP8.5), the projected warming is 1.3°C and 2.7°C, respectively.
386 The Fifth Assessment Report (AR5) of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) projections in rainfall are
less certain with a high degree of variability which indicates that average annual rainfall may remain the same, but there
will be increase in the intensity for extreme rainfall events.171 The NextGen Report states that future changes in rainfall
are uncertain but could range from wetter to drier, depending on the South Pacific Convergence Zone (SPCZ). The SPCZ is
one of the main climate drivers in the south Pacific and is influenced by the presence of El Niño and La Niña.

387 Southwest Pacific tropical cyclone (TC) activity projection for a 2°C global warming indicates a likely decrease in the total
number of TCs, and a possible increase in the frequency of severe (category 4-5) TCs. The projected increase in average
TC intensity, combined with sea level rise and increases rainfall rate would increase TC impacts.
388 Resulting Impacts: Fiji is considered a high-risk country due to its vulnerability to natural hazards, ranking 75th out of 193
countries in the World Risk Report 2023. The country faces significant impacts from TCs and floods, with annual asset
losses exceeding F$500 million, reaching over 5% of the GDP. In extreme cases like a 100-year fluvial flood, losses could
surpass F$2 billion, affecting the transport and building sectors the most. Droughts, particularly during El Niño events,
have led to reduced crop production and the need for emergency water and food supplies in Fiji. Climate change poses a
threat to food security, especially in coastal areas impacted by sea level rise and salinity intrusion. Traditional crops
exhibit more resilience to climate change than non-traditional ones, but staples like rice, taro, and yams remain
vulnerable. Fiji's limited capacity to manage and adapt to climate risks contributes to health risks and increased poverty
rates. Natural hazards like TCs and floods annually push around 25,700 people into poverty, disproportionately affecting
communities reliant on subsistence fishing and facing water security challenges. Changing weather patterns also threaten
sectors like agriculture and tourism, critical to Fiji's economy, as evidenced by the increasing impact of 124 natural
hazards over the past 37 years, with TCs, floods, and earthquakes being the most frequent occurrences.
Chad
389 Between 1971 and 2022, 62 natural disasters were recorded in Chad, of which 68 percent (42 events) occurred since
2000 (EM-DAT, 2024). Successive droughts have affected the food security and livelihoods of households across large
swathes of the country, with 1.5 million people affected in 1981-85, and 2.4 million people affected in 2009-2010. The
most recent drought in 2022 affected 2.1 million people while floods in the same year rendered 121,088 people
homeless. Floods and droughts have also been associated with outbreaks of disease, and with undernutrition. Together,
these disasters led to a total of 10,556 recorded deaths, of which two thirds were a result of viral or bacterial disease
epidemics such as cholera, meningitis and measles.
390 Over the past 10 years, IFRC has launched 18 Disaster Relief Emergency Fund (DREF) operations supporting the national
Red Cross society in Chad; and raised a further 30 emergency appeals to mobilise resources to respond to 21
emergencies, targeting 5.8 million people affected by emergencies.
391 Studies have shown a continuous increase in temperatures, as well as increased variability in rainfall in the subregion
since the 1990s. After a sequence of wet years covering the 1950s and 1960s, followed by a sequence of dry years in the
1970s and especially dry years in the 1980s, inter-annual variations have become more irregular since the 1990s, though
with relatively better rainfall. Overall precipitation in Chad has been above average over several years since the 1990s,
particularly in the Sahelian zone, but with variability in its distribution over the year. The spatial distribution of
precipitation has changed, with the retreat of the 300 mm and the 1,200 mm isohyets.
392 Air temperature is expected to increase by 2.1°C to 4.3°C (very likely range) by 2080. Relative to pre-industrial levels, the
median temperature increase from climate models in Chad is 2.1°C in 2030, 2.6°C in 2050, and 3.5°C in 2080 under
RCP6.0. The number of very hot days per year is also expected to increase across the country with a high degree of
certainty. For the RCP6.0 scenario, the median of the multiple models (averaged over the entire country) predicts 17
additional very hot days per year in 2030, 31 additional days in 2050 and 49 additional days in 2080, compared to 2000.
In some parts of the country, particularly in the center, this equates to over 300 very hot days per year by 2080.
393 Projections of precipitation and variations in rainfall for 2030, 2050 and 2100 vary greatly, according to the country’s
zones owing to the high natural variability from year to year and high level of uncertainty and differences between
models. The more conservative models would lead to a reduction in precipitation while the models with higher emissions
driving higher global temperature increases suggest higher precipitation, with higher variability. Critically, all models
project more variability in precipitation than the pre-1980 situation.
394 Chad remains among the poorest and least developed countries in the world and is ranked 119th of 125 countries of the
global hunger index 2023, with a level of hunger classified as serious. A combination of high poverty, frequent conflicts,
and the risk of both droughts and floods have placed Chad as the lowest ranked country overall on the ND-GAIN index,
with a score of 27.0.

=== PAGE 112 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 109
395 With rain-fed agriculture accounting for almost 46% of GDP in 2019, and 77% of the labour force working in agriculture,
the food production and livelihood systems in Chad are highly dependent on climatic factors, particularly rainfall patterns
and distribution. The effects of high temperatures, and of hunger, are more acute for children, the elderly, and those
with chronic diseases.
396 Chad also faces severe environmental degradation, exemplified by the drying up of Lake Chad, increased desertification,
declining fish stocks, the disappearance of certain animal and plant species, and soil degradation (National Adaptation
Plan, 2022). Increased competition for access to pasture and water, soil depletion and lower agricultural productivity
have the potential to exacerbate existing conflict factors or contribute to new forms of dispute.
397 The proposed project aims to provide technical support and capacity building at national, institutional level to ensure
essential climate services can be delivered on a sustainable basis. Improved data on vulnerability and risk, knowledge
management, governance of multi-hazard EWSs and disaster preparedness/disaster management will be improved at
national and sub-national levels. The intervention addresses the fact that people’s information needs are not being met,
in the face of changing climate patterns with increased exposure to the impacts of droughts and floods, where they can
no longer rely solely on traditional knowledge and experience. The project will equip communities with relevant and
timely risk education, training and advice on adaptation and preparedness measures and early warning information to
reduce both the loss of life and the economic impact of disasters. It will support the piloting, and integration of early
action protocols by WFP and the Red Cross, into national systems and will engage with communities on their needs in
terms of information, preparedness and disaster management to ensure these processes are inclusive, needs-based and
people-centered.
Ethiopia
398 Ethiopia's climate varies significantly across its regions, classified into three primary zones based on seasonal rainfall
patterns. The northern and central western areas experience a single rainy season, with peak precipitation occurring in
July and August. The southern areas are characterized by two distinct rainy seasons: a short rainy period from September
to November and a long rainy period from March to May. The eastern and central parts experience two rainy periods: a
spring season from February to May and a summer rainy season from June to September (Paleoclimate Research
Institute, 2021). The variability in Ethiopia's rainfall is influenced by large-scale climatic phenomena such as the El Niño-
Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and sea surface temperatures (SSTs) in the Indian and Pacific oceans. SSTs, with their gradual
variations, affect long-term rainfall patterns and are crucial for improving the accuracy of regional-scale climate
predictions (World Meteorological Organization, 2022)
399 Climate change poses a significant threat to Ethiopia’s development, exacerbating existing vulnerabilities. The country
faces high impacts from natural hazards and increasing climate variability, which threaten its development goals.
Ethiopia's ambitious reform agenda aims to address these challenges amidst conflict and inflation. Balancing
development needs with climate adaptation and mitigation efforts is crucial for ensuring sustainable growth (World Bank
Group, 2023).
400 Ethiopia is committed to a green development path, adopting various policies, strategies, and plans to guide its climate
interventions. The legal framework for climate action includes specific sectoral responsibilities and coordination
mechanisms. However, gaps and overlaps in institutional mandates require further refinement. Ethiopia's climate change
targets and commitments are integrated into public expenditure management, with efforts to mainstream climate action
across sectors and levels of government (World Bank Group, 2023).
401 Climate change impacts various sectors in Ethiopia, including water, agriculture, energy, transport, and urban
development. The country faces significant water challenges, with variable and unpredictable rainfall affecting millions of
people. Essential adaptation measures include improving storage efficiency and integrated watershed management. The
agricultural sector must become more productive and climate-resilient, while energy, transport, and urban infrastructure
need to be adapted to withstand climate impacts. Additionally, diversifying the economy through mining and tourism can
enhance resilience (World Bank Group, 2023).

=== PAGE 113 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 110
402 Climate change has profound implications for Ethiopia's macroeconomic stability and poverty levels. Rising temperatures
and increased rainfall variability threaten economic growth and exacerbate poverty. Structural reforms are crucial to
expanding fiscal space and enabling private sector participation in climate adaptation. Managing residual risks and
mobilizing external finance are essential for addressing climate impacts. Supporting the most vulnerable populations
through targeted interventions is critical to building resilience and ensuring equitable development (World Bank Group,
2023).
403 Ethiopia faces significant economic losses from various climate hazards. Droughts cause substantial economic damage,
with a drought event having a 1-in-5 year return period leading to losses exceeding US$1 billion, and a 1-in-100 year
drought event resulting in losses of over US$3 billion. Flooding also has a severe impact on GDP, with a flood event with a
25-year return period causing a 3.3% deviation in GDP baselines, and a 100-year flood leading to a 7% deviation.
Additionally, heat stress results in significant losses due to its impact on labor productivity and livestock yields.
Infrastructure damage, particularly to roads and bridges, can incur annual costs of up to US$755 million under certain
scenarios. These economic impacts highlight the urgent need for effective climate adaptation and mitigation strategies in
Ethiopia (World Bank Group, 2023). The country faces critical challenges, including ethnic conflicts and climate-related
risks such as droughts and floods, which impact agriculture and water resources. Effective climate services and EWSs are
essential for enhancing resilience (Food and Agriculture Organization, 2021).
Somalia
404 Somalia is one of the most climate-vulnerable countries in the world. Somalia is ranked 178 out of 182 countries on the
ND-GAIN Index 2024, with the least capacity to respond and recover from extreme weather events.172 Located in the
Horn of Africa, Somalia extends south of the Equator northward to the Gulf of Aden, between sub-Saharan Africa and the
Middle East. As a predominately arid and semi-arid country with a hot desert climate173, the country is susceptible to
both droughts and flash floods. Prolonged dry seasons result in water scarcity, reduced grazing land, reduced livestock
production, livestock perishes, reduced agricultural productivity, food insecurity, and ultimately, famine and the loss of
human life.174 Somalia’s chronic climate-associated shocks, including cycles of floods, droughts, and locust infestation, are
compounded by increased conflict and insecurity, and have aggravated the nation’s growth and slowed the transition
from fragility. Climate change has exacerbated this vulnerability by increasing the frequency, persistence and intensity of
droughts in Somalia.175
405 Historical and projected climate change impacts in Somalia are drought and flood, although Somalia is also affected by
cyclones and coastal flooding is also classified as being high.176 Daily temperature maximums have increased over the last
two decades177 and are projected to continue over the next decade.178 The very southern areas of Somalia are projected
to experience extreme heat, and the southern and some parts of the northern areas are projected to experience very
high heat.179 Climate change projections suggest that the duration, frequency and intensity of droughts will increase by
the end of the 21st Century under all scenarios and that drought areas will increase by 16 per cent, 36 per cent and 54
per cent under increasing Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs) (2.6, 4.6, 8.5 respectively).180 At the same time,

higher rainfall and runoff are expected across the various climate scenarios, leading to increased flash flooding.181 The
frequency and intensity of heavy precipitation events are projected to increase with potential impacts of flooding and soil
erosion.182
406 Drought is a critical issue for Somalia, which disparately affects nomadic and agro-pastoral communities who are more
vulnerable to such droughts. During 2015 – 2022, 6.1 million people were affected by the drought, and 760,000 - 1.2
million people were displaced by drought.183 However, the following year of 2023 saw a further 468,000 people impacted
by flood, including 247,000 displaced people.184 Somalia experiences regular river floods and flash flooding that result in
major economic impacts and damage, as well as many human casualties, with riverine flooding typically occurring along
the Juba and Shabelle Rivers in southern Somalia and flash flooding tending to occur in the north along intermittent
watercourses.185 Yet, intense rainfall events and subsequent floods have become more frequent, resulting in water runoff
on the earth's surface, washing away fertile soil and causing widespread devastation. Most recently, the 2023 Deyr flood
has been reportedly the worst flood Somalia has faced, resulting in total damages of US$126.6 million and total losses of
$49.5 million across sixteen districts, mostly affecting agriculture, livestock, and WATSAN and transport.186 Around 2.48
million people were affected, with over 1.2 million displaced from their homes. 187 The floods also resulted in the loss of
188 lives.188 Cyclones, such as Cyclone Sagar (2018) and coastal inundation, tend to affect northern Somalia’s Somaliland
and Puntland regions189 rather than the southern areas.

409 Under SSP3-7.0, projected precipitation patterns show increased regional variability by mid-century and drier dry seasons
nationally. Annual precipitation is expected to rise by 14.48 mm from Cambodia's 1995–2014 reference period over
2020–2039. Conversely, a decrease of 11.27 mm is projected over 2040–2059, with southern and eastern provinces
seeing the most significant increases and northern areas experiencing the greatest decreases in annual precipitation.
410 Climate change will likely exacerbate Cambodia's vulnerability to extreme weather events such as floods and droughts,
which can damage infrastructure, disrupt agriculture, and lead to food insecurity. Rising temperatures and changing
precipitation patterns may affect water resources and biodiversity, threatening ecosystems and livelihoods—additionally,
sea-level rise risks coastal areas, potentially displacing communities and impacting the nation's economic stability.

Appendix 3: Eligibility criteria for project Outputs and Activities
The proposals should meet the requirements of the EW4All initiative (Sendai framework Target G). They should have a strong rationale describing the circumstances that
justify using this programmatic approach. The proposals should also be closely aligned with national strategies and policies based on the national climate investment
priorities.
The proposals should be designed to satisfy the following criteria:
1. They should have a clearly defined governance structure for decision-making and ensuring country ownership. This structure should be compatible with the global
project structure and organization to ensure smooth coordination and collaboration at the global level and with other participating countries throughout the
duration of the programme.
2. The outputs of the proposal must be closely aligned with the activities listed under Output 2 of the global funding proposal. This will directly influence the design
of the log-frame of the proposal which must be compatible with the logical framework of the global funding proposal.
3. The proposal design process must include comprehensive engagement with government agencies and national, regional as well as global focal points of the four
EW4All pillar leads. All these partners must be facilitated to contribute to proposal design and given an opportunity to weigh in on the proposed activities. This
consultative process must ensure the respective governments retain full ownership of the design process.
4. The support of multilateral agencies and non-governmental agencies should be ensured for countries with challenges emanating from fragility and conflict.
Proposals designed for FCAS states should demonstrate appropriate governance arrangements and mechanisms to implement proposed activities.
5. The proposal should meet the reporting requirements for both physical and financial reporting.
6. The proposal needs to be fully compatible with the monitoring, evaluation and learning system and knowledge management framework provided in the global
funding project.
7. The projects should demonstrate sustained impact of investments on a continued basis and should specifically provide for the development of an Operations and
Maintenance plan in the initial period of implementation.
8. The proposal should adhere to the legal arrangements and frameworks of the global project and all contractual structures should assure continued operations of
the sub-project.
9. The proposal should demonstrate ownership of the respective country government to take onboard and absorb the investments proposed. It should also
demonstrate financial and economic sustainability and cost efficiency.
10. The proposal should be compliant with environmental and social safeguards and ensure environmental and social risks are within the GCF risk category “C” or low
risk.

=== PAGE 140 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 137
H
11. The proposal must be designed in accordance with the GCF template for funding proposals including all relevant annexes.
The criteria for eligibility of country proposals are based on the following principles. These are closely aligned with the GCF investment criteria.
1. Impact potential: Following criteria will be used to determine the project’s impact potential
a. The project must clearly set out the specific risks and vulnerabilities, under current and future conditions of climate change, that the project aims to address,
articulating a clear causal narrative between specific activities and their objective of reducing vulnerability or climate risk. Projects that include arguments that are
well evidenced and quantified using reliable data sources and information will be prioritized.
b. The project must clearly describe the adaptation benefit that is expected to be generated by the implementation of the project activities.
c. The project must align to GCF adaptation result areas.
2. Paradigm shift potential: The proposal should demonstrate its potential to catalyze impact beyond a one-off project investment by:
a. Clearly describing how the project outcome will be sustainable in the long run through securing additional public and/or private financing and building the capacity
of national institutions to implement similar activities without GCF funding.
b. Demonstrating the potential of being replicated elsewhere in the same country or other countries in region.
c. Promoting innovation such as, through the development and/or adoption of new technology or approaches which can contribute to more accurate forecasts,
improve dissemination of and access to early warning information or allow communities to set up autonomous early warning and alarm systems.
d. Promoting sharing of knowledge and learning within and with other countries and contribute to the global project knowledge sharing.
3. Sustainable development potential: The proposals should demonstrate sustainable development potential by identifying at least one positive co-benefit from the
following with associated indicators.
a. Economic co-benefits –explicitly aim at poverty reduction.
b. Social co-benefits – human health and social development through improved food and nutrition security and reduced loss of life resulting from the impact of
extreme weather events.
c. Environmental co-benefits –improved ecosystem services and biodiversity.
4. Gender: The project must meet the gender criterion independently of the environmental, social and economic co-benefits. The project must fall under the UN
Gender Equality Marker 2 or 3 .

=== PAGE 141 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 138
H
5. Needs of the Recipient: The proposal must meet the need of the recipient by :
a. Overcoming barriers related to technical, institutional and/or financial barriers to meeting the objectives of the four pillars of Multi Hazard Early Warning Systems
as described in the Early Warnings for All Executive Action Plan.
6. The project must strengthen the capacity of National Meteorological and Hydrological Services and National Disaster Management Agencies institutions to deliver
effective MHEWS, enhance coordination and improve governance.
7. Country Ownership: The project must demonstrate alignment with national priorities climate priorities as reflected in nationally determined contributions (NDCs),
national adaptation plans (NAPs) and/or national disaster risk reduction plans. It must also demonstrate stakeholder engagement in developing the project,
including consultation with relevant stakeholders among government and civil society organizations and with climate vulnerable communities across all relevant
climate related hazards. Finally, the project must demonstrate engagement with national designated authorities (NDAs) in developing the project.
8. Efficiency and Effectiveness: To demonstrate efficiency and effectiveness the project should demonstrate that grants from GCF are being used to offset the
incremental cost of climate resilient investments, provide targeted climate resilient technical assistance, or for non-revenue generating outputs and non-market
elements. By blending grants from GCF with additional grants and/or loans in order to augment the volume of financing available for strengthening MHEWS,
disaster response and adaptation and better tailor concessionally to achieve transformative investments which would otherwise not proceed.
In addition to these criteria, the project must have a framework to manage environmental and social risks and impacts of the activities through the design of and
implementation of an Environmental and Social Management Framework (ESMF). The ESMF must adhere to compliance benchmarks UNDP as its AE, as per the terms set
forth in the AMA.

II. Summary of the Secretariat’s assessment
2 .1 Programme background
3.
The Multi-country Project Advancing Early Warnings for All is an intervention aimed at
promoting climate-resilience among vulnerable communities in Antigua and Barbuda,
Cambodia, Chad, Ecuador, Ethiopia, Fiji, and Somalia, by helping to institute relevant policies
and governance mechanisms for end-to-end MHEWS, establishing early warning system (EWS)
infrastructure and setting up systems for its long-term operation, and supporting local
capacities in the generation and dissemination of early-warning products. The objective of the
project is to strengthen the resilience of vulnerable communities in the participating countries
through enhancing production of actionable multi-hazard early warnings and impact-based
forecasts, strengthening of communication and last-mile dissemination channels, and building
capacity for the effective use of early warnings and advisories for early and anticipatory action,
with a view to reaching 80 per cent of the most vulnerable communities in the targeted seven
co untries.
4.
The project’s seven target countries face growing disaster risk resulting from increasing
prevalence and severity of different types of hazardous events, which pose adverse impacts for
both the social and natural systems in the countries, including exacerbated food, water, health
and livelihood insecurity, and infrastructure and economic losses. The countries are faced with
extremely high levels of vulnerability to climate change, with limited readiness to access
knowledge, or technical and financial capacity to build the resilience of communities and
climate-proof their social and economic infrastructure.

5.
The project will overcome these challenges by accelerating the development of EW4All
projects in the participating countries, enhancing the enabling conditions for the
implementation of EW4All actions that meet each participating country’s needs, and rolling out
EW4All investment activities in the seven countries based on the Climate Information and Early
Warning System (CIEWS) paradigm shift and EW4All target G (Sendai Target G) as selection
criteria. It will support the countries to establish and sustain EWS infrastructure, set up systems
for its long-term operation, expand the coverage of end-to-end MHEWS and support local
capacities in the generation and dissemination of early-warning products, and help institute
re levant policies and governance mechanisms for end-to-end MHEWS.
6.
The project is requesting USD 103.25 million of GCF financing. The total cost of the
project, including co-financing, is USD 114.59 million, with co-financing primarily in the form of
cash and in-kind grants from the governments of the participating countries, EW4All pillar
leads, and the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP). The programme will also
receive parallel financing of USD 40.10 million from the Systematic Observations Financing
Fa cility (SOFF).
7.
In terms of environmental and social safeguards (ESS), this proposal has been
categorized as environmental and social (E&S) risk category C. The review by the Secretariat
confirms the E&S risk category assigned by the AE.

III. Assessment of performance against investment criteria
Scale: High
3. 1 Impact potential
12.
Currently, one-third of the world’s population, communities in Africa, least developed
countries and small island developing states being particularly affected, lacks comprehensive
coverage by early warning systems. At the launch of the EW4All Initiative in March 2022, United
Nations Secretary General Antonio Guterres called on all governments, financial institutions,
and civil society to support this crucial effort to ensure that every person on Earth is protected
by early warning systems by 2027.
13.
The proposal presents a robust climate change context and demonstrates how the
ambitious EW4All targets can be achieved through an integrated and comprehensive global
project that supports the establishment of bespoke country-led enhancements to MHEW) in the
target countries. All seven countries that are targeted by the project are faced with significant
climate variability and change, affecting livelihoods, food security, and economic stability. Since
the 1970s, extreme weather events have led to agricultural losses, food crises, water scarcity,
flooding, and environmental degradation. The countries face a wide range of climate risks and
ha zards, including:
(a)
Hurricanes, extreme rainfall, droughts, and rising sea levels in Antigua and Barbuda;
(b)
Floods, extreme heat and longer droughts in Chad;
(c)
Increased intensity and frequency of extreme and slow-onset climatic events such as
melting of glacier cover, increased variations in sea-surface temperature, increased
floods and intensified droughts in Ecuador;
(d)
More frequent intense temperatures and droughts, increased frequency and intensity of
extreme rainfall events, more severe cyclones and increased floods, flash floods and
landslides, sea level rise, and increased storm surges and coastal erosion in Fiji;
(e)
More erratic rainfall, prolonged dry spells and worsening drought conditions, wild land
and forest fires, and intensified rainfall events leading to severe flooding, land and
mudslides in Ethiopia;
(f)
Exacerbated flooding and drought risks resulting from more intense rains, a delayed
rainy season and longer dry seasons, unexpected dry periods during the rainy season,
and untimely rains in Cambodia; and
(g)
Drought, floods, cyclones and extensive coastal flooding in Somalia.
14.
The project seeks to support the countries to address these climate challenges by
harnessing the crucial role that climate information and early warning play in enabling
individuals, communities, and organizations to take appropriate measures to minimize the

=== PAGE 154 ===
GCF/B.41/02/Add.06
Page 154
potential impact of the disasters that the climate hazards would create. The project aims to
achieve this by supporting concrete investment in infrastructure and systems needed to
observe weather events, forecast climate hazards and provide vulnerable communities and
public and private sector decision makers with advance notice of the potential hazards in a way
that would be timely enough to enable them to prepare and respond before the hazards occur,
an d thereby save lives and livelihoods and reduce damage and losses.
15.
The project will support at least 26.34 million direct beneficiaries and 51.66 million
indirect beneficiaries. It would effectively increase climate-change resilience among this large
number of people (at least 80 per cent of the population) across the seven countries by
providing technical assistance, implementation support for installation and operation of early
warning infrastructure and systems (component 1), and support for strengthening of climate
information and early warning governance and coordination frameworks and processes in the
countries (component 2). These interventions are all vital in ensuring that the countries attain
the kind of climate information and early warning systems that will be effective and sustainable
in supporting communities and businesses to undertake adequate anticipatory action in
response to the threats that climate hazards pose to their lives, livelihoods and social and
eco nomic systems and infrastructure.
16.
The project will specifically support adaptation and resilience-building across seven
core areas for local climate resilience-building in the seven countries: climate change-adapted
agriculture, forestry, agroforestry, water and health, energy efficiency, renewable energies, and
climate-resilient infrastructure and coastal areas (Antigua and Barbuda, Fiji and Somalia). The
gra nt finance will cover additional costs of public early warning investments.
17.
Within the context of majority of these countries, where a significant percentage of the
population (over 80 percent in Ethiopia, Chad and Somalia) derive their livelihoods from
climate-sensitive sectors such as rain-fed, subsistence agriculture, access to climate information
an d early warnings remains a major challenge.
18.
The universal access target of the EW4All programme aims to ensure that it will
ultimately benefit 100 per cent of the target countries’ population, as everyone can use climate
information for dynamic decision-making, planning, and reducing the risks associated with
climate variability and change over a range of decision timelines. The proposal is designed to
ali gn with this target.
19.
The benefits and impact potential of this intervention is therefore assessed to be very
significant.
Scale: High
3. 2 Paradigm shift potential
20.
The updated Strategic Plan for the GCF 2024–2027 (USP 2) notes that GCF can
substantially contribute to the EW4All Initiative. This is evidenced by strong support from the
Board with an MHEWS target of supporting up to 60 countries. Realizing this target requires
aligning the GCF pipeline to the EW4All priorities with the aims of prioritizing support for the
most vulnerable, optimizing the impact of investments, coordinating various investments
so urces and improving innovation to deliver quality at scale in a timely manner.
21.
GCF has a range of tools and approaches that could be harnessed to deliver the USP 2
and EW4All targets. These include the projects and programmatic approaches and ongoing
work under the simplified approval process through the Climate Risk and Early Warning
Systems Initiative (CREWS)–simplified approval process scaling up framework and fast-
tracking approaches. The proposal has been co-designed by the EW4All pillar leads (World
Meteorological Organization, UNDRR, International Telecommunication Union and
International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, International

Telecommunication Union) and a broad range of public- and private-sector partners. The
ambitious targets required a coordinated approach by all the pillar leads and partners. A
meeting with all pillars leads, SOFF and CREWS was held in Bangkok, 3–5 May 2023 to develop
a conceptual framework (EW4All Global support programme) for the timely delivery of the
EW 4All targets.

24.
The EW4All Facility will be established that supports the preparation of four to five
projects (including multi-country programmes) for GCF Board approval annually. This should
result in systematic and technically sound, predictable project maturation, increased quality of
projects, local partner-owned and implemented, co-invested by donors. Other projects will be
developed following this initial project. The approach has the potential to meet the USP 2 target
of covering 60 countries by 2027. This proposal is the first attempt to operationalize the EW4All
co nceptual framework at scale through a programmatic approach.
25.
The project demonstrates a high paradigm-shift potential in that it seeks to deliver a
shift of disaster risk management processes in the target countries from reactive approaches
that are focused on response to impacts of climate hazards and disasters, towards an approach
that also prioritizes preparedness and anticipatory action, where vulnerable communities and
decision makers in climate-sensitive sectors have easy access to widely available reliable
sci ence-based climate information and early warnings.
26.
The project promotes an approach that fosters the development of an integrated and
comprehensive MHEWS value chain, which integrates long-term financing strategies to enable
the sustainability of the operation and maintenance of the MHEWS infrastructure and systems.
The project uses lessons learned from previous work, such as the Afghanistan Community
Resilience Programme, to inform the design of climate information and early warning systems
and processes in a way that has the potential for scaling up and replication across the globe,
pa rticularly in fragile and conflicted affected situations.
27.
The project demonstrates a paradigm-shift potential across all the components of the
project and ensures the strategic focus is maintained over the long term.

28.
The project presents an innovative and strategic approach to promoting and increasing
the participation of the national and local governments, communities and local-level private-
sector actors in the development and implementation of CIEWS.
Scale: High
3. 3 Sustainable development potential
29.
According to UNDRR, advances in early warning systems and preparedness have saved
many lives and significant financial resources. People-centred, MHEWS can effectively minimize
harm by triggering timely and well-prepared actions. These systems are among the most proven
and cost-effective methods for reducing disaster deaths and losses. However, as at 2022, only
half of the world’s countries have such systems, with even lower coverage in developing
countries, where less than half of the least developed countries, and only one-third of the small
isl and developing States are protected.
30.
The project will significantly reduce the exposure of poor and vulnerable communities
to natural hazards and will thereby be instrumental in helping these communities to safeguard
their lives, assets and economic resources from potential damage from such hazards. These
avoided human and economic losses and the resultant development of climate risk-resilient
local and national economies will in the long term yield vast social, economic and environmental
benefits for the vulnerable communities and for the sustainable development aspirations and
go als that the global community seeks to achieve.
31.
The project contributes directly towards efforts to achieve the Sustainable Development
Goals (SDGs), especially SDG 1 (No poverty); SDG2 (Zero hunger); SDG 9 (Industry, innovation
and infrastructure); SDG 11 (Sustainable cities and communities); SDG 13 (Climate action); and
SD G 15 (Life on land).
32.
The project also significantly aligns/contributes to the GCF targeted results for 2024–
20 27 (USP 2), specifically:
(a)
Target 1. Developing countries directly supported to advance nationally determined
contribution/national adaptation plan/long-term strategy implementation (four
developing coun tries);
(b)
Target 3. CIEWS(project areas in the four countries would be protected by robust early
warning system s);
(c)
Target 4. Food(prom ote investm ent in transformative agricultural practices);
(d)
Target 5. Ecosystems(promoteinvestment in ecosystem-based adaptation measures);
(e)
Target 6. Infrastructure (social and community infrastructure made resilient through
investmentinclimate-proofing);
(f)
Target 7. Clean energy (renewable energy s ources to drive the interventions); and
(g)
Target 9. Adaptation and locally-led action(the proposal is an adaptation proposal).
33.
The economic, social and environmental co-benefits that the project offers would be
achieved and sustained through capacity-strengthening that the project will provide to the
participating countries to enhance their ability to develop, operate, maintain and sustainably
manage climate information and early warning systems and dissemination channels. This will
contribute directly to building awareness of climate hazards, and capacity to mitigate the risks
tha t they pose and adequately respond to their impacts.
34.
The sustainable development potential of this investment is therefore estimated to be
high.

=== PAGE 157 ===
GCF/B.41/02/Add.06
Page 157
Scale: High
3. 4 Needs of the recipient
35.
The project targets some of the world’s most vulnerable countries, where water, food
and livelihood insecurity conditions arise from the various hazards posed by extreme climate
va riability, which are compounded by the political fragility in some of the target countries.
36.
The target communities are facing severe challenges from climate change threatening
their current livelihood strategies, and yet, they lack reliable access to usable climate
information and early warning systems to support their need, and effort to secure their
livelihoods and natural capital from the impacts of the climate hazards that afflict their
localities. The current local livelihood, food, water and health systems in the participating
countries are not able to withstand the pressure from climate hazards. Through the
development of MHEWS, the proposed interventions will help communities to use advance
information to develop strategies for safeguarding and transforming their livelihood options,
local food, water and health systems as well as ecosystems to become resilient to climate
ha zards, thereby building the resilience and adaptive capacity of the vulnerable communities.
37.
The target countries are heavily indebted and do not have sufficient resources to invest
in the actions to safeguard their populations from climate-induced hazards and the associated
livelihoods, water and food insecurity. The countries and beneficiaries are currently struggling
to access usable climate information and early warnings that they need to prepare and secure
their well-being, livelihood and food, water and health systems. Without access to climate
information and early warning, the local communities and economies in the target countries will
not be able to prepare and develop, in a timely fashion, the relevant the safeguards and safety
nets that they need. The project will fill an important gap through working with key global,
national and local institutions in both the public and private sectors to foster long-term
solutions for enhanced access and use of climate information and early warnings for building
resilient infrastructure and health, water, food and livelihood systems.
Scale: High
3. 5 Country ownership
38.
Country ownership is well embedded in the project, which is fully aligned with the
climate change and broader development aspirations, strategies and policies of all seven target
countries. The project will promote the development of capacity among local governmental and
non-governmental actors in the target countries to disseminate and use climate information and
early warnings to identify their own solutions and to prepare for and undertake anticipatory
action. The project also places an important focus on ensuring better synergy with ongoing
reg ional and national strategies and actions being implemented in the target countries.
39.
The project is aligned with the nationally determined contributions, national adaptation
plans, climate change policies and programmes, as well as the GCF country programmes of the
target countries. Furthermore, the project has been developed with the strong participation and
commitment of the governments concerned, as well as the participation and commitment of
other national and local-level stakeholders, involving all levels of stakeholder groups, including
gra ss roots, women and youth.
40.
The AE is the UNDP, which, along with the four early warning pillar leads that are
participating in the project as implementing partners, has a long-standing presence in all the
target countries, and a wealth of experience working with stakeholders and dealing with the
development and environmental challenges in the countries. UNDP offers a unique structure as
well as experience and partnerships that will facilitate meaningful engagement and involvement
of all relevant stakeholders in the target countries in the successful implementation and scaling
up of the programme activities and outputs.

=== PAGE 158 ===
GCF/B.41/02/Add.06
Page 158
41.
The architecture of the project consists of a Project Board and Project Management Unit
at the country level where the country governments, acting through relevant national
institutions, will participate directly in the governance and management of the project and its
activities. This will bolster the integration of local contexts and ownership in the project’s
act ivities and outputs.
42.
The project is built on well-designed stakeholder consultations that were conducted
throughout the project development process, ensuring local knowledge, innovation and
sustainability, and participation is fully embedded in the design of the project.
Scale: Medium to high
3. 6 Efficiency and effectiveness
43.
The overall EW4All action plan proposes an investment of USD 3.1 billion over five
years, which equates to just USD 0.50 per person per year. This funding aims to enhance
disaster risk knowledge and management, improve observation and forecasting, and strengthen
the dissemination and communication of warnings, as well as preparedness and response
capabilities. To achieve these goals, this proposal plans to leverage existing pooled funding
mechanisms like CREWS and SOFF as well as global multilateral funds, including development
ba nks.
44.
This programme will directly support poor and vulnerable communities in the
participating countries to strengthen their ability to secure, diversify and transform their own
adaptive capacity and livelihood systems. It will target 26.84 million direct beneficiaries and
51.26 million indirect beneficiaries and will drive innovation and transformation by providing
access to climate information and early warning for communities and businesses to use in
undertaking anticipatory action to protect themselves from potential climate hazards and
dis asters.
45.
The funding amount is well justified to provide the support needed to safeguard lives,
livelihoods and local health, water and food systems and to provide innovative approaches and
lessons for transforming climate governance in the participating countries and around the globe
in general. The project is fostering an enabling environment for private- and public-sector
investments in climate information and early warning systems. It aims to achieve this through
the structuring and deployment of a global support mechanism for EW4All and of a value-chain
approach to addressing the barriers to EW4All; and through developing robust and sustainable
CIEWS and thereby foster an innovative approach to helping countries to access long-term
fin ancial innovation for EWS and maintain their sustainability.
46.
The project also has an innovative exit strategy that will enable scaling up its approach
across the globe and will build access and partnership between global actors and governments,
communities and businesses to tackle local climate-change challenges with innovative and
locally appropriate and developed solutions based on reliable and science-based climate
information.
IV. Assessment of consistency with GCF safeguards and policies
4. 1 Environmental and social safeguards
47.
The programme is categorized as C for environmental and social impacts and risks in
accordance with the GCF Revised Environmental and Social Policy and the accreditation level of
the AE. While most of the activities are focused on enhancing risk knowledge, upgrading
information and forecasting systems, capacity-building, technical assistance, disaster
preparedness and planning and information dissemination in seven countries, small

=== PAGE 159 ===
GCF/B.41/02/Add.06
Page 159
infrastructure works will be undertaken under output 2. Output 2 will involve the procurement
of goods and equipment to upgrade and/or strengthen forecasting services in the seven selected
countries, which includes installation or upgrading of hydrometeorological stations, installation
of water storage tanks, installation of toilets and minor improvements to existing access paths.
The upgrading and installation works will have minimal physical footprints. An ESMF has been
prepared to include an assessment of all the associated E&S risks and impacts, proposed
mitigation measures, including through an environment and social code of practice, which
would guide the implementation of minor works. There will be no displacement of people or
their livelihoods as a result of programme interventions. No work will be undertaken on sites of
cultural, historical or environmental importance. New installations will be sited on government
property or public areas free of encumbrances, with existing access so that operation and
maintenance (O&M) tasks will not require the crossing of private lands, biodiversity areas or
other zones that would pose any impact to the environment, workers or communities (including
zones where there are ongoing conflicts). The ESMF will guide safeguard implementation as the
specific activities and locations are not fully known at project preparation stage. The ESMF will
be the basis for the screening of subprojects during implementation, and includes exclusion
criteria where activities considere d as category A or B will not be considered for programme
financing. Nevertheless, all activities will be required to apply any national regulatory permits
tha t would apply to minor works.
48.
The project is multi-country in nature and will be implemented in countries that have
been classified by the World Bank as fragile and conflict-affected states (i.e. Chad, Ethiopia and
Somalia). Any subproject located in these countries will develop a corresponding conflict
sensitivity analysis informed by consultations to assess institutional needs and capacities so
that interventions will be designed in a way that ensures they will not create or exacerbate
conflicts and ideally will contribute to peace. In such countries, no minor works will take place
in areas where there is ongoing conflict or where works could exacerbate existing tensions.
49.
At the programme level, a global Project Management Unit will be established within
UNDP which will include a Project Manager), Technical Advisor, Monitoring and Evaluation and
Learning Officer, Communications Expert, and a Safeguards, Gender and Inclusivity Expert
(SGIE). The Project Manager will work together with the SGIE to oversee overall compliance
with the ESMF. At the country level, a national Project Management Unit will be established as
well. It will include a national Project Manager who will work with the national SGIE to ensuring
compliance with E&S measures laid out in the ESMF. The national SGIE will provide capacity-
building for central and field staff, contractors, and community members who will be involved
in ESMF and environmental and social code of practice implementation. Periodic monitoring of
ESMF implementation will be undertaken by the national SGIEs with oversight from the global
SG IE.
50.
A global stakeholder engagement plan (SEP) has been developed through extensive
stakeholder consultations at the national and local levels, including some vulnerable groups in
the seven countries from 2023 to 2024. The global SEP provides a framework for the overall
programme, outlining the stakeholders, methodologies, grievance redress mechanism (GRM),
and timelines for engagement during the programme duration. Country-specific SEPs have been
prepared to more accurately capture country and local contexts and will be updated as needed
during programme implementation once the specific locations are known. During project design
and implementation, special considerations for vulnerable groups will be taken into account.
The programme will ensure that they are meaningfully consulted and that their needs and
constraints are considered. The global Project Manager, global SGIE, national Project Manager,
and national SGIE will be working together to implement the SEPs. A programme-level GRM and
a country-level GRM will be established and communicated through stakeholder engagement
sessions. The GRMs will facilitate complaints related to the E&S performance of the programme.
The UNDP Accountability Mechanism and GCF Independent Redress Mechanism will also be

Indigenous Peoples
are potentially present in most of the countries covered by the funding proposal. The

applied to any activity implemented by the national-level projects involving Indigenous Peoples.

on, abuse and harassment (SEAH) safeguarding.
52.
SEAH risks are
included in the social and environmental screening report and have been assessed as low risk.
Potential SEAH issues may arise from interaction of project workers with communities during

activities to address SEAH risks that include training on SEAH and the code of conduct as part of
capacity building for various programme actors, such as local contractors; timelines;
responsibilities for implementation and monitoring. The grievance redress mechanism (GRM) is
described in the ESMF and includes information disclosure and stakeholder engagement.

centred, and gender-responsive, including facilitating confidential reporting and ensuring safe
and ethical documentation of incidents, and protocols for reporting incidents and the follow-up
actions that will be taken. The Fund’s independent redress mechanism will also be available to
stakeholders.
4. 2 Gender policy
53.
The AE has provided a gender analysis and action plan and therefore complies with the
GCF Gender Policy. The gender assessment identifies barriers to equitable participation and
benefit-sharing in MHEWS. Women face restricted access to early warning information and
communication technologies, particularly in rural and marginalized areas, due to lower digital
literacy, socioeconomic disadvantages, and cultural norms. Gender roles often limit women’s
involvement in decision-making and disaster preparedness, as their primary responsibilities for
unpaid care work reduce opportunities for active participation. Additionally, systemic issues
such as the underrepresentation of women in leadership positions, lack of gender-disaggregated
data, and minimal integration of gender-sensitive policies in disaster risk management
exacerbate these disparities. Vulnerable groups, including women with disabilities, Indigenous
women, and those in rural areas, face compounded challenges in accessing resources, safe
evacuation facilities, and targeted interventions during emergencies.

=== PAGE 161 ===
GCF/B.41/02/Add.06
Page 161
54.
The gender action plan proposes a comprehensive set of actions to address these
challenges by mainstreaming gender considerations across MHEWS. The gender action plan
defines activities, indicators, and targets for women’s participation and benefit with
corresponding timelines, budget and gender expertise. Key actions include increasing women’s
representation in decision-making and leadership roles, enhancing gender-responsive data
collection and analysis, and promoting community-based training programmes tailored to
women’s needs. It intends to develop accessible, multichannel early warning dissemination
systems, prioritizing formats that reach women and marginalized groups effectively. The plan
emphasizes capacity-building initiatives to empower women as agents of change in disaster
preparedness and response. Furthermore, it underscores the need for gender-sensitive
infrastructure in evacuation sites, integrating separate facilities and addressing safety concerns.
Institutional capacity will be strengthened to ensure gender equity in disaster risk governance,
with mechanisms to monitor progress through gender-focused indicators. Each country will
have its own GAP that its gender staff will report on to the global PMU which will in turn
consolidate inputs for annual reporting to the Fund.

4. 5 Results monitoring and reporting
69.
The funding proposal contains a programme-level theory of change demonstrating three
outcomes that will focus on distinct dimensions of the global EW4All initiative. The
programme's overall goal is to contribute to enhanced avoidance of the adverse effects of
climate change and adaptation of lives, livelihoods, and assets to climate hazards through
effective early warning systems. While the implementation of EWS in each country needs to
consider the respective country’s context and specificities, the AE is planning to submit
ind ividual theories of change for each country investment.
70.
The adaptation impact of the programme stems from increasing resilience to climate-
change hazards in the population of the seven targeted countries. The approach to estimating
direct and indirect beneficiaries of these country-level investments is provided under the
impact potential investment criteria. The AE will submit further information on applying this
approach in the country context and outputs within the individual country-level document. The
impact estimates will be reviewed and finalized once this information is available, and hence,
the Secretariat expects a revision in the present beneficiary figures.
71.
The programme’s logical framework is predominantly in line with the requirements of
the Integrated Results Management Framework, with a few identified areas for improvement.
The potential for a paradigm shift and the selection of enabling environment indicators are
appropriately addressed. Given the programme’s focus on adaptation, the logical framework has
applied the core 2 indicator and related supplementary indicators. While country and sex-
disaggregated targets have been provided for the indicators, targets for supplementary
indicators are only partially consistent with the indicator definitions. The AE has proposed
conducting baseline assessments in the first year of project implementation to inform the
targets and baseline for the indicators. The programme-specific logical framework is high-level
and requires the inclusion of indicators specifically on reporting results from output 3 on the
implementation of activities related to the four pillars of EW4All in the targeted countries. To
ensure the required granularity and robustness for measuring GCF and programme-specific
indicators, the AE will be submitting country-level logical frameworks that will be mapped to
pr ogramme logical frameworks before project approval by the Board.
72.
The programme proposal contains an M&E plan, laying out the role and responsibilities
of AE for various M&E activities and reporting to GCF as per various policy requirements. The
programme will conduct an interim and final independent evaluation as per the GCF Evaluation
Policy.
4. 6 Legal assessment
73.
The Accreditation Master Agreement was signed with the Accredited Entity on 5 August
2016, and became effective on 23 November 2016, which was amended and restated pursuant

=== PAGE 164 ===
GCF/B.41/02/Add.06
Page 164
to a first amendment and restatement agreement dated 16 March 2023, and which became
eff ective on 3 May 2023 (the “AMA”).
74.
The Accredited Entity has provided a legal opinion/certificate confirming that it has
ob tained all internal approvals and it has the capacity and authority to implement the project.
75.
The proposed multi-country Programme will be implemented in Antigua and Barbuda,
Chad, Cambodia, Ecuador, Ethiopia, Fiji, and Somalia. The GCF has signed bilateral agreements
on privileges and immunities with one of these seven host countries, namely Antigua and
Barbuda. In the remaining six countries, namely Chad, Cambodia, Ecuador, Ethiopia, Fiji, and
Somalia, GCF is not provided with privileges and immunities. This means that, amongst other
things, GCF is not protected against litigation or expropriation in these countries, which risks
need to be further assessed. Moreover, the ability of GCF to undertake redress activities and/or
investigations in such countries may be hindered due to the absence of privileges and
im munities for relevant GCF personnel.
76.
Therefore, it is recommended that the Board considers whether disbursements of GCF
proceeds should only be made after the GCF has obtained satisfactory protection against
litigation and expropriation in the countries, or has been provided with appropriate privileges
an d immunities for GCF and its personnel.
77.
To address the matters raised in this section, it is recommended that any approval by
the Board is made subject to the following conditions:
(a)
Signature of the funded activity agreement in a form and substance satisfactory to the
GCF Secretariat within 180 days from the date of Board approval; and
(b)
Completion of the legal due diligence to the satisfaction of the GCF Secretariat.

I. Assessment of the independent Technical Advisory Panel
1.1 Overview
1.
This is the first submission of the proposal for the Multi-country Project Advancing
Early Wa 1 rnings for All (EW4All) programme under the GCF standard proposal approval Early
pWraorcneisnsg.s Tfohre A fulln Edxiencgu ptirvoep Aocstaiol nis P plaarnt of a global initiative to advan ce EW4All by 2027, as
announced by the United Nations Secretary General in March 2022and articulated in the
2
. Presented as an umbrella programme, the funding
proposal includes a global component as well as prioritized support to seven participating
countries across four geographies: Antigua and Barbuda, Cambodia, Chad, Ecuador, Ethiopia,
Fiji, and Somalia.
2.
The objective of the programme is to accelerate the design and implementation of
EW4All through coordinated global support involving all the key actors across the early
warnings value chain. Additionally, the project will directly support the financial and technical
needs of seven participating countries to enhance the production of actionable multi-hazard
early warning systems (MHEWS) and impact-based forecasts. This information will be
disseminated to effectively reach the most vulnerable communities in each of the seven
countries and to trigger preparedness, early and anticipatory actions. To illustrate how this will
work in practice, one country funding proposal for Ecuador has been submitted alongside this
funding proposal. The accredited entity has clarified to the independent Technical Advisory
Panel (iTAP) that the remaining six country proposals are expected to become available by the
end of January 2025.
3.
The funding proposal responds to several challenges related to MHEWS: (i) insufficient
financial resources and limited capacities to access financing at country and community levels;
(ii)inadequate policies and strategies for inter-agency coordination, data-sharing and
governance for preparedness and response; (iii) limited technical, scientific and institutional
capacities for a comprehensive MHEWS; (iv) ineffective dissemination of early warning
information to climate-vulnerable communities; (v) insufficient national- and local-level
disaster preparedness and anticipatory action planning; and (vi) limited opportunities for
women and other marginalized groups to engage with and benefit from early warning systems.

goals, through context-specific activities that address the four key pillars of MHEWS
namely: (i) disaster risk knowledge and management; (ii) detection, observations,

4

The proposal outlines how the impacts of climate and climate-related hazards can wreak

8

global resources and collaboration, and by enhancing the enabling environment, output 1 could
help to accelerate efforts towards universal coverage of early warning systems by 2027. By
helping to improve the effective ness and reach of end-to-end MHEWS in seven participating
